title: Chicago Bears week 9 power rankings roundup: Among the best
summary: With an emphatic win Monday night against the Seattle Seahawks, the Chicago Bears have launched into the Super Bowl contender conversation. This team is for real. They have a great quarterback and coach. Their defense has been elevated with the addition of Jeffery Simmons. The team has fought the regression narrative. They’ve fought the “yeah […]
full_text: SEATTLE, WASHINGTON - NOVEMBER 02: Caleb Williams #18 of the Chicago Bears and Sam Darnold #14 of the Seattle Seahawks embrace after the game at Lumen Field on November 02, 2026 in Seattle, Washington. (Photo by Steph Chambers/Getty Images) | Getty Images With an emphatic win Monday night against the Seattle Seahawks, the Chicago Bears have launched into the Super Bowl contender conversation. This team is for real. They have a great quarterback and coach. Their defense has been elevated with the addition of Jeffery Simmons. The team has fought the regression narrative. They’ve fought the “yeah but…” caveats that came with their wins and the “but what about…” that came with the losses. Now they have to work against the hype and the target on their back. How high are they in this week’s rankings? WCG – Aaron Leming 7. Chicago Bears (6-2) Deadline Status (and needs): Buyers Defense was a need going into the offseason, and it remained a need heading into the season. Despite playing better than expected, it made sense that Chicago was still an impact piece (or two) away from being considered a legitimate Super Bowl contender. Even after adding Jeffery Simmons, additional defensive line help or a starting-caliber cornerback should still be a priority. Another sneaky need: tight end depth, following the season-ending injury to Cole Kmet. The Athletic – Chad Graff and Josh Kendall 4. Chicago Bears (6-2) Last week: 5 Monday: Beat Seahawks 34-17 Reality check: The bull’s-eye is on them now The addition of Jeffery Simmons paid immediate dividends for the Bears defense. The new defensive tackle, acquired from Tennessee for two first-round picks, had six tackles and a sack on Monday night. Caleb Williams became the first quarterback this season to throw for more than 200 yards against the Seahawks, and the offense put up the most overall yards (363) of anyone this season against Seattle. The Bears are officially contenders. Yahoo Sports – Frank Schwab 4. Chicago Bears (6-2, LW: 5) Biggest need: Still defense, though the big move was made The Bears’ front office understood the assignment. Chicago traded two first-round draft picks to Tennessee for defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons. If there’s a bigger move at the deadline from any team, it’ll be a surprise. Simmons is exactly what the Bears’ defense needed as a disruptor on the line, and he notched a sack in his Chicago debut on Monday night against Seattle. Chicago clearly feels like it’s a contender now and was willing to sacrifice some high future draft picks for a shot at making a deep playoff run. That doesn’t mean the Bears should be done on defense, though any other move wouldn’t be major. A mid-round draft pick for pass rushing help would continue to improve the defensive front. A reunion with Khalil Mack would make a ton of sense. But make no mistake: The Bears already made their all-in move. “Super Bowl teams all have what we call a ‘red-level’ interior defensive lineman,” Bears general manager Ryan Poles said of the Simmons trade, via the Chicago Sun-Times. “You need one. “We’ve been searching, but sometimes the draft doesn’t provide that to you. Free agency doesn’t really [provide them]; it’s very hard for guys to get out of the building when they have all of those things that we’re talking about. [Simmons] was an opportunity that we had to jump on.” NFL.com – Nick Shook 3. Chicago Bears (6) Those who were familiar with Jeffery Simmons’ game knew he’d make an immediate difference for a Chicago front that needed an elite disruptor. The rest of the football world quickly learned about him in Monday night’s 34-17 road win over the defending champion Seahawks. Simmons elevated the Bears’ front by multiple levels, pressuring Sam Darnold and eventually attracting double teams that freed Montez Sweat for more one-on-one rushes in what doubled as a preview of the conundrum every team will have to navigate going forward. Chicago isn’t just an offensive machine anymore; this is a team with a defense that just might be able to complement Caleb Williams and Co. CBS Sports – Pete Prisco 4. Chicago Bears (8) They went into Seattle and beat up the Seahawks. The Jeffrey Simmons trade paid off right away with a dominant first game. USAToday – Nate Davis 2. Chicago Bears (2): QB Caleb Williams and newly acquired DT Jeffery Simmons certainly sowed fresh hope in front of a national audience on Monday night that Chicago might get its first NFL title in four decades after Da new-look Bears knocked off the reigning Super Bowl champion Seahawks. In Seattle. In prime time. Quite a statement win. ESPN NFL Nation – Courtney Cronin Week 8 result: Beat the Seahawks 34-17 Week 8 ranking: 7 Best in-season trade acquisition ever: DE Montez Sweat in 2023 Three seasons before the Bears sent three draft picks, including two first-rounders, to Tennessee to acquire All-Pro defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons, GM Ryan Poles got aggressive in 2023 to land Sweat. Chicago sent a 2024 second-rounder to Washington in exchange for Sweat, who led both the Commanders (6.5) and Bears (6.0) in sacks in 2023, making him the first player in NFL history to lead two different teams in sacks in the same season. Sweat recorded his first double-digit-sack season and reached similar production in 2025, when he led Chicago with 10 sacks. Coach Ben Johnson called that season the best of Sweat’s career. — Courtney Cronin Pro Football Talk – Mike Florio Bears (No. 8; 6-2): The Bears are NOT who we thought they were — they’re serious contenders to win the whole thing. What do you think of this week’s rankings? Let us know in the comments.

title: Bears vs. Seahawks Game Balls: The Nation Takes Notice
summary: The Chicago Bears can win a Super Bowl. This year. The team left no doubt about that fact on Monday night at Seattle’s Lumen Field. The Bears thoroughly dominated the defending Super Bowl champions, in their own house, from bell to bell. This happening just one week after defeating last year’s Super Bowl runner-up New […]
full_text: SEATTLE, WASHINGTON - NOVEMBER 02: Jeffery Simmons #99 of the Chicago Bears celebrates a win against the Seattle Seahawks at Lumen Field on November 02, 2026 in Seattle, Washington. (Photo by Steph Chambers/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Chicago Bears can win a Super Bowl. This year. The team left no doubt about that fact on Monday night at Seattle’s Lumen Field. The Bears thoroughly dominated the defending Super Bowl champions, in their own house, from bell to bell. This happening just one week after defeating last year’s Super Bowl runner-up New Englad Patriots. Also one week ago, the Seahawks defense kept Patrick Mahomes and the Kansas City Chiefs out of the end zone entirely. This week, the Bears went on a methodical, 17-play drive to score a touchdown on their first possession of the game against that same defense. In defeating the Seahawks, as well as the Patriots last week, the Bears became the first team in NFL history to defeat both of the previous year’s Super Bowl teams in back-to-back weeks. That’s a heck of a stat. Now, let’s get to the game balls. Offense Game Ball: QB Caleb Williams Despite most of the NFL world now acknowledging the fact that Williams is a top tier quarterback, it feels like Monday night’s game took that one step further. As I browse social media and the usual talking heads throughout the sports world, I’m starting to see a general consensus now that not only is #18 top-tier, he is elite. As in, a top five quarterback in the league. A Chicago Bears quarterback. Elite. We’ve been waiting a long time for this, and we absolutely deserve it. Williams did something to the Seahawks that no other QB has done this year – throw for 200 yards. And the Seahawks have played some pretty accomplished QBs and big names this year: Mahomes, Brock Purdy, Drake Maye, Justin Herbert, and Bo Nix to name a few. None of them accomplished this feat. It took Williams barely half the game, surpassing 200 yards less than five minutes into the third quarter. And he did so on one of the most spectacular plays of the game. Caleb Williams became the first player with 200+ passing yards against the Seahawks this season on this play pic.twitter.com/eBATND2yrE — Underdog NFL (@UnderdogNFL) November 3, 2026 The Bears’ QB finished the night 24/34, 247 yards passing, one touchdown, zero interceptions, and a passer rating of 101.0. You’ve got to think the Williams has firmly entered the MVP discussion and will remain there for the rest of the season. Defense Game Ball: DT Jeffery Simmons Did the Bears give up too much for Simmons? If I’m the Titans, I’m thinking they didn’t give up enough. It can’t be overstated how much of a difference Big Jeff made for the Bears defense from the very first play he was on the field. Those bright orange sleeves might as well have been a flashing warning sign to the rest of the league for the remainder of this season. Not only do the Bears have an elite offense; they now have a defense that opposing teams will (and should) fear. That’s a combination that wins championships. Trade for Jeffery Simmons… IMMEDIATELY gets a sack. CHIvsSEA on ESPN Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/jVPBx4MzcS — NFL (@NFL) November 3, 2026 In commanding so much attention from the offensive line, Simmons helped other Bears defenders in the front four look like All Pro candidates. Montez Sweat was a beast. Austin Booker continued to look the part of up and coming young star. Hell, James Lynch even had an interception, catching a ball that Booker tipped late in the game. Simmons was on the field for 48 plays, and the Seahawks were held to just 3.0 yards per play (including three sacks and an interception) during those snaps. There were eight plays that Simmons was not on the field, and Seattle averaged 13.3 yards per play during those snaps. That kind of says it all. Simmons finished the night with six tackles, one sack, two tackles for loss, one pass defended, and one QB hit. And this is just the beginning. Simmons had only been with the team for a little bit over 72 hours on Monday night. Expect this train to keep rolling ahead at full speed in the week’s ahead. It hasn’t been this exciting to be a Bears fan in a very long time. Relish it. Who would have received your game balls? Let us know in the comments section below. The best team in the NFL resides in Chicago.
author: Ryan Droste

title: Jeffery Simmons’ biggest contribution to Bears might be reactivating Montez Sweat
summary: The play seemed innocuous enough at the time—just another errant throw by Seattle Seahawks quarterback Sam Darnold against a rapacious Chicago Bears front to force a punt late in the game. But I pointed something out to my brother on the text thread that I thought was the cause: He’d seen, as he had for […]
full_text: Nov 2, 2026; Seattle, Washington, USA; Chicago Bears defensive line Montez Sweat (98) reacts after a sack against the Seattle Seahawks during the third quarter at Lumen Field. Mandatory Credit: Joe Nicholson-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The play seemed innocuous enough at the time—just another errant throw by Seattle Seahawks quarterback Sam Darnold against a rapacious Chicago Bears front to force a punt late in the game. But I pointed something out to my brother on the text thread that I thought was the cause: He’d seen, as he had for much of the night, newly acquired defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons and defensive end Montez Sweat lined up on the same side of the formation, and he was thinking more about them than he was about delivering an accurate football. They didn’t get home, but they pushed the pocket enough around him and into his throwing window that he lost his composure and threw a bad ball. There was a lot of that for Darnold and the Seahawks offense, which was the first to go against this new-look Bears defensive unit with Simmons at the center. To be fair to Darnold, that fear wasn’t entirely unfounded. A Bears defense that has struggled for much of the last two years to get pressure with just four rushers has apparently solved that issue in one masterstroke by trading for Simmons, one of the NFL’s best interior pass-rushers. Defensive coordinator Dennis Allen, who had been making ends meet without an elite front four by spamming blitzes, let the big dogs eat on Monday Night Football, and they left no crumbs. But as hellacious as Simmons (two pressures, a sack, and an 86.9 pass rush grade) was in the Bears’ 34-17 beatdown of the Seahawks—arguably the best defensive debut we’ve seen since Khalil Mack’s in 2018—the effect he had on Sweat, his old college teammate at Mississippi State, might’ve been the biggest takeaway from last night. Sweat, who was just coming off of a two-game suspension for violating the NFL’s PED policy, had his best game of the season with four pressures and a sack. (He would’ve had even more if it hadn’t been for a few untimely penalties in the secondary.) Maybe it was the layoff. Maybe it was the addition of his old friend Simmons, with whom he already seems to have insane chemistry. Maybe it was primetime football. Maybe it was all of the above. Whatever the reason, Sweat looked as good as he ever has in a Bears uniform. The Bears traded for and signed Sweat to a four-year, $98 million contract extension back in 2023 for games like this. But too often, he hasn’t had the running mates, especially on the interior, to maximize his skills, which are less those of a truly elite pass-rusher and more of a strong running mate to an alpha dog. Now, Chicago went and got him one, and the difference, even in a small sample size, is enormous. This was one game, of course, and the Bears will have some tough tests up ahead—the Detroit Lions, who swept the Bears last year, the AFC South-leading Jacksonville Jaguars, and AFC-leading Buffalo Bills, to name a few. (Plus, they need to get revenge on the Packers for that drubbing a couple weeks back without Caleb Williams.) But if the Bears are going to get this version of Sweat alongside Simmons, not to mention what other ways general manager Ryan Poles might improve the defense, Chicago might just be the scariest team in the NFL. The best team in the NFL resides in Chicago.
author: Khari Thompson

title: The Best Team in the NFL is the Chicago Bears
summary: The Chicago Bears are dominating the NFL, and the rest of the league is finally starting to notice. Maybe it’s because so many people hate Caleb Williams and they won’t believe it. Maybe it’s because the Bears have been so bad for so long, it’s hard to believe this is actually them. Or maybe it’s […]
full_text: SEATTLE, WASHINGTON - NOVEMBER 02: Caleb Williams #18 of the Chicago Bears celebrates a win against the Seattle Seahawks after the game at Lumen Field on November 02, 2026 in Seattle, Washington. (Photo by Steph Chambers/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Chicago Bears are dominating the NFL, and the rest of the league is finally starting to notice. Maybe it’s because so many people hate Caleb Williams and they won’t believe it. Maybe it’s because the Bears have been so bad for so long, it’s hard to believe this is actually them. Or maybe it’s that Caleb Williams was hurt and the Bears went 2-2 in the 4 games he missed all or part of the game. Whatever the reason, the way the Bears have played the last three games leaves you with only one logical conclusion: The Chicago Bears are the best team in the NFL. These stats speak for themselves: Since Caleb Williams has returned from injury, the Chicago Bears have led for 158:33 of 180 minutes. They have only been tied at 0-0. They have never trailed. — Bill Zimmerman (@BillTZimmerman) November 3, 2026 The Bears are dominating right now. And they aren’t dominating the Tennessee Titans and the Arizona Cardinals. In the last two weeks, the Bears did this against the two teams that met in the Super Bowl just nine months ago. The way this team is playing, and with the addition of Jeffery Simmons, something has happened with my expectations that I haven’t had since I was a child. Never in my adult life have I truly believed the Bears can win the Super Bowl. Maybe that makes me overly critical. Maybe that just makes me a realist, but let me try to explain. To me, there are two types of good teams: playoff contenders and Super Bowl contenders. The Bears have been playoff contenders on more than one occasion. In 2018, you knew they were headed for the playoffs. During the Lovie years, you knew the Bears were good enough to play additional football in January. But did you ever truly believe they were going to win a Super Bowl? Did you truly believe it? Or did you just hope they could? In 2006, I never truly believed they could beat the Colts. How was Rex Grossman going to beat Peyton Manning? In 2018, if the Bears did, in fact, take down Sean McVay again and reach the Super Bowl? Did we really think Matt Nagy and Mitch Trubisky could outduel Bill Belichick and Tom Brady? You could hope that things would align just perfectly and somehow, someway, the Bears could pull out a miracle win and bring home a title, but did you truly believe they were a Super Bowl contender? The last time I felt this way was in 1987. The Bears still had Jim McMahon. Walter Payton was still on the roster. The ‘85 defense was still largely intact. This was the last time I felt this way. I was 10. Did I actually know what I was watching? No, of course not. I was a hopeful child who believed my team could win. Why not? They won just two years before; why couldn’t they do it again? I didn’t understand that Payton was on his last legs. I didn’t understand that McMahon had no chance of staying healthy. I didn’t understand how much Wilber Marshall would be missed and that other key pieces on the defense were aging. I didn’t understand the context. Now I do. I’ve never had this belief and this level of confidence in this team in my adult life. The Bears have the coach. They have the quarterback. They have the offensive line. They have the weapons. They have the defense. The Bears have everything they need to win it all. The team isn’t perfect. If they can land Khalil Mack and make this defensive line even stronger, they should. If they can land a CB and beef up their secondary, it’s a must. Spend what you have to do to make this happen. Draft picks are for teams that aren’t drafting with the last spot in each round, and that’s where the Bears are headed if they keep this up. This Chicago Bears team can win the Super Bowl. That should be the expectation. If the Bears aren’t playing a game in Los Angeles on February 14th, I’m going to be disappointed. That’s an awesome feeling to have on November 3rd. Is there a team you are afraid of in the NFL? The only team that should give you any concern in the NFC is the SF 49ers. In the AFC, it’s the Buffalo Bills. Are you afraid of the Kansas City Chiefs? I’m not. Right now, the Bears have a more talented roster. They have the better coach. They have the better quarterback (Yes, I know what I said). This offense is the best in the NFL. When it’s rolling, no defense in the league can stop it. Ask the Seahawks; they stop everyone and still gave up 34 points. This defense, with Jeffery Simmons, is a whole new ballgame. As we talked about last week, Simmons is so good, he makes everyone around him better. We saw that already in his first game. Montez Sweat, Austin Booker, Devin Bush- they all looked fantastic. The Chicago Bears have arrived. There’s no team in the league better than this one. You can have concerns about the secondary; you can have concerns about their depth; you can have concerns. You should have concerns. No team in the league is perfect. But despite any of those concerns, one thing is clear: The best team in the NFL resides in Chicago.
author: Bill Zimmerman

title: Bengals Film Room: Dexter Lawrence shines in a forgettable day for the defense
summary: The Cincinnati Bengals had to force overtime in order to defeat the Tennessee Titans this past week. There were plenty of bad performances on both sides of the ball, including the Titans scoring 36 points on the day. That shouldn’t take away from just how dominant Dexter Lawrence was again. Lawrence finished with 5 run […]
full_text: The Cincinnati Bengals had to force overtime in order to defeat the Tennessee Titans this past week. There were plenty of bad performances on both sides of the ball, including the Titans scoring 36 points on the day. That shouldn’t take away from just how dominant Dexter Lawrence was again. Lawrence finished with 5 run stops on the day, the most on the team. He was a force against the run all game long. One specific play in the first half, he was able to bring the ball carrier down by just using one arm. As with most plays, he certainly had an argument for a holding call here, but it didn’t even matter ultimately. I’ll just go ahead and make the play with one arm. You are a beast Dexter Lawrence. pic.twitter.com/076d8C1wrb — Bengals & Brews (@BengalsBrews) November 2, 2026 Don’t let the defense giving up 36 points take away from how good Dexter Lawrence was again yesterday pic.twitter.com/zXXOU2qhrs — Bengals & Brews (@BengalsBrews) November 2, 2026 Dexter Lawrence had 7 tackles yesterday, most of them were at or behind the line of scrimmage pic.twitter.com/17oQBEJv9q — Bengals & Brews (@BengalsBrews) November 2, 2026 Dexter was credited with just 2 pressures on the day, which was his lowest mark of the season. However, one of those pressures led to the sack that ultimately forced overtime. If he doesn’t make that play, the Titans were getting close to field goal range for their kicker. Lawrence consistently faced double teams, as he does on a weekly basis. When they try to block him with one guy, it is almost guaranteed to end up with the lineman being pushed back into their own quarterback. My goodness Dexy pic.twitter.com/2ewv8g9s0s — Bengals & Brews (@BengalsBrews) November 2, 2026 Dexter Lawrence for Defensive Player of the Year pic.twitter.com/jAIX4lgdqD — Bengals & Brews (@BengalsBrews) November 2, 2026 Demetrius Knight Jr. was credited with the safety the Bengals forced during the second half, as he should have been, but Dexter Lawrence was also right there to help make the play if he didn’t. In a game that went to overtime, every play mattered. Dexter Lawrence was certainly in his share of pivotal plays all game long. Demetrius Knight and Dexter Lawrence with the safety pic.twitter.com/AtW2cKOkyh — Bengals & Brews (@BengalsBrews) November 2, 2026 At one point during the game, it seemed like we were even going to see a big man touchdown from Lawrence. After a strip sack by Boye Mafe, Lawrence recovered the fumble. He was tripped up after the recovery, but man, it is always a sight to behold when a big man gets rumbling up the field. Boye Mafe forces the fumble and Dexter Lawrence scoops it up for the turnover. I thought we were about to see an electric touchdown rumble for a moment… pic.twitter.com/vZTUsXTZiv — Bengals & Brews (@BengalsBrews) November 2, 2026 Lawrence finished the game on Sunday with 2 pressures, a sack, the fumble recovery, 5 run stops, and 7 total tackles. He has been well worth the 10th overall draft pick that the Bengals gave up to acquire him via trade this season. I think he deserves to be in the conversation for the Defensive Player of the Year. While you always hate to give up 36 points in general, that is a game the Bengals would have lost the last few years. Dexter Lawrence making critical plays in critical moments was one of the differences compared to previous years.

title: Bengals Film Room: Chase Brown starting to heat up?
summary: The Cincinnati Bengals survived an overtime thriller 43-36 on Sunday against the Tennessee Titans. No one expected the game to be that close, but that is life in the NFL. If you start out slow, you are typically in for a dogfight the rest of the day. That is something that the Bengals continue to […]
full_text: The Cincinnati Bengals survived an overtime thriller 43-36 on Sunday against the Tennessee Titans. No one expected the game to be that close, but that is life in the NFL. If you start out slow, you are typically in for a dogfight the rest of the day. That is something that the Bengals continue to keep doing. There has been a lot of chatter about trading for a running back, specifically Jonathan Taylor. While Taylor is a great back, I have not been of the belief that he necessarily elevates this team dramatically. For a guy that would cost premium draft capital to acquire, he would be joining a Bengals team that will always be pass-first. When you pass the ball a lot, you need a player that is a high-level pass protector and can catch the ball out of the backfield. To me, they already have that guy in Chase Brown. Brown caught eight passes for 46 yards on Sunday. He had a fantastic touchdown reception, but it was called back due to a holding call on Dylan Fairchild. Brown is a reliable target as a pass catcher, and that is something the Bengals will need to continue leaning on as an extension of the running game this season. Dylan Fairchild robbed us from a really nice touchdown reception by Chase Brown. pic.twitter.com/xIEMxMwZFq — Bengals & Brews (@BengalsBrews) November 2, 2026 Chase Brown had 8 receptions versus the Titans pic.twitter.com/5HECR42S1h — Bengals & Brews (@BengalsBrews) November 2, 2026 Good luck as a linebacker trying to cover Chase Brown out of the backfield pic.twitter.com/rnlGIRdi7V — Bengals & Brews (@BengalsBrews) November 2, 2026 The thing that Brown has improved the most on since his time in the NFL is his pass protection. He has turned himself into one of the best pass protectors in the league this season. He has a 78.2 pass-blocking grade and has consistently flashed by picking up blitzes all season. For a team that loves to throw the ball, it’s so critical to have guys like Brown and Perine who take pride in being good blockers for Joe Burrow and the offense. Dylan Fairchild has to play better and Chase Brown was in a tough spot there but I love his physicality as a blocker this year. pic.twitter.com/KIooiULKp9 — Bengals & Brews (@BengalsBrews) November 2, 2026 While it wasn’t a massively productive rushing performance for Brown on Sunday, it felt efficient. Brown had 12 carries for 55 rushing yards. That totals out to 4.6 yards per carry in the game. I thought he has looked more elusive, quick to hit the hole, and has been running his best of the season over the last two weeks. Chase Brown finished the game against the Titans with 55 rushing yards and 46 receiving yards pic.twitter.com/vE8UkWeGRX — Bengals & Brews (@BengalsBrews) November 2, 2026 Chase Brown pic.twitter.com/x0MTHMO5Vj — Bengals & Brews (@BengalsBrews) November 2, 2026 If Chase Brown is the running back #1 for the rest of the season, you have to hope that this is the start of him coming on for the rest of the season. He has been a player who has started a bit slower statistically in the past. Just last season, he did not have a rushing game over 50 yards until Week 7. He still finished the season with over 1,000 rushing yards. If the Bengals want to compete in the playoffs, they’ll need more balance in the running game. Chase Brown starting to heat up would go a long way toward accomplishing that.

title: Browns preparing to start Shedeur Sanders at QB against Saints
summary: Wednesday morning, breaking news emerged on the Cleveland Browns’ quarterback situation as the team placed starter Deshaun Watson in the concussion protocol. The team released the following statement: During the first quarter of Sunday’s game against the Steelers, Deshaun took a helmet-to-helmet hit. The ATC spotted called down to the sideline, and the Unaffiliated Neurotrauma […]
full_text: JACKSONVILLE, FLORIDA - SEPTEMBER 13: (L-R) Shedeur Sanders #2 of the Cleveland Browns and Deshaun Watson #4 take the the field for warmups prior to the game against the Jacksonville Jaguars at EverBank Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Jacksonville, Florida. (Photo by Don Juan Moore/Getty Images) | Getty Images Wednesday morning, breaking news emerged on the Cleveland Browns’ quarterback situation as the team placed starter Deshaun Watson in the concussion protocol. The team released the following statement: During the first quarter of Sunday’s game against the Steelers, Deshaun took a helmet-to-helmet hit. The ATC spotted called down to the sideline, and the Unaffiliated Neurotrauma Consultant (UNC) administered a gameday concussion evaluation. Deshaun was cleared by the UNC and returned on the Browns’ next offensive series. As part of the protocol, the team’s medical staff evaluated him again postgame and Monday morning. Both times he showed no symptoms, passed his evaluations, and was cleared. On Tuesday morning, he reported to the medical staff that he began experiencing concussion symptoms Monday night and was immediately placed in the concussion protocol. This is the hit that resulted in a roughing the passer penalty on Pittsburgh, and led to Watson being pulled from the game for a few plays while Shedeur Sanders replaced him. As mentioned in the Browns’ statement above, Watson returned on the next series and played the remainder of the game in the team’s 27-6 loss. Deshaun Watson took a hit to the helmet and is likely getting checked for a head injury. Doesn’t seem like much so hopefully he can return to the game pic.twitter.com/YdUiiEOElP — Jeff Mueller, PT, DPT (@jmthrivept) November 1, 2026 Obviously, the biggest storyline for the Browns the remainder of the week will be whether he clears the protocol or not. Last week, right tackle Tytus Howard did not practice Wednesday-Friday while in the protocol, but then magically cleared it on Saturday and started. If Watson is out, then Sanders would start his first game of the 2026 NFL season. It’s certainly a unique situation for the Browns’ quarterback situation. At the start of the season, many fans wanted Sanders to start over Watson. However, Watson has led five game-winning drives in the team’s 5-3 start to the season, which has led to more fans at least tolerating watching him. The metrics still show he’s been a below average quarterback, though, so if Sanders indeed starts, he’ll have a chance to shift the narrative again to whether he should remain the team’s starter. It probably couldn’t come at a better time, too, because the Saints’ defense is among the worst in the NFL, and the Browns then return home for a four-game stretch.

title: What did the loss to the Steelers show about this Browns team?
summary: There was a lot on the line in the Cleveland Browns Week 8 matchup against the Pittsburgh Steelers, and it unfortunately did not go Cleveland’s way. It would’ve been a huge opportunity to assert their dominance in the AFC North, but the team instead fell to 5-3. It was never really close, and the final score of 27-6 was disappointing. One of the […]
full_text: There was a lot on the line in the Cleveland Browns Week 8 matchup against the Pittsburgh Steelers, and it unfortunately did not go Cleveland’s way . It would’ve been a huge opportunity to assert their dominance in the AFC North, but the team instead fell to 5-3. It was never really close, and the final score of 27-6 was disappointing. One of the biggest factors in the matchup was the Steelers’ ability to get pressure on Deshaun Watson . Watson struggled to escape Pittsburgh’s pass rush and was sacked eight times on the day. Taking that many sacks makes it incredibly difficult to get anything going offensively. The sacks weren’t entirely Watson’s fault. The offensive line really struggled in this matchup and showed their weaknesses. As many expected, the Browns’ defense struggled to stop the run in this game, allowing 200 rushing yards and three rushing touchdowns. Teams will continue to exploit this part of Cleveland’s defense if they don’t improve. AFC North opponents will always bring a physical style of play, and if the Browns want a chance to win the division, they will need to match that physicality on defense. full_text: The Cleveland Browns have changed their roster up a bit after losing to the Pittsburgh Steelers 27-6 in the rubber match on the road. Their practice squad saw activity on Tuesday. RELATED: BROWNS WAIVE RB AUDRIC ESTIME The Browns waived/released WR Bub Means, P Wes Pahl, OG Vershon Lee, and OT Andrew Coker from their practice squad. In corresponding moves, they signed WR Xavier Guillory, OG Austin Blaske, and OT Xavier Truss to the practice squad. This leaves one roster spot on the practice squad. Estime will not be filling that spot, as he was claimed by Cleveland’s Week 9 opponent, the New Orleans Saints. Guillory (6’-2”, 210 pounds) went undrafted in 2025 out of Arizona State, then signed with the Baltimore Ravens and was placed on their practice squad last year and this season until he was waived on October 13. He runs a 4.58 and has never been on a main roster. Blaske (6’-5”, 310 pounds) played for North Carolina and went undrafted this year. He then signed with the Los Angeles Rams and was a last-day cut, then signed to their practice squad. Truss (6’-7”, 320 pounds) played for Georgia, where he was part of two National Championship teams and went undrafted in 2025. He spent time with the Denver Broncos, New Orleans Saints, the Browns, and the Philadelphia Eagles. He has spent time on practice squads and played in seven NFL games while with the Saints. The Eagles waived him on October 27. Truss played for Cleveland head coach Todd Monken while with Georgia.

summary: It is Week 9 of the 2026 NFL season, and the Cleveland Browns are coming off their first AFC North loss of the season. Overall, the Browns went down by 1.7 spots from week-to-week to have an overall ranking of 16.0. Considering the magnitude of their loss to the Steelers, that’s not all-too-bad of a […]
full_text: (Photo by Justin K. Aller/Getty Images) | Getty Images It is Week 9 of the 2026 NFL season, and the Cleveland Browns are coming off their first AFC North loss of the season. Overall, the Browns went down by 1.7 spots from week-to-week to have an overall ranking of 16.0 . Considering the magnitude of their loss to the Steelers, that’s not all-too-bad of a drop. Plus, Cleveland did split the season series with Pittsburgh, which could play a big factor down the road for divisional tiebreakers. Here is a summary of how the Cleveland Browns are viewed across mainstream media outlets in NFL Power Rankings heading into Week 9 of the 2026 NFL season. CBS Sports – No. 17 (down 3 spots) The early success went bye-bye in the loss to the Steelers. They were dominated on both sides of the ball, which is not a good look. ESPN – No. 16 (no change) Best in-season trade acquisition ever: CB Tyson Campbell in 2025 In October 2025, the Browns traded Greg Newsome II to the Jaguars for Campbell, along with a swap of late-round picks, which gave two underperforming cornerbacks a change of scenery. In a man-based scheme that fits Campbell’s skill set, he has formed one of the NFL’s better cornerback duos with Denzel Ward. Since Campbell made his debut with Cleveland in Week 6 of the 2025 season, he is tied for the 15th-most pass breakups in the NFL (15). NFL.com – No. 15 (down 3 spots) The Browns received the reality check they needed in Pittsburgh on Sunday, getting bullied by the Steelers in all-too-predictable fashion. Deshaun Watson was sacked eight times behind an unpredictable offensive line, Cleveland wasted a monster day from Harold Fannin Jr., and its most important defenders were constantly seen chasing Steelers ball-carriers in vain. At 5-3, the Browns are still in a solid place and should benefit from a serving of humble pie. Pittsburgh smashed the entire dish in their face in Week 8. Sporting News – No. 16 (down 1 spot) The Browns are starting to spring more leaks in their run defense, but the bigger problem up front is their offensive line, which gave up eight sacks on Deshaun Watson and helped to produce only 34 rushing yards in Pittsburgh. Watson is on pace to be sacked an NFL-high 70 times, which would challenge the record set by fellow former Texan David Carr. Yahoo Sports – No. 16 (no change) Biggest need: A reality check Like the Raiders, it’s fun for a team that has had almost no success to start 5-2. An uncompetitive loss to the Steelers on Sunday should put the Browns in a more realistic mindset. They can’t keep living off last-minute wins, and their poor quarterback situation makes their level of success unsustainable. The five wins have already put the Browns in a bad spot to find a quarterback solution in 2027, but that’s a conversation for next offseason. The Browns can still be partial sellers without hurting their playoff hopes for this season. Receiver Jerry Jeudy is tradable and there are plenty of teams that could use him. Offensive tackle Dawand Jones, a backup who could provide depth elsewhere, can also be available. But with a promising young core, the Browns have to be careful to not get ahead of themselves despite a 5-3 record. Bleacher Report – No. 16 (down 4 spots) Days after Jared Verse’s comments about Pittsburgh, the Browns were comprehensively outplayed by their division rivals. Cleveland got outplayed, outcoached, and out-physicaled by the Steelers on Sunday while continuing a couple of alarming trends. The Browns fell behind early, again, and they committed more penalties (nine) than any playoff hopeful should. Considering how uncompetitive the Browns have looked in blowout losses to the Steelers and Jacksonville Jaguars, it’s fair to wonder if they actually are a playoff-caliber team. It would be easier to take Cleveland seriously if it had at least one convincing victory on its resume. USA Today – No. 16 (down 1 spot) DE Jared Verse got taken down Sunday, but he’s still searching for his first sack eight games into his Browns career. title: Browns: Run defense is scary. And not in a good way.
summary: The Cleveland Browns faced some questions on the defensive side of the ball heading into the 2026 season. The biggest concern was how Mike Rutenberg would handle being a defensive coordinator for the first time, especially since he was taking over for the highly regarded Jim Schwartz, who had been in charge of Cleveland’s defense […]
full_text: (Photo by Lauren Leigh Bacho/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Cleveland Browns faced some questions on the defensive side of the ball heading into the 2026 season. The biggest concern was how Mike Rutenberg would handle being a defensive coordinator for the first time, especially since he was taking over for the highly regarded Jim Schwartz, who had been in charge of Cleveland’s defense for the past three seasons. Outside of a Week 1 disaster against Jacksonville, the defense has been one of the consistent bright spots in Cleveland’s 5-3 start. One area that has been an issue, however, is the run defense, which has been up and down through eight games. When the run defense has been good, it’s been pretty good, as the Browns held Carolina, Baltimore, and Pittsburgh (in the first meeting) all under 100 rushing yards. Rico Dowdle breaking tackles on his way to the end zone! CLEvsPIT on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/XuFdbhhI61 — NFL (@NFL) November 1, 2026 But when it has been bad, it has been bad and steadily getting worse. Cleveland allowed an average of 132.2 rushing yards to Jacksonville, Tampa Bay, and the New York Jets. But in the last two games, Tennessee rushed for 141 yards, while the Steelers piled up 200 rushing yards in Sunday’s rematch. What’s worse, after allowing just one rushing touchdown in the first six games, the Browns have allowed a total of six in just the past two games. So what is going on? Is it a lack of effort? Are opposing offenses figuring out the defense? Or is the defense wearing down from having to carry so much of the burden while the offense has struggled? According to head coach Todd Monken, it is a combination of the last two items : “I don’t see it as a mindset. Our guys play their rear ends off – they’re physical. Every game’s different, every week is different. We’ve got to play better on the road. We’ve got to play from in front. That will give us a chance to play the run better and force them to make calls. But there are a number of things we’re going to have to do to change, because we’re going to continue to see those types of runs, those schematic runs against the attack style, and where we go from here. “We weren’t at our best the last couple of weeks in stopping the run. All right, now what? What are we going to do to stop the run? What are we going to do to put ourselves in a position where we’re always trying to make a team one-dimensional, no doubt, but where we can mitigate those long plays.” It is worth pointing out that, despite the hand-wringing over Schwartz leaving the team, the Browns have been good at stopping the run for the better part of the past two decades. According to numbers pulled by Chris Easterling at The Beacon Journal, the Browns are currently ranked No. 24 against the run as they are allowing 126.9 yards per game. Only once since 1999 have the Browns allowed less than 100 yards per game in a season, and that came in the winless campaign of 2017. Even under the great and mighty Schwartz, the Browns struggled, as in his three seasons the defense allowed 105.5 rushing yards per game (2023), 129.7 in 2024, and 116.4 in 2025. It doesn’t seem as if the offense is in any hurry to put a full game together, so the defense is going to have to tighten up against the run if there is any hope of not having the season spiral away. This week will be a good test to see if the coaches can make any meaningful changes as the Browns face a New Orleans team that is No. 28 in rushing yards (86.0), No. 30 in yards per carry (3.52), and just fired its offensive run coordinator. If the Browns can’t keep the Saints under control on the ground, there is no telling how bad things may get the rest of the way.

title: Cowboys roundtable discussion: Arizona loss, Cowboys defense, head coaching
summary: Every week, we gather to discuss the latest news about the Dallas Cowboys and seek our writer’s perspective on each headline. Welcome back to the roundtable. This week we have Jorge Guajardo, Dyllan Rivers, Tom Ryle and Sean Martin.  Who deserves the majority of the blame for the collapse against Arizona? Mike – Brian Schottenheimer, and for me, it’s not even […]
full_text: Mandatory Credit: Jerome Miron-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Every week, we gather to discuss the latest news about the Dallas Cowboys and seek our writer’s perspective on each headline. Welcome back to the roundtable. This week we have Jorge Guajardo , Dyllan Rivers , Tom Ryle and Sean Martin. Who deserves the majority of the blame for the collapse against Arizona? Mike – Brian Schottenheimer, and for me, it’s not even a debate. Christian Parker’s defense deserves criticism for the collapse, but Schottenheimer’s play-calling, poor game management and complete inability to close out games are becoming impossible to defend. What makes it worse is the complete lack of logic behind his rushing decisions. Dallas had been averaging 5.6 yards per carry running left compared with just 2.0 yards running right, yet on Javonte Williams’ 24 carries, only eight went to the left. How do you identify such an obvious advantage and then fail to exploit it? The frustrating part is that Denver had already handed Dallas a blueprint just one week earlier. Sean Payton exploited Arizona’s aggressive defense with a beautifully designed screen pass to the left (yes to the left), allowing RJ Harvey to race 52 yards for a touchdown. That was a perfect example of using creativity to get a running back into space. Schottenheimer had that evidence staring him in the face, yet showed little of the same imagination. For me, Schottenheimer’s biggest weakness is his conservatism when Dallas gets ahead. Instead of attacking opponents and putting games beyond reach, he becomes predictable, cautious and far too concerned with protecting a lead. Jorge – The person really at fault is Jerry Jones. He’s run this franchise somewhat like a despot running a small island nation with precious resources. Subsequently, a festering culture of losing has smoldered for decades, and losses like Sunday are commonplace, frankly. Even so, Schottenheimer is the guy with the headset on that players ultimately call coach, and his tenure in Dallas has been poor. It’s hard being a coach in Dallas given the circumstances with the Joneses, but man, just look at everybody that leaves this place once they land on stable ground. Sunday’s game was just another example of two wrongs not making a right with the dull duo of JJ and Schotty. Sean – Not to sound like a broken record, but we all might end up doing so thanks to not being able to look away from the obvious, but this one is on Schottenheimer to me. We went from Mike McCarthy is the right hire because he wants to work with Dak Prescott, and at the time Kellen Moore, to McCarthy gets to bring in his own OC and that being Schottenheimer, to Schotty is the man in charge and now can’t figure out how to get a first down with Dak Prescott, CeeDee Lamb, and George Pickens. Hell, the head man can’t even figure out how to get all three of these players on the field at the same time in this latest loss. It’s horror show stuff. Schottenheimer got the ultimate do-over card in year one when we all accepted the Eberflus defense was bad enough to not be able to fairly evaluate anything else, just to be as bad at calling an offense as Eberflus was at calling a defense in year two with the same personnel. Horror. Show. Tom – Not much to add, although I would add that the culture seems to be a real issue. This team just seems to have no real fight in it, and certainly does not seem to be working together. Now we have the Cowboys being treated as a laughingstock after blowing that game, and that is not going to help the morale. Maybe that falls back on the head coach, but you’d hope that some of the players would be trying to do something themselves to change the attitude. Dyllan – Players need to play. Coaches need to coach. Neither party involved did much of either in the second half. Coach Schottenheimer’s game management has proven to be abysmal this season, rearing its ugly head once again against Arizona. Players began missing tackles and committing drive-continuing penalties. Everything went from near perfect in the first half to a cataclysmic nightmare in the second. When that happens, the blame falls at the feet of every person involved. Tyler Allgeier finished with 147 rushing yards. Is the problem poor tackling, blown assignments, or simply a lack of physicality from Dallas? Mike – It’s all three, but for me, the biggest problem is poor defensive discipline and a complete lack of physicality. Players were losing their assignments, failing to maintain gap discipline, taking poor angles, and missing tackles. But what frustrates me most is how easily Arizona bullied Dallas at the line of scrimmage. There was no aggression, no accountability and very little resistance once Allgeier reached the second level. When it’s all three you have to look at Christian Parker to take responsibility for all this, and he’s sitting firmly on the hot seat already. Jorge – All of the above. Tackling has been an issue all year, and the lack of physicality has been a staple of the Dallas Cowboys defense even when they were recently good. Both go hand in hand; the same goes for the assignments. Christian Parker is failing as a DC, and the same issues have bubbled up all year. When you mix all three shortcomings into defensive performance, you get exactly what you saw on Sunday. The fact that the Cowboys defense isn’t okay at any of these three things is an indictment of Parker. Sean – I would include being out of position within the poor tackling category if I had to choose one of your buckets here, so tackling for me. Guys are expecting the first line of defense to make plays that they aren’t, which leads to the second level missing tackles, and then the third. There’s no swarming to the ball or visible effort to care about getting the guy with the ball on the ground before at least a positive gain every time. Tom – I heard someone during the SNF postgame talk about how none of the units on defense were really unified. They just seem to be playing the game in isolation, with no teamwork. The three levels of the defense have to support one another, and that is just not happening. Dyllan – Pre-snap alignment hurt them at times. Throwing shoulders instead of wrapping up occurred more than once. It looked like nobody wanted to take the bull by the horns in the second half and say, “enough is enough.” It’s troubling to see that against what’s supposed to be an inferior team. What does Brian Schottenheimer need to change about his late-game managemen t to be trusted to close out games when the Cowboys are ahead? Mike – Right now, I simply don’t trust Brian Schottenheimer to close out games when Dallas has a lead. He needs to understand that protecting a lead doesn’t mean abandoning what made the offense successful. Keep attacking defensive weaknesses and trust your playmakers. His clock management and play selection all need serious improvement. Good coaches know when to be aggressive and when to manage a game. Schottenheimer currently seems to confuse managing a lead with playing not to lose. Jorge – I hate to sound cliché, but he needs to coach to win the dang game. Too often he coaches not to lose, only to lose in the most enfeebling ways possible. Trust your playmakers, cut them loose, put your line in a position to succeed, give the defense different looks. He gets really cute with his play calls, overthinks the hell out of everything and worst of all, just shows no urgency whatsoever. He is the worst possible coach for this team with the DNA it has; he’s way too laid back, and it shows. Constantly taking opportunities, moments and plays for granted, I don’t think I’ve ever seen a coach so disinterested in winning and trying to get better. With that said, he has to give up playcalling, and he absolutely cannot be trusted to close out games. Sean – Again, like we’ve basically been saying for two years now, get the ball to your best players. Not to be a prisoner of the…
author: Mike Poland

title: Brian Schottenheimer report card: Out-coached again in another loss
summary: Do you remember when you were a kid and your parents always hounded you about how much better of a student you would be if you just applied yourself? No… just me? Well, for what feels like the 100th time this season, Brian Schottenheimer brought home a failing report card to his disappointed parents, and […]
full_text: Photo by Perry Knotts/Getty Images | Getty Images Do you remember when you were a kid and your parents always hounded you about how much better of a student you would be if you just applied yourself? No… just me? Well, for what feels like the 100th time this season, Brian Schottenheimer brought home a failing report card to his disappointed parents, and his lack of ability to properly understand how to attack his opponent based on tape is very concerning. Even after putting up 30 points in the Cowboys 33-30 loss, Schottenheimer (along with Christian Parker) was the clear problem for the Cowboys. Whether it’s failed challenges, ultra-conservativeness, questionable fourth-down play calls, extreme lack of creativity, or the stubbornness to establish the run, the Cowboys offense is consistently put on hard-mode week in-and-week out. The first half was filled with inefficient runs, setting the Cowboys up behind the chains and trying to convert on third-and-longs way too much. After torching the Philadelphia Eagles on the ground in week seven, the Cowboys were dedicated to replicating their running game success against the Cardinals, and they finished the game with 39 carriers for 93 yards (2.4 yards per carry). With the running game hurting them a ton in this game, the Cowboys relied on Dak Prescott, CeeDee Lamb, and Ryan Flournoy to carry the load. The only problem was the passing concepts looked eerily similar to how it did in Weeks 1-6. Very little motion, few bunch sets, and basic, static route concepts that make things extremely difficult for anyone to create separation in the passing game. With the run game setting them back, and the lack of modern day passing concepts making things very easy to defend, the Cowboys found themselves stalling out in the second half and blowing a two-possession lead with just four minutes to go in the game. The main concern with Schottenheimer (outside of everything else we’ve already touched on) is his inability to close games out as a play-caller. For his entire tenure at the head coach and play-caller for the Cowboys, Schottenheimer has called the game was too passive. His inability to understand how poor his defense has been for a year-and-a-half now has cost this football team wins. For a coach who has a $60-million dollar quarterback, two highly paid wide receivers, and an offensive line loaded with highly paid players and first-round picks, Schottenheimer puts more faith in his defense and special teams than he does his talented and highly-paid offense. The end of the first half field goal attempt was the first of many signs of this throughout the game. With 11-seconds left in the first half and a timeout in his back pocket, Schottenheimer elected to run the football for a minimal gain and send out Brandon Aubrey for a 61-yard field goal attempt. Aubrey, who has struggled mightily with the longer field goal attempts so far this season, missed the field goal, and the Cowboys carried a 14-3 game into half. Why not try to gain 10-15 yards with a timeout in your back pocket and the entire field at your disposal? The next drive that had a heavy weight on his grade was the Cowboys second to last drive in the fourth quarter. With the ball on the Cardinals 20-yard line up three points, the Cowboys ran Javonte Williams up the middle for no gain to get the Cardinals to burn their last time out, which was the right call. The next play call perfectly encases all of Schottenheimer’s warts as a play-caller. With the two-minute warning looming, the Cowboys were in a perfect position to go for the jugular. Instead, with CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens standing on the sideline, Schottenheimer dialed up a slow developing play-action pass with everyone on the field and in the stadium knowing the Cowboys should and would be passing. The result? An L.J. Collier sack losing six yards. On 3rd-and-16, Schottenheimer did what he often does in less than ideal down and distances, runs Williams straight into a brickwall for a minimal gain. Brandon Aubrey came on to give the Cowboys a six-point lead with a minute to go and no timeouts for the Cardinals. In most instances, that’s enough to win the football game, but the Cowboys defense had other plans, as they often have in 2026. The decision to run play-action with Lamb and Pickens on the sideline, with a chance to ice the game was absolutely mind-boggling. Schottenheimer commented on his choice of personnel, pointing to a similar package earlier in the game on the Ryan Flournoy touchdown pass in the second quarter. I would certainly hope Schottenheimer understands the difference between a 3rd-and-1 in the first quarter of a 7-0 game and potentially the last play from scrimmage when the defense is forced to play aggressive to create negative plays from the offense, but who really knows right now. Play-Calling F Fourth-Down Decisions C I loved Schottenheimer’s decision to go for the fourth down on the opening drive of the game, but absolutely hated the play call and formation that got stuffed. Timeout Usage F Team Preparation F It was all pretty ugly, yet again. What grade would you give to Brian Schottenheimer on Sunday?

title: Cowboys Week 9 opponent: A look at the 2026 Indianapolis Colts
summary: The Dallas Cowboys head to Indianapolis for a Week 9 matchup against a franchise, not unlike the Cowboys, that appears to be falling apart in real time. The Colts enter Sunday’s game at 2-6, riding a four-game losing streak after getting embarrassed 42-7 by the Jacksonville Jaguars. But the losing record is only part of […]
full_text: The Dallas Cowboys head to Indianapolis for a Week 9 matchup against a franchise, not unlike the Cowboys, that appears to be falling apart in real time. The Colts enter Sunday’s game at 2-6, riding a four-game losing streak after getting embarrassed 42-7 by the Jacksonville Jaguars. But the losing record is only part of the story. Indianapolis has already fired general manager Chris Ballard, traded away two of its biggest stars and opened the door to moving more players before the Nov. 10 trade deadline. That could make the Colts a very different team by the time Dallas takes the field. Jonathan Taylor is drawing serious trade interest, wide receiver Josh Downs has requested a trade, and quarterback Daniel Jones is coming off another miserable performance. For Dallas, this is a chance to take advantage of a team facing significant uncertainty. But the Cowboys are 3-5 themselves, and after blowing a 14-point fourth-quarter lead against Arizona, they can’t afford to overlook anyone. Daniel Jones is struggling, but Indianapolis is sticking with him The biggest question surrounding Indianapolis is what to do at quarterback. Daniel Jones was pulled during Sunday’s blowout loss to Jacksonville after throwing two interceptions, and the conversation immediately shifted to whether Anthony Richardson would get another opportunity to start. Steichen answered that question Monday, confirming that Jones will remain the starting quarterback for Week 9 against Dallas. Richardson entered the Jacksonville game late and completed both of his pass attempts for eight yards, but the coaching staff apparently believes Jones still gives the Colts their best chance to win. That is becoming a difficult argument to make. Through eight games, Jones has completed 162 of 268 passes for 1,542 yards, five touchdowns and nine interceptions. He has also been sacked 22 times and has a 68.7 passer rating. His 60.4% completion rate is a career low, and his five passing touchdowns are not a good sign for an offense that entered the season expecting to compete. Against Jacksonville, Jones completed 19 of 28 passes for 144 yards, one touchdown and two interceptions before being replaced. The Colts managed just seven points, turned the ball over three times and never looked capable of making the game competitive. The offensive line has not helped. Indianapolis has allowed 22 sacks in eight games, and Quenton Nelson’s departure makes an already difficult situation even more complicated. Jones will work behind a reshuffled offensive line against a Dallas defense that desperately needs to generate pressure. Jonathan Taylor could be playing his final game in Indianapolis The biggest trade storyline in Indianapolis centers on running back Jonathan Taylor. One of the league’s most productive running backs is suddenly available, and the Colts are reportedly engaged in active discussions with multiple teams ahead of the trade deadline. According to NFL Network’s Ian Rapoport and ESPN’s Adam Schefter, the Colts are open to moving Taylor, with the Denver Broncos, Green Bay Packers, Minnesota Vikings, New York Giants and Seattle Seahawks among the teams that have shown interest. Taylor has been one of the few consistent bright spots for Indianapolis this season. Through eight games, he has rushed for 610 yards and eight touchdowns on 148 carries, averaging 4.1 yards per attempt. He has also added 21 receptions for 202 yards, giving him 812 yards from scrimmage. Most rush TD this season Josh Allen 9 Jonathan Taylor 8 Javonte Williams 8 Christian McCaffrey 8 3 players tied 7 pic.twitter.com/8LyyxYTY5f — PFF (@PFF) November 1, 2026 The numbers are impressive, especially considering how much the offense has struggled around him. Taylor entered Week 8 among the league leaders in rushing touchdowns and has been one of the Colts’ most dependable offensive weapons. However, his performance against Jacksonville reminded everyone that even an elite running back cannot carry an entire team. Taylor managed just 23 rushing yards on eight carries and added 24 receiving yards. He also fumbled during the blowout. Taylor has acknowledged the trade speculation but has not requested a move. He recently said he remains proud to wear the Colts uniform and is focused on controlling what he can control. Still, the organization has already shown that it is willing to move established players as it reshapes the roster. There is a legitimate argument for keeping Taylor as a centerpiece of the rebuild, particularly after signing him to a two-year, $44 million extension in August. But with Indianapolis sitting at 2-6 and already moving important veterans, a trade would not be surprising. Josh Downs wants out, and the Colts’ receiving corps is changing Taylor is not the only offensive player whose future in Indianapolis is uncertain. Wide receiver Josh Downs has requested a trade, adding another layer to the Colts’ ongoing roster shake-up. Downs has been one of the team’s most productive receivers this season, leading Indianapolis with 30 receptions for 330 yards and one touchdown through eight games. He has become an important target for Jones, particularly in the short and intermediate passing game. Josh Downs is wide open ‼️ 📺 CBS pic.twitter.com/w2M7uc1aW6 — Indianapolis Colts (@Colts) November 1, 2026 His request came after Indianapolis traded Quenton Nelson and DeForest Buckner, two established leaders who were central to the team’s identity. Downs is entering the final year of his rookie contract, and with the Colts seemingly shifting toward the future, he could be another player moved before the deadline. Downs isn’t the only receiving option Dallas needs to consider. Veteran Keenan Allen has recorded 36 receptions for 325 yards and a touchdown, while second-year tight end Tyler Warren has added 34 catches for 231 yards and two touchdowns. If Downs is still in the lineup Sunday, he will be an important underneath target for Jones. If he is traded, Indianapolis will have to rely even more heavily on Allen and Warren to provide consistency in the passing game. The Cowboys’ secondary remains one of the team’s biggest weaknesses, so even a struggling Indianapolis offense could find opportunities if Dallas allows receivers to work freely underneath as they have all year. The Colts’ defense has its own problems after trading DeForest Buckner The Colts’ defensive situation has changed dramatically following the trade of DeForest Buckner to San Francisco. Buckner was one of the team’s most important defensive players, and his departure leaves a significant hole along the defensive line. Indianapolis has recorded 16 sacks and two interceptions through eight games, while opponents have accumulated 2,748 total yards. Defensive tackle Adetomiwa Adebawore and Buckner tied for the team lead with four sacks each before the trade, while edge rusher Laiatu Latu has two. Without Buckner, the Colts will need other players to take on larger responsibilities along the defensive front. That is a difficult adjustment for a team already struggling to stop opposing offenses. The Colts have allowed 1,054 rushing yards through eight games, averaging nearly 132 yards per contest. That ranks among the league’s weaker run defenses, and Buckner’s departure could make the challenge even greater, with Indianapolis also struggling to create turnovers this season. Indianapolis is in free fall, but Dallas cannot afford another letdown The Colts have lost four consecutive games with defeats to Pittsburgh, Tennessee, Minnesota and Jacksonville. Their latest loss was ugly: a 42-7 defeat in which Jacksonville averaged nearly seven yards per play, and Indianapolis struggled to produce anything offensively. The numbers paint a bleak picture. Indianapolis has scored just 15 offensive touchdowns through eight games, committed nine interceptions and has a minus-11 turnover ratio. The team has also allowed 2,748 yards while producing only 2,329 of its own. The…

title: Cowboys news: Jerry Jones likes the direction of his defense
summary: Before halftime, the Dallas Cowboys led the Arizona Cardinals 14-3, and Christian Parker’s defense played lights-out. Something changed in the second half, and the defense gave up four straight touchdown drives to end regulation, and the Cowboys lost in overtime. Through it all, Jerry Jones said he still believes in his defense and sees the […]
full_text: Photo by Perry Knotts/Getty Images | Getty Images Before halftime, the Dallas Cowboys led the Arizona Cardinals 14-3, and Christian Parker’s defense played lights-out. Something changed in the second half, and the defense gave up four straight touchdown drives to end regulation, and the Cowboys lost in overtime. Through it all, Jerry Jones said he still believes in his defense and sees the unit trending in the right direction. Jerry Jones on Cowboys’ defense: ‘I like the way we’re trending’ – Tommy Yarrish, DallasCowboys.com The Cowboys owner and general manager still believes in Christian Parker. “We’ve been changing,” Jones said. “We’ve changed out on our defense, we’ve changed out our coaching staff, complete coaching staff. We’ve changed out the majority of the players, really. And in today’s building of a team, you do it with a combination of draft, which draft picks have to have a little seasoning most of the time.” “And therein lies the inconsistency that we’re seeing, even within a game where we played so well in the first half and came back and didn’t play as well in the second half. That is a disappointment, but not a surprise… It does not call for massive, or not massive, it does not call for very succinct, important changes because I like the way we’re trending.” The Cowboys’ defense is turning 30-point games into losses. And jeopardizing jobs – Mac Engel, Fort Worth Star-Telegram Will the Cowboys’ continued disappointment cause a shake-up in the coaching staff at the end of the season? Jerry will not fire Schottenheimer during this season, but after it feels plausible. Schottenheimer is in the second year of a four-year contract, and while Jerry hates the idea of paying a coach to not coach, he will not want another year of what he’s currently watching. The problem remains the same as it has been for years. The defense under first-year, first-time defensive coordinator Christian Parker continues to play at a level that is no longer bewildering but a state that will get people fired, most notably himself. Cowboys’ Brandon Aubrey problem is affecting them in more ways than one – Levi Dombro, The Landry Hat Brandon Aubrey hasn’t been the same clutch long-distance kicker this season. Although Aubrey’s kickoffs are undeniably the best in the league, which give Dallas better field position than any other team in the NFL, his field goals have been an issue. On Sunday against the Arizona Cardinals, he had makes from 31, 35 and 41, and he made all three extra points. He missed from 61, though. Download the SB Nation app today! Fewer ads Seamlessly jump between communities and conversations Faster commenting and posting experience! Download the SB Nation app on iOS or Android . George Pickens Could Force the Cowboys to Trade Him – Michael Gallagher, Heavy on Cowboys The Cowboys would net some quality draft capital if they moved on from George Pickens. Pickens is playing on the one-year franchise tag ($27.3 million), and a second tag next offseason would cost Dallas about $32.8 million. That’s a problem. Cornerback Joey Porter Jr. is also playing without an extension and wants upward of $30 million per year — and the Cowboys only get one tag. An extension won’t be cheap either. Solak estimates Pickens would command north of $33 million per year, worryingly close to the $34 million CeeDee Lamb makes. Past/Present: Oklahoma names Jason Witten offensive coordinator for remainder of 2026 season – Tommy Yarrish, DallasCowboys.com It’s the year 2028, and Jason Witten is being introduced as the next head coach of the Dallas Cowboys. Former Cowboys tight end Jason Witten was named the offensive coordinator and play caller for the remainder of the 2026 season by the University of Oklahoma. Witten was hired as the Sooners’ tight ends coach at the start of the year for his first collegiate coaching job, and now takes over the offense after Oklahoma’s decision to dismiss offensive coordinator Ben Arbuckle.
