title: How Brian Schottenheimer is failing the Cowboys
summary: Watching the Dallas Cowboys in 2026 has become a tiring experience. We are not even halfway through the season, and things are already looking bleak. Losing is never fun, but watching them underachieve has become a weekly ordeal that has turned into pure exhaustion. Every Sunday, it’s a new level of disappointment. There’s talent on […]
full_text: Photo by Ron Jenkins/Getty Images Watching the Dallas Cowboys in 2026 has become a tiring experience. We are not even halfway through the season, and things are already looking bleak. Losing is never fun, but watching them underachieve has become a weekly ordeal that has turned into pure exhaustion. Every Sunday, it’s a new level of disappointment. There’s talent on this team, but the leadership and tactical execution have brought about regular failures that are tough to sit through. The most recent collapse against the Arizona Cardinals serves as more evidence that head coach and play-caller Brian Schottenheimer is fundamentally not the guy to help this franchise return to glory. The issues start with Schottenheimer’s bizarre tendencies. He routinely fails to make the basic decisions that would maximize his team’s probability of winning. One example is his weird habit of running quarterback sneaks down at his own goal line. Instead of trusting his playmakers or scheming an effective play, he plays scared and chooses to waste a down, putting the offense in a tough spot. Every time he does this, the Cowboys have punted three plays later. Another example is his treatment of Brandon Aubrey. We all know that Aubrey is one of the league’s most lethal kicking weapons, but Schottenheimer finds ways to turn that into a disadvantage for the Cowboys. Rather than pressing and trying to pick up extra yards to give him a more reasonable field goal attempt, the head coach contentedly runs the ball and settles for a short gain. His confidence in Aubrey treats those situations like an automatic three points instead of working for a shorter attempt. He unnecessarily creates high-stress kicking situations that have resulted in blocks and misses. The team also cannot stop repeating the same mistakes. They look uncoached at times, committing the same self-inflicted errors week after week. Are we sick of neutral zone infractions yet? Every week. Early and often. It’s just the same penalties over and over. It’s become an epidemic. Whatever the coaches are doing to discourage this practice is not working. They keep jumping early. As a play-caller, Schottenheimer is equally frustrating. The team doesn’t have much of a rushing attack, as the offense has struggled to deploy the physical ground game they so confidently promote during the summer. It’s been ineffective, and there have been moments when he has completely abandoned it, essentially acknowledging defeat. That admission might be a little easier to accept if the offense possessed a high-powered aerial attack that many believe should accompany having one of the best wide receiving duos in the league. But they don’t. For some reason, the team’s most explosive receiving weapons are underutilized. Schottenheimer fails to create mismatches, and the offense becomes very stagnant at times. No pre-snap motion or creative blocking schemes. The Cowboys’ offense has turned into a predictable entity that defenses can absolutely shut down at certain points in the game, and those moments are extremely harmful. Under Schottenheimer, the Cowboys constantly invent new ways to lose football games. Against the Cardinals, it was the inability to run out the clock. Earlier in the year, against the Ravens, it was a goal-line debauchery that couldn’t win the game. Both instances put the pressure back on a porous defense to come through, and sadly, they did not. The Cowboys don’t just lose. They actively engineer their own downfall through a blend of situational ineptitude and executive panic. But if you listen to Schottenheimer’s postgame press conferences, he seems completely detached from reality. His media appearances have turned into comedy shows, highlighted by delusion and a lack of awareness. He stands at the table and claims to be a problem solver, yet no problems ever get solved. He throws out tired clichés and empty promises about how things need to get cleaned up, but each week the same chaos ensues. The Cowboys are a 3-5 football team, and sadly, it’s fitting for who they are. Each week, they are favored against these bad teams because, on paper, they should be beating them. They have more talent. But none of that matters when the coaching puts them at such a disadvantage. Star players become average, and average players become bad. So far, the evidence strongly suggests that Schottenheimer is not a head coach capable of leading an NFL team to victory, and with each new week, this is becoming more and more obvious. This is a subtle example of being outcoached. Mike LaFleur takes his final timeout on the north side of the two-minute warning. It dares the Cowboys to pass on second down. That's fine, but they play scared, and he knows it. The result? A sack and no chance to run out the clock. pic.twitter.com/U7Kjbvfbmr — Dan Rogers (@DannyPhantom24) November 1, 2026
author: Dan Rogers

title: Rashan Gary’s inexcusable penalty opened the door to final collapse
summary: The Cowboys should have had Arizona facing a desperate decision on a fourth down. Either go for a risky first down on 4th-and-10, or take a safe field goal that would still leave Dallas up seven. Instead, Rashan Gary handed them a lifeline. With Dallas leading 27-17 late in the fourth quarter, Gary’s roughing-the-passer penalty […]
full_text: Mandatory Credit: Jerome Miron-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The Cowboys should have had Arizona facing a desperate decision on a fourth down. Either go for a risky first down on 4th-and-10, or take a safe field goal that would still leave Dallas up seven. Instead, Rashan Gary handed them a lifeline. With Dallas leading 27-17 late in the fourth quarter, Gary’s roughing-the-passer penalty wiped out an incompletion and gave the Cardinals a fresh set of downs. One play later, Arizona was in the end zone. Suddenly, a game the Cowboys should have closed out became another nervous finish, ultimately ending in a 33-30 overtime defeat. Dallas had already weathered one Arizona response. After taking a commanding 24-10 lead early in the fourth quarter, the Cowboys allowed Tyler Allgeier to score again, cutting the margin to just seven. However, the Cowboys’ offense then put together a lengthy possession, before Brandon Aubrey’s 35-yard field goal upped the lead to 27-17 with 3:54 remaining. With the clock working in their favor, Dallas should have held on to the victory. Dallas needed the defense to make Arizona earn every play. Instead, on third-and-10 from the Dallas 29 with 2:23 remaining, Gardner Minshew’s pass towards the end zone fell incomplete. However, Gary committed an unnecessary helmet-to-helmet hit on the quarterback, giving Arizona 15 yards and an automatic first down at the Dallas 14. This turned fourth-and-10 into another scoring opportunity for Arizona without the Cardinals having to complete a pass. It was an inexcusable mistake from a veteran defender. The punishment was immediate. Minshew found an uncovered Trey McBride for a 14-yard touchdown on the next snap. The extra point cut Dallas’ lead to 27-24, and Arizona had scored before the two-minute warning. The timing of Gary’s mistake made the penalty even more damaging. Arizona still had the two-minute warning to stop the clock during Dallas’ next possession. Gary’s error had helped the Cardinals quickly get into the end zone, preserving a realistic chance of regaining possession. This desperate comeback now had a viable path forward. Gary does not carry all the blame for what followed. The coverage failure on McBride’s touchdown, the offense’s inability to close and the final defensive collapse each deserves scrutiny. But his penalty was the moment Dallas surrendered a major advantage it had already earned. With Arizona running short of chances, the Cowboys supplied another one for free. For a team trying to prove it could win consecutive games, that lack of discipline was painfully costly, and this was the turning point of the game.
author: Mike Poland

title: The Cowboys and the cruel art of collapse
summary: The Dallas Cowboys are bad at football. That’s a tough reality to live in. For months we have been clinging to the hope that a stellar offense with a gradually improving defense would be the magic ticket to help this team pick up steam and start rolling down the stretch of the season. We have […]
full_text: Photo by Ron Jenkins/Getty Images The Dallas Cowboys are bad at football. That’s a tough reality to live in. For months we have been clinging to the hope that a stellar offense with a gradually improving defense would be the magic ticket to help this team pick up steam and start rolling down the stretch of the season. We have some bad news. Nothing’s rolling. The defense remains terrible, and the offense has started to join in by underperforming at unpopular moments in the game. The whole thing culminates in disappointing outings and losses to what we think are inferior teams. One after the other. The latest letdown elevates the frustration to another notch. That’s because it appeared like they were onto something by building a 14-point lead, but things inevitably fell apart. What happened this time? Taking a closer look paints an uncomfortable picture. To start off, it’s important to note that these two teams aren’t too far off when it comes to ability. They both now have the same record, and this one went down to the wire, so it tracks. That’s why it was misleading when the Cowboys got off to an early lead. It wasn’t because of sheer dominance. It was just luck. When you look at what went on early in the game, the Cowboys benefited greatly when a Jonathan Mingo muffed punt bounced right back into his hands. They were also fortunate that backup tight end James Mitchell was right there to fall on a Javonte Williams fumble in the end zone. Even Shemar James’ interception that he returned deep into Arizona territory bounced right into his arms after it deflected off the Cardinals’ receiver. You could make a strong case that this game would’ve remained a lot tighter had the ball bounced a little differently. It hurts because the Cowboys let a 14-point, fourth-quarter lead get away from them, but look on the bright side – they shouldn't have even had that lead. The Cowboys got some good luck in this game, and they still blew it. pic.twitter.com/8zDmoaLXOn — Dan Rogers (@DannyPhantom24) November 2, 2026 But hey, that’s football, and Cowboys fans certainly aren’t going to complain when some breaks go their way. The Cardinals kept dropping passes, committed a lot of false starts at terrible times, and even shanked the game-winning extra point at the end of regulation. Bad teams do bad things, and the Cardinals did their fair share. Offensively, you might be inclined to think the Cowboys scored 30 points and that’s more than enough. The offense did their part. But did they? They did score six times, three touchdowns and three field goals, but a close look shows the offense didn’t look all that great. One of their touchdowns came from that before mentioned fumble recovery in the end zone, and the only reason they were down that far was because of the interception return. The Cowboys’ other two touchdowns came from improv plays where Dak Prescott started to scramble. In fact, on one of those scrambles, he ran into the end zone. When you step back, you see an offense that sputtered quite a bit. They didn’t have any creative play calls to free up players. They often didn’t have the correct protection set up, giving Cardinals defenders free shots in the backfield. And even when they just needed to get one lousy first down to run out the clock, they couldn’t pull it off. The result was 261 total yards against the defense that gives up the most points in the league. An offense with Prescott, CeeDee Lamb, George Pickens, and several first-round offensive linemen couldn’t get the job done in critical moments. As unimpressive as this unit was, they were still outfailed by the defense. Oh, the defense. What a weird game it was for this group. It’s weird because, unlike the offense, they were never meh. They were either great or dreadful. There was no in-between. They started off really sharp. The pressure was there, the coverage was decent, and they were making hard-hitting tackles. The Cardinals couldn’t get anything going. To understand this, let’s offer some perspective. With 90 seconds left in the first half, the Cowboys led 14-0. The Cardinals hadn’t scored any points yet. With 90 seconds left in the third quarter, the Cowboys led 17-3. The Cardinals only had a field goal through almost three quarters of football. The defense finished with five sacks and two takeaways. They were making plays, but then they went from playing really well to absolutely horrid. What happened? This is the frustrating part. The Cowboys got comfortable. Instead of playing disciplined, sound football, they wanted to annihilate the Cardinals and got caught overpursuing. On the big running plays, it was a collection of failures. The defensive line didn’t maintain their gaps. Instead, they were aggressive and attacked upfield. With holes available, the defensive backs took poor angles and completely whiffed with their tackling. Manageable gains turned into monster plays for the Cardinals. Those two big running plays allowed Arizona to get back in the game because they were fast strikes. And when the Cowboys offense couldn’t finish things on their end, the Cardinals were given more chances to attack, and the defense wasn’t equipped to fend them off. It's so frustrating that when Arizona's offense needed a big conversion with the defense coming at them, they schemed a play. The same was not true for the Cowboys offense. One team had Dak Prescott. The other had Gardner Minshew. That's all you need to know about the coaching. pic.twitter.com/CZBV8SgiTz — Dan Rogers (@DannyPhantom24) November 2, 2026 Many will say that Minshew Mania saved the day. That’s not what went down. Sure, credit Minshew for making plays, but he wasn’t pulling off any Houdini escapes or threading any needles. He just calmly capitalized on coverage breakdowns by the Cowboys’ defense. On the Cardinals’ final two touchdowns, one to Trey McBride and another to Michael Wilson, there wasn’t a defender anywhere close on either play. It was easy, and quite honestly, we all watched helplessly knowing it was coming. There was no Minshew Magic. There was only Parker Tragic. Overpursing Weak tackling Taking poor angles Lack of gap integrity Coverage breakdowns The same stupid penalties Outsmarting the Cowboys' defense is not hard to do. You just gotta wait it out and push the right buttons. — Dan Rogers (@DannyPhantom24) November 2, 2026 If there’s a silver lining, it’s that the Cowboys do have talented pieces. Unfortunately, that doesn’t mean anything if this team can’t find a way to use them correctly. Both the offense and defense are having mental lapses and breakdowns. And it keeps happening week after week with no end in sight.
author: Dan Rogers

title: 2026 NFL Week 9 Power Rankings: Cowboys proving no bottom exists
summary: Don’t you dare think that we have reached the bottom. The Dallas Cowboys are proving over and over again that such a place does not exist. There is always lower to go. Just a few weeks ago we thought that losing to Jalon Daniels and the Tampa Bay Buccaneers was the end of the black […]
full_text: Photo by Stacy Revere/Getty Images | Getty Images Don’t you dare think that we have reached the bottom. The Dallas Cowboys are proving over and over again that such a place does not exist. There is always lower to go. Just a few weeks ago we thought that losing to Jalon Daniels and the Tampa Bay Buccaneers was the end of the black hole. Maybe you feel like that was more embarrassing than what happened last week, but the point is we at least have to have the conversation which proves that things are not fun. It is just barely November and the season feels over for the Cowboys. This isn’t something that only fans of the team who have been around for forever are saying because we are tired… this is universal opinion and belief. Let’s get to this week’s power rankings. 1. Buffalo Bills (LW: 1) Kings stay kings. It was a bummer that last week’s game against Baltimore lost juice when Lamar Jackson was hurt. 2. San Francisco 49ers (LW: 2) How many points will they beat the Cowboys by next week? 3. Detroit Lions (LW: 3) I’ve said before… I really doubted them this year. They have proven me very wrong. 4. Chicago Bears (LW: 4) Ben Johnson sure can coach. And yes… we all know. 5. Jacksonville Jaguars (LW: 5) Welcome back. 6. New England Patriots (LW: 7) They just do the simple things right. Over and over and over again. That is so much harder than it seems. 7. Cincinnati Bengals (LW: 9) They are headed to Spain this week! 8. Denver Broncos (LW: 16) I was also very wrong about the Broncos. The offense I think is still a little to be determined, but the defense is incredible. 9. Seattle Seahawks (LW: 6) Monday night was definitely a stumble. 10. Green Bay Packers (LW: 13) We really need them to start losing for draft pick purposes. 11. Minnesota Vikings (LW: 8) The undefeateds have all fallen. Cheers to the ‘72 Dolphins. 12. Pittsburgh Steelers (LW: 18) Look at Mike McCarthy. 6-2 and in first place with a bye to rest. Must be nice. 13. Los Angeles Rams (LW: 14) Perhaps they are turning into the top team everybody envisioned them to be. We need to see more. 14. Atlanta Falcons (LW: 11) It really seemed like they were turning into a team that could be feisty. Last week was dreadful, though. 15. Kansas City Chiefs (LW: 12) On some level it was strange to see them in a pickle and not find the only way to pull it off. They are going to have to work harder than normal this season. 16. New York Giants (LW: 15) Back from the bye, but they will likely crush the Eagles and fully announce themselves as the soon-to-be NFC East winners. 17. Cleveland Browns (LW: 17) They were humbled a bit last week. 18. Baltimore Ravens (LW: 10) All the best to Lamar Jackson. This franchise feels a bit at a crossroads at quarterback. 19. Tampa Bay Buccaneers (LW: 19) A win is a win and they are stacking them. 20. Las Vegas Raiders (LW: 23) At least they are fun. 21. Arizona Cardinals (LW: 25) What is there to even say anymore? 22. Carolina Panthers (LW: 21) They gave Green Bay all they could handle. 23. Houston Texans (LW: 22) Welcome back as well. 24. Dallas Cowboys (LW: 20) Embarrassing. 25. Washington Commanders (LW: 29) Maybe they will jump Dallas in the standings, too. 26. New Orleans Saints (LW: 24) Did you know Boise State unveiled a Kellen Moore statue? We are all getting old. 27. Philadelphia Eagles (LW: 26) At least they know they need to reset. 28. Indianapolis Colts (LW: 27) How many yards for Jonathan Taylor this week? 29. New York Jets (LW: 28) The Cowboys of the AFC. 30. Miami Dolphins (LW: 30) Very gross. 31. Tennessee Titans (LW: 31) They might also give the Cowboys a tough time. 32. Los Angeles Chargers (LW: 32) The toughest of tough scenes. ESPN : 23 (LW: 20) Sigh. Best in-season trade acquisition ever: Package in 1989 RB Herschel Walker deal Regardless of whether the credit for the trade goes to Jerry Jones or Jimmy Johnson, it altered the Cowboys’ trajectory into becoming a three-time Super Bowl champion. They were 0-5 when they traded Walker, ending the 1989 season at 1-15. It wasn’t the five players the Cowboys received from Minnesota that were important, but rather the conditional draft choices that would come if players Dallas acquired were cut the next offseason. Ultimately, the trade landed them Emmitt Smith, Kevin Smith and Darren Woodson, and gave them flexibility to make other moves. Without the trade of Walker, the Cowboys of the 1990s probably never would have existed. — Todd Archer NFL.com : 24 (LW: 22) And again… sigh. Remember when that guy in the AT&T Stadium bowels described a Cowboys loss as “embarrassing” a few weeks ago? Well, that individual would have been spot on again on Sunday. Dallas disintegrated against the Cardinals, blowing a 17-3 lead and surrendering 467 yards to Arizona. It’s a loss that feels too devastating to have occurred in Week 8. It’s where the Cowboys are right now, though: They pin their hopes on their passing game, haven’t improved enough defensively and can only hope the running game produces. That’s simply not a winning formula. USA Today : 25 (LW: 23) The lowest ranking so far. They had been 69-0 at home when nursing a lead of at least 14 points in the fourth quarter … but that was before Sunday. Yahoo : 25 (LW: 20) And again. Biggest need: Adding to the defense, maybe At some point the Cowboys need to have an honest conversation about themselves, which seems impossible after team owner Jerry Jones proclaimed everyone is letting head coach Brian Schottenheimer down. Jones has talked about making big trades, and already made one in-season for cornerback Joey Porter Jr. A putrid defense that let Gardner Minshew tear it apart in the fourth quarter and overtime on Sunday needs a lot of help. But, is a team that has losses at home to a Buccaneers team led by an undrafted rookie quarterback and to a Cardinals team that came back from a 14-point deficit in the fourth quarter really a defensive piece away from contending for a Super Bowl? Probably not. It puts the Cowboys in a weird place. They’re not out of the NFC East race because the division isn’t good. They’re also not very good themselves. It’s not even outlandish for the Cowboys to look in the mirror after that hideous loss to the Cardinals and admit they should be sellers. That would require self-awareness, which isn’t abundant in Dallas. CBS Sports : 22 (LW: 20) Not quite as far of a dip. What in the hell was that against the Cardinals? That’s the kind of loss that gets a coach fired. Jerry Jones said it’s not happening now, but Brian Schottenheimer better get it going. The Athletic : 22 (LW: 18) Same spot. Reality check: Jerry Jones is big mad The Cowboys owner said after the game, one in which Dallas blew a 24-10 lead in the final 11 minutes, that he doesn’t expect to make a head coaching change during the season, but he didn’t rule out doing something . “This is something we will take a good hard look at,” Jones said. “That was a total team effort out there for us. We have to be, for our fans, better than that.” Dallas has lost three of its last four. ProFootballTalk : 26 (LW: 21) The lowest ranking of the group. Offseason hype, in-season tripe. title: Cowboys rookie report: Caleb Downs, Malachi Lawrence hurt
summary: Dallas had another win within reach, but a fourth-quarter embarrassment ended in a 33–30 overtime loss to Arizona. For the rookie class, LT Overton supplied a takeaway, Malachi Lawrence generated some pressure, and Caleb Downs’ afternoon ended early with a concussion.  But here is how each rookie fared this week, listed in draft order, and […]
full_text: Mandatory Credit: Kevin Jairaj-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Dallas had another win within reach, but a fourth-quarter embarrassment ended in a 33–30 overtime loss to Arizona. For the rookie class, LT Overton supplied a takeaway, Malachi Lawrence generated some pressure, and Caleb Downs’ afternoon ended early with a concussion. But here is how each rookie fared this week, listed in draft order, and any undrafted players worth noting after that. Caleb Downs (55 defensive snaps | 4 tackles | 0 TFL | 0 sacks | 0 INT | 0 passes defended | 0 QB hits | 0 pressures) Downs offered some resistance against the run and was credited with two run stops, one extremely impressive one on fourth down on the goal line. His coverage was less encouraging with all three targets against him completed for 49 yards. His day then ended after he suffered a concussion attempting to tackle Tyler Allgeier on the running back’s fourth-quarter touchdown reception. There were useful contributions near the line, but too much production allowed through the air. Malachi Lawrence (40 defensive snaps | 0 tackles | 0 TFL | 0 sacks | 0 INT | 0 passes defended | 1 QB hit | 2 pressures) Lawrence’s pass rush provided more than his empty tackle column suggests. He produced two pressures on 24 pass-rush snaps and registered a quarterback hit, although he could not turn those opportunities into a sack. Across 40 defensive snaps, Dallas needed more finishing production from its first-round edge defender, especially when it mattered most in the closing portion of the game. He injured his ankle in the game and could miss some time. Jaishawn Barham (16 defensive snaps | 1 tackle | 0 TFL | 0 sacks | 0 INT | 0 passes defended | 0 QB hits ) Barham had a limited role behind Shemar James and DeMarvion Overshown. His coverage results were modestly encouraging allowing one reception for six yards on two targets. However, one tackle and no plays behind the line made this another quiet outing. His small workload limits how much can be concluded about the performance. LT Overton (39 total snaps | 0 tackles | 0 TFL | 0 sacks | 0 INT | 0 passes defended | 0 QB hits | 1 pressure | 1 fumble recovery) Overton delivered the rookie group’s clearest positive when he recovered Bam Knight’s fumble after Overshown forced the ball loose late in the second quarter. Securing that possession mattered. His work elsewhere was quieter, with one pressure on 19 pass-rush snaps and no tackles or sacks. The recovery was valuable, but Dallas still needs more consistent disruption from his defensive opportunities. Camden Brown (10 ST snaps | 0 targets | 0 receptions | 0 receiving yards | 0 TD) Brown’s involvement remained almost entirely on special teams. With just one offensive snap and no targets, there was no meaningful receiving performance to evaluate. Staying involved on game day is a step forward, but his offensive opportunity remains extremely limited.

title: Broncos at Panthers preview: Denver aims to avoid the “trap”
summary: The Denver Broncos are riding high. They’re on the heels of a massive win over the rival Kansas City Chiefs that puts them in first place in the AFC West. The 28-24 win over the Chiefs also puts Denver in the hunt for home-field advantage. Yes, it’s only eight games, but after the gauntlet the […]
full_text: DENVER, COLORADO - NOVEMBER 01: Felix Anudike-Uzomah #91 of the Kansas City Chiefs tackles Jonah Coleman #20 of the Denver Broncos in the fourth quarter of a game at Empower Field At Mile High on November 01, 2026 in Denver, Colorado. (Photo by Matthew Stockman/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Denver Broncos are riding high. They’re on the heels of a massive win over the rival Kansas City Chiefs that puts them in first place in the AFC West. The 28-24 win over the Chiefs also puts Denver in the hunt for home-field advantage. Yes, it’s only eight games, but after the gauntlet the Broncos have faced, sitting at 6-2 and where they are is impressive. Now come the Carolina Panthers, who just got trucked on Thursday Night Football by the Green Bay Packers. As a result, the Panthers fired their defensive coordinator. Since Carolina plays in the NFC South, it leads the division at 3-4 and will be highly motivated to get back on track at home this Sunday. Denver is currently the -3-point road favorite at FanDuel Sportsbook. The total sits at over/under 43.5 points, with a lean toward the over at -118. Offensive Rankings Denver : Thirtieth in total offense (273.0 yards per game), 26th in rushing offense (92.6 YPG), 25th in passing offense (180.4 YPG), 22nd in scoring offense (21.5 points per game). Carolina : Ninth in total offense (363.7 yards per game), 22nd in rushing offense (102.0 YPG), fifth in passing offense (261.7 YPG), ninth in scoring offense (25.4 points per game). Defensive Rankings Denver : Twenty-fifth in total defense (355.3 yards per game), 25th in rushing defense (127.9 YPG), 20th in passing defense (227.4 YPG), 11th in scoring defense (20.6 points per game). Carolina : Twenty-third in total defense (349.6 yards per game), 30th in rushing defense (140.7 YPG), 10th in passing defense (208.9 YPG), 28th in scoring defense (27.6 points per game). Here are the MHR staff’s keys to Sunday’s game. Don’t fall into the “trap” Sean Payton owns the NFC South. Dating back to his New Orleans Saints days, he knows the division and how to beat these teams. However, the Broncos have historically struggled in the early games on the East Coast. On top of that, Denver is coming off a brutal stretch of games and is on the heels of a ginormous win. Not to mention, the bye is after this Sunday’s game. It’s natural to take the foot off the gas and think, “We got this.” In other words, the “trap game.” Don’t fall into that trap. It’s imperative for the Broncos to remain focused on the task at hand. Build on the win over Kansas City with the goal of playing a complete game. — Ian St. Clair Score more points than Carolina My advanced analytics came through once again. For the 6th time this season, the Broncos have scored more points than their opponent and won. Following this trend, if they do that this Sunday against the Panthers, they will improve to 7-2. — Scotty Payne Stop the run Scotty’s analytics are spot on. One of the best ways to ensure his analytics remain proven correct is to limit the Panthers’ ability to run the football. That forces Carolina into a one-dimensional attack and allows the defensive line to eventually pin its ears back and make Bryce Young as uncomfortable as the back of a Volkswagen. — Adam Malnati Keep feeding Jonah Coleman Good things happen when you run the ball effectively. We saw that for the Broncos in their past two victories. Last Sunday, rookie running back Jonah Coleman was solid on the ground for the Denver. He certainly deserves the majority of carries moving forward. The Panthers have one of the worst run defenses in the league and give up nearly 5 yards per carry. Why not pound the ball on the ground and keep giving Coleman a chance to prove himself even more? It seems like a great opportunity to see him shine. — Christopher Hart What are your keys to Sunday’s game?
author: Ian St. Clair

title: Statistical dive into Denver Broncos record-tying 15th straight win in one-score games
summary: The Denver Broncos have now won 15 straight regular season games that were decided by one-score (8 or fewer points). This ties the 2007-2008 Peyton Manning-led Colts. Since the start of the 2025 season the Broncos are 16 and 2 in one-score games in the regular season (1-1 in the post-season). This is a big […]
full_text: The Denver Broncos have now won 15 straight regular season games that were decided by one-score (8 or fewer points). This ties the 2007-2008 Peyton Manning-led Colts. Since the start of the 2025 season the Broncos are 16 and 2 in one-score games in the regular season (1-1 in the post-season). This is a big change from 2024 when the Broncos were 1-6 in one-score games. The positive change for the Broncos in being able to win one-score games has coincided with Chiefs forgetting how to win one-score games. They were 11-0 in one-score games in 2024 and they have gone 3-10 since. As good as the Broncos have been in one-score games since the start of the 2025 regular season, the 49ers have had the same winning percentage, 0.889, just in half the games. They are 8-1. The two worst teams are the Chiefs and the Titans. Both have a 0.231 win percentage. Both in 13 games (3-10). Many of these one-score games have involved Bo Nix leading a fourth quarter comeback (4QC) and a game-winning drive (GWD). Both can only occur in the 4th quarter or overtime and can only happen in a win. If the QB leads a drive to take the lead and then the defense allows a GWD by the opposing QB, the Bronco QB does not get either. Bo Nix has now started 42 NFL games and has lead 12 4QC and 15 GWD. Those are the highest values for any QB at this point in his career in NFL history. Comparing Bo Nix to some other notable QBs at this same point (roughly) in their careers. pic.twitter.com/Nwh2pHX6i0 — Joe Mahoney (@ndjomo76) November 2, 2026 The only QBs who are close is in 4QC are Tom Brady and Justin Herbert. Both have 10 in the first 3 starting seasons. Dak Prescott is the only one who is close in GWD. He had 14 in his first 48 starts (first 3 seasons). Tom Brady is the career leaded in 4QC with 46. He did that in 333 career starts. Bo has 12 in 42. Brady had one every 7.24 starts in his career. Bo has one every 3.50 starts. Brady also has the most GWD in his career with 58. He had one GWD every 5.74 starts. Nix has one every 2.80 starts. Bo’s numbers are best in history (min 32 GS) for both 4QC and GWD. Now some context, it takes a special set of circumstances to get either a 4QC or a GWD. There is some luck involved. The 3 and out drive for the FG after the interception in OT against the Seahawks gained 8 yards. But Bo Nix still got a GWD for that drive. That was luck and good, good defense. So a QB needs to be playing for a team with a good defense to get either. Tom Brady had this early in his career as Belicheat almost always had good to great defenses. QBs also need to be on a team with decent offense: good enough to keep the game at least close, but not good enough to win in blow-outs. By the same token, if the defense is inconsistent, the QB might be on the wrong side of blow-out losses. If the Bronco offense ever figures things out (they had four 3-and-outs last game), the opportunities for these two stats should go away because the Broncos will be playing with leads. That is what the Bronco defense is designed to be at its best – rushing the passer and defending against the pass with a lead. That didn’t work too well at the end of the last game, but when both starting safeties are out, it changes things. For historical context, as a rookie Nix had 3 4QC and 3 GWD. Last season he had 5 and 7. He already has 4 and 5 this season. However, the 5 GWD is not the most in the NFL. Somehow PFR is showing the Browns with 6 GWD when they only have 5 wins. That makes no sense until you realize that they credited two different QBs with a GWD (Shedeur Sanders and Deshaun Watson) for the same game. I have never seen that before. The Broncos are currently 22nd in scoring at 21.5 ppg with a full 8 weeks of the season completed. The rushing offense is tied for 25th at 3.78 yards per carry (tied with Dallas). Although part of that is a result of just how ineffective JK Dobbins has been so far this season as a runner. His 3.26 yards per touch is tied for 3rd worst among RBs with 35 or more carries. Only Kendre Miller and Dameon Pierce have been worse this season. Contrast that with RJ Harvey and Jonah Coleman who (aided by long catches) are near the top of the league in yards per touch for RBs. Comparing RBs Yds/Touch – for the Broncos it doesn't get much clearer as to who should be getting the ball. pic.twitter.com/geR6f6monu — Joe Mahoney (@ndjomo76) November 2, 2026 The Broncos converted 2 of 11 third downs against the Chiefs and now sit at dead last in the NFL on 3rd down conversion rate at 29.7 percent. The Commanders are second worst at 31.9%. The Bengals have been the best so far this season at 52.9 percent. The 49ers at 50.0 percent exactly are second. Thankfully the Broncos have been able to convert on 5 of 6 4th downs, but 3rd down efficiency needs to improve or this team won’t make the playoffs. Jeremy Crawshaw is 4th in net yards per punt and he is tied for the league lead in punts downed inside the 10 at 10 (tied with Michael Dickson). He is also leading the league in “Inside the 10” points (trademarked) with 45. See below. For this a punter gets one point for a punt downed at 10, 2 for one downed at the 9, etc. While Crawshaw has yet to get one downed at the one or two this season, he has 10 of his 41 punts downed at or inside the 10. 41 punts is tied for most in the league (with the Eagles’ punter). The sack total for the defense sits at 23 after 8 games. They are 3 behind the league leading Steelers, but Kermit has always been hard to sack, so getting him twice last game is admirable. The Lions and Vikings are also ahead of the Broncos with 24 and 25 and they both have only played 7 games. The Bronco defense is looking to become the first team in NFL history to lead the NFL in sacks for three straight seasons.

title: Broncos News: Who needs picks when your offense is lacking?
summary: Every year that passes, I like having draft picks more and more. I fully understand that they are all essentially a roll of the dice, but I’d rather have a bunch of chances at improving the team than not. In general, I’m not normally about trading picks mid-season. I think this is the perfect time […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - SEPTEMBER 27: Breece Hall #20 of the New York Jets plays against the Detroit Lions at Ford Field on September 27, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Gregory Shamus/Getty Images) | Getty Images Every year that passes, I like having draft picks more and more. I fully understand that they are all essentially a roll of the dice, but I’d rather have a bunch of chances at improving the team than not. In general, I’m not normally about trading picks mid-season. I think this is the perfect time and place to let those picks fly. We just went through the wringer of our schedule where we easily could have had 6 losses at this point instead of 6 wins. This team is trending up, and the offense needs help. A play-making running back makes way too much sense. This team legitimately has deep playoff run potential. Shove those chips in the middle on this team this year. Jonathan Taylor may cost a 2nd, 3rd, and 5th. Breece Hall may be slightly less. Tony Pollard could sneak into the picture for the Broncos. Honestly, I don’t care which one. Any of them will help this team finish the season strong. This doesn’t mean I’m not a believer in Jonah Coleman. I absolutely love Coleman. Right now we’re one injury away from asking Bo Nix to throw 40+ passes a game. I think shoring up the room with an infusion of talent makes way too much. Most of the fans I interact with are chomping at the bit for a trade. I’d love to hear from you all in the comments whether you’re for or against a trade. Do you value the picks over a veteran back? title: NFL Power Rankings for Week 9: Are they beginning to Bo-lieve?
summary: Four straight wins and sitting in the number two seed in the AFC. That’s where the Denver Broncos are heading into Week 9, which means the national media has to start paying attention and most did in their power rankings this week. If I had to be honest with where each team is at in […]
full_text: DENVER, CO - NOVEMBER 1: Jonah Coleman #20 of the Denver Broncos runs with the football during the second quarter against the Kansas City Chiefs at Empower Field at Mile High on November 1, 2026 in Denver, Colorado. (Photo by Justin Edmonds/Getty Images) | Getty Images Four straight wins and sitting in the number two seed in the AFC. That’s where the Denver Broncos are heading into Week 9, which means the national media has to start paying attention and most did in their power rankings this week. If I had to be honest with where each team is at in the NFL, I would probably put the Broncos somewhere around 4th and 5th right now. I think the Buffalo Bills, San Francisco 49ers, Chicago Bears are all playing more complete football right now. From there, you could split hairs between our Broncos and teams like the Detroit Lions and Jacksonville Jaguars. If Denver keeps winning, however, they’ll continue be harder and harder to ignore. The media will be forced to start bo-lieving in this football team team. Here’s how the Broncos are doing in this week’s power rankings around the web: NFL.com – 6th Denver recorded a huge win over the Chiefs with a frantic fourth-quarter comeback that should give Broncos fans hope the team can climb out of its offensive struggles before long. There were signs that it’s starting to turn for the better: Bo Nix pushed the ball downfield successfully a few times, Jonah Coleman broke out in a fashion that usually leads to an increase in importance, and the defense once again finished the job. If the Broncos can follow this trajectory, they’ll round into top form by December — and thanks to Sunday’s triumph, they’ll be right in the thick of the race for the AFC West crown. NBC Sports – 4th They out-chiefed the Chiefs. ESPN – 4th The Broncos acquired Hall of Famer Gary Zimmerman just before the start of the 1993 regular season, so the wayback machine had to be fired up to get to the best in-season trade. The Broncos acquired Moses from the Bills via a one-for-one swap for Dwight Harrison. Moses played nine full seasons for the Broncos after the 1972 season, averaging at least 17 yards a catch in eight of those years and having 44 total touchdown catches. He is in the team’s Ring of Fame and played on the franchise’s first Super Bowl team in 1977. Yahoo Sports – 9th The idea that the Broncos could make a big move for Jonathan Taylor is dubious only because Sean Payton’s history of using committees at running back without a standout workhorse. And the team has to be intrigued by rookie Jonah Coleman, who has played well and came up with two big plays to give Denver the lead in a huge win over the Chiefs on Sunday. Perhaps Taylor or another big-time back could solve some issues on the offense. Or maybe it’s a receiver or a tight end, after the Evan Engram signing in 2025 has been a dud. Even some depth on the offensive line isn’t a bad idea. The Broncos are set on defense, so their focus can be how to add an impact piece to an inconsistent offense. USA Today – 3rd If they don’t have your respect yet, then how about this nugget – they’ve won five consecutive home games against former league MVPs. This 6-2 squad has also survived the most brutal stretch of its schedule and is set up to coast to another AFC West crown if it can take care of business. Fox Sports – 2nd I’ve still got my worries about Bo Nix. At some point, the Broncos are going to need a lot more from him. But he’s doing enough right now, especially for a team that can’t run the ball effectively. He makes enough big plays — though usually they are short passes that someone turns into a big play — and doesn’t make many big mistakes. In fact, he’s gone five straight games without an interception. With a coach like Sean Payton and a defense playing as well as the Broncos’ is, that’s more than enough. For now. CBS Sports – 5th They have a lot of late-game magic to win games. That formula has worked for this team, but for how long? NY Times – 3rd The rookie running back led Denver in rushing (41) and receiving (63) yards on Sunday and is a delight to watch, but the hot rumor coming out of this game was that the Broncos might be in the Jonathan Taylor trade discussions. If that comes to fruition, the offense will be better, but we’ll miss Coleman. What do you think of these power rankings? Share in the comments section below!

title: Broncos vs. Chiefs: The No Bull Review
summary: Hear me out, Broncos Country. There are a lot of you out there who need to lock in. Eat your veggies, take your vitamins, get some cardio regularly, and don’t forget to mix in some strength resistance training. Especially those of you who, like me, have been watching this team for more than a couple […]
full_text: DENVER, COLORADO - NOVEMBER 01: Alex Singleton #49 of the Denver Broncos celebrates after his team's 28-24 win against the Kansas City Chiefs at Empower Field At Mile High on November 01, 2026 in Denver, Colorado. (Photo by Matthew Stockman/Getty Images) | Getty Images Hear me out, Broncos Country. There are a lot of you out there who need to lock in. Eat your veggies, take your vitamins, get some cardio regularly, and don’t forget to mix in some strength resistance training. Especially those of you who, like me, have been watching this team for more than a couple of decades. The heart attack Broncos are alive and well. Mile High Magic lives forever. Don’t you dare for one second EVER give up on this team. From Sean Payton to Bo Nix to Nik Bonitto to the ball boy, this team is built to win come hell or high water. They have absolutely no give-up in them. They are the Rocky Balboa of the NFL, and the Kansas City Chiefs just got knocked the hell out. Offense I’m done getting frustrated with this offense, in all honesty. They had me pulling out my hair for 3 quarters. Constant inability to convert 3rd downs. Giving carries to the objectively worst running back on the team and trotting him out as the starter. Wide receivers who are incapable of getting separation. Tight ends who were paid big bucks to come catch passes and can’t even snag one catch. My current theory about their ineptness is that Nix is playing it safe to avoid getting buried due to turnovers. He isn’t forcing contested catches unless he has to, for the most part. They believe in their defense to a fault and are very comfortable chipping away until they have to go guns blazing at the end of the game. Quarterbacks Bo Nix is my quarterback. I love this guy. The dude can make every throw (whether or not he tries to early in the game). He’s got the most frigid of fluids running in his veins when it gets down to crunch time. He’s not without faults worth talking about, though. That attempt to throw to Trautman backwards was the most ghastly thing I’ve seen from the Broncos offensive backfield since a Paxton Lynch dab. He also threw a pass into the dirt on 3rd and 10 when Waddle was streaking with plenty of separation from the chaser and the safety. He’s also far too timid on 3rd down, throwing short of the sticks. He’s got to work with Payton on how to have reads further down the field that he’s comfortable with at 6, 8, and 10-12 yard depths. The other thing for him to improve on is navigating throwing windows. He had far too many tipped passes this game, and it cost the team big time on 3rd down. But man, you have to love that sprinkling of amazing we get to see from him every game. His throw down the sideline to Sutton was perfection. His ability to wait for plays to develop and deliver the ball to open runners gave us big gains by Coleman, Waddle, and Trautman. Line The only nit to pick with the line really from this game is training them up on driving into their defenders or chopping their arms when they raise them to bat down passes. I thought the line played very well in this game. Their run blocking has been improving every week. Many of our successful throws were due in large part to excellent blocking up front, giving Nix time to get the ball out. Running Backs Jonah Coleman is the truth. He’s a better back than anyone else we have on the roster and needs to take over the starting role immediately. This young man had 11 runs for 41 yards and a touchdown and 4 catches for 63 yards. He’s a power runner who has excellent vision and burst to go with it. JK Dobbins needs to stop getting a starting role just because he’s a veteran. He certainly does have a run here or there that looks good. The problem is that he gets stuffed for very little gain far too often. He deserved getting benched after losing 8 yards on a run play. This offense is far too fragile for him to try playing Barry Sanders on his Lance Ball skillset. Receivers Courtland Sutton may be a bit long in the tooth. He may have lost a step. He put in some great work this week against the Chiefs. Sutton showed supreme focus to catch his long pass over the middle that was tipped by the defender. His sideline go doesn’t look like much on film, but that was a timing route that required him to be in stride between defenders. Sutton caught all 4 of his targets for 53 yards and, as always, had some great blocks in the run game that don’t show up on the stat sheet. Jaylen Waddle bailed out an awful offensive start after the 8-yard loss by Dobbins by getting a 35-yard pass deep down the middle of the field. He scored his touchdown on a tricky little trips play that had him stutter while Franklin ran upfield in front of him to spring him open for an easy score. He also nailed the 2-point conversion on a deep crossing route behind that caught the deep defender flat-footed. If you look at the stat sheet, Troy Franklin shouldn’t really be mentioned with 1 of 3 catches for 3 yards. He got us an 18-yard pass interference call, though, and that counts for something in my eyes. Keep grinding, Troy! Adam Trautman hasn’t gotten as many opportunities this year, but he showed up in this game. He had a big catch downfield for 22 yards after his defender slipped in the 4th quarter and ended the game with 2 catches for 30 yards. Nate Adkins snuck out into the flat for a TD catch on 4th and goal. I love what Adkins brings to the game. He’s strong as hell as a blocker and is a shifty route runner for a big guy. Defense What a gutsy performance from this defense. While they had both their starting corners return for this game, they lost their last standing starting safety when Brandon Jones left the game early. That left them with Taylor Rapp, Devon Key, and JL Skinner holding down the fort at safety. It was a rough go, and Patrick Mahomes took full advantage of the weakness, along with our flaws in coverage from the inside linebacker position. The Chiefs do a great job against Denver with their quick-throw game, as has been their plan for a few years now. They know their line can’t hold up to the pressure of our defense, which leads Mahomes to get the ball out quickly. The Chiefs scored 24 and honestly should have scored another 6 to seal the game had they not ultra-choked while poor return coverage, poor pass coverage on Kelce, luck, and practically God himself tried to hand them the game. But give credit to Vance Joseph and this defense. Bo Nix gets all the talk about comeback wins over the past few years. But none of those stats go in the record books without this defense, and I know Nix would tell you the exact same thing. This defense is absolutely stacked with guys who answer the bell with ice water in their veins when the game is on the line. I honestly feel like both Payton and Joseph have a specialty in coaching players on how to execute no matter what. This team knows how to put bad plays behind them and dial in for the next one. We got big plays all over on this defense that found a way to close out this game and get us back on top of the AFC West. Front 7 Malcolm Roach is a damned playmaker in the trenches, and I don’t think we give him enough credit for how consistent he is up front. While he may have been brought in to stop the run originally, he’s learned how to shed blocks and crash down to get sacks, which we all saw in the last play of the game. He also had a batted pass, tackle for loss, and a quarterback hit in this game to go along with his game-winning sack. Speaking of that sack, let’s give a quick shout-out to Jonathan Cooper, who is the main reason that sack happened. His rush off the edge was great technical work. He bull-rushed the RT back, stepped into him to make it seem like he was stopped, and then burst out to the left to get around him and force Mahomes upfield into the sack. Alex Singleton is still playing his ass off out there. He got smoked for a touchdown early (any play with him in man coverage on a back is a bad…

Mandatory Credit: David Reginek-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Detroit Lions linebacker Jack Campbell offered an update on Wednesday on his progress via an official statement from the team. It means more to us than words can express. I’m incredibly encouraged by the progress I’ve made in such a short period of time. I have full movement in my lower body, and I’m continuing to make progress with movement in my upper body. I know there’s still work ahead, but I remain very optimistic. I’m taking things one day at a time, staying positive, and focusing on getting better. My faith in God has never been stronger. I know He has a plan for me, and I trust in that plan. I know there may be challenges ahead, but with my faith, my family, and so many people in my corner, I know we’ll get through this. I especially want to thank the athletic trainers and medical personnel who responded and cared for me on the field. I know those were difficult moments, and I’m incredibly grateful for the professionalism, compassion, and care you showed me. The way you handled everything and looked after me when I needed it most is something I’ll never forget. From the bottom of my heart, thank you. I also can’t say enough about the incredible care I’ve received from the medical team at Henry Ford Hospital and the Detroit Lions medical staff. They’ve been amazing to me and my family throughout this process, and I’m truly grateful for everything they’ve done. To my teammates, coaches, and everyone in the Lions organization, I want you to know how much I love and appreciate you. This team is a family to me, and the way everyone has been there for me means everything. I’m proud to be a Detroit Lion and couldn’t ask to be surrounded by a better group of people. One thing I’ve learned about Detroit is that this city is built on toughness, resilience, and grit. That’s exactly how I’m going to approach this challenge. Please continue to keep me and my family in your prayers. We feel the love, and I can’t thank everyone enough. God is good. My faith is strong. Jack Campbell

title: 5 Lions vs. Dolphins thoughts after watching Miami’s loss to Patriots
summary: To turn the page from Week 8 to Week 9, I spent some time early this week watching the Miami Dolphins’ most recent game to see what’s in store for the Detroit Lions. Here are my five Lions vs. Dolphins thoughts after watching Miami’s 24-19 loss to the New England Patriots. Note: It’s worth mentioning […]
full_text: Nov 1, 2026; Miami Gardens, Florida, USA; Miami Dolphins quarterback Malik Willis (2) drops back to throw a pass during the first quarter against the New England Patriots at Hard Rock Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Rich Storry-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect To turn the page from Week 8 to Week 9, I spent some time early this week watching the Miami Dolphins’ most recent game to see what’s in store for the Detroit Lions. Here are my five Lions vs. Dolphins thoughts after watching Miami’s 24-19 loss to the New England Patriots. Note: It’s worth mentioning that it was a very rainy day in Miami, particularly at the start and end of the game. Malik Willis holds onto the ball for a loooooong time There could be a lot of reasons for it, but Willis holds onto the ball way too long in the pocket. Per NFL Pro, Willis’ 3.05 average seconds to throw is third-longest in the league. Is it taking Willis too long to go through his progressions, is he too hesitant to trust his eyes, or is his young receiving corps just not getting open? It’s hard to say from my vantage point, but it certainly is an opportunity for the Lions to get home against Willis. Thus far, Willis has taken 21 sacks—the seventh most in the NFL—and the Dolphins have the second-highest sack rate in the NFL (10.3%). The Patriots got to Willis five times in the first half, before backing down a little in the second. This could be a big Tyleik Williams game Miami had an extremely hard time stopping Patriots nose tackle Cory Durden in this game. He set career highs in pressure (three), quarterback hits (three), and sacks (1.5). Prior to this game, Durden had never recorded a sack and only had two quarterback hits since starting his NFL career, coincidentally in Detroit, in 2023. Miami is particularly vulnerable on the right side of the line, where second-year right guard Jonah Savaiinaea is the 66th (out of 75) PFF-graded guard (47.9), and right tackle Austin Jackson is the lowest-graded tackle in football (44.6). Williams is having a strong start to his second season, remaining a force in the run game (Dolphins rank 21st in EPA/rush, 24th in success rate) while growing as a pass rusher. Obviously, look out for Alim McNeill, too, who is currently only behind Broncos defensive tackle Zach Allen in PFF pressures from interior defenders (31). The Lions’ run game should find success Last week, the Lions found success pounding the rock right up the middle of the Vikings’ defense. That should be the game plan once again against the Dolphins. Rhamondre Stevenson toughed out 82 yards on 19 carries (4.3 YPC), as the Patriots produced a 45.2% success rate on the ground—ninth-highest of all Week 8 performances. For the year, Miami ranks 21st in EPA/rush allowed and 30th in success rate (43.9%). So they aren’t giving up a ton of explosive plays on the ground, but you can certainly grind them down. I would not be surprised to see another solid workload from Sione Vaki. But Miami does have some dudes on defense Miami’s defense as a whole won’t likely be up for the task against the Lions’ high-flying offense. The Dolphins rank 24th in points per game allowed (25.9) and 25th in yards per play allowed. However, there are a couple of players who are playing well and capable of game-changing plays. The first is edge rusher Josh Uche. While Uche only has two sacks this year (one against the Patriots), he’s produced PFF’s ninth-highest run defense grade among edge defenders (76.0). On the next level, rookie linebacker Jacob Rodriguez flashed against the Patriots. He had a teach-tape punchout and was second on the team with eight tackles. His rookie season has seen some ups and downs, but don’t be surprised if he makes a big play or two against the Lions. The game wasn’t as close as the score While the Dolphins only lost by five and they held a 10-point lead at halftime, this game did not feel like it was truly competitive between the teams. For one, the Patriots made a ton of mistakes in the first half. They fumbled inside their own red zone, missed a 40-yard field goal, and had a ton of untimely penalties (seven in total). In the second half, the Patriots dropped an easy interception, and they had a game-clinching pick erased by an away-from-the-play offsides penalty. And the Dolphins only made it close thanks to a prevent-defense touchdown with just over two minutes, because a Patriots defender fell down for an easy 35-yard touchdown. On a per play basis, the Patriots produced more yards per play (5.3 vs. 4.5), and had a much higher success rate (49.1% vs. 43.8%). If you take away garbage-time stats, the difference is even bigger in success rate (52.9% vs. 39.3%). Did we really get beat that bad? Comparing offensive success rates for NFL games in Week 8: pic.twitter.com/i4tQhlOtNa — Sam Hoppen (@SamHoppen) November 2, 2026 If the Lions can avoid making self-inflicted mistakes, they should be able to win comfortably, despite the fact that Miami has kept each of their last four games within a touchdown.

title: Mailbag: Could the Detroit Lions target a linebacker at NFL trade deadline?
summary: The NFL trade deadline is now less than a week away. If teams want to add talent via a trade, it must happen by 4 p.m. ET on Tuesday, November 10. After that, the only talent acquisition can come via free agency or waivers. The Detroit Lions’ interest in a cornerback is no secret. The […]
full_text: Oct 18, 2026; Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, USA; Philadelphia Eagles linebacker Zack Baun (53) in action against the Carolina Panthers Lincoln Financial Field. Mandatory Credit: Bill Streicher-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The NFL trade deadline is now less than a week away. If teams want to add talent via a trade, it must happen by 4 p.m. ET on Tuesday, November 10. After that, the only talent acquisition can come via free agency or waivers. The Detroit Lions’ interest in a cornerback is no secret. The team openly admitted they were involved in talks for Joey Porter Jr., although the Dallas Cowboys apparently outbid them. Cornerback sure seems like it’s still on the table, but could Detroit’s strategy shift after losing several players to injury on Sunday against the Minnesota Vikings? With rookie Jimmy Rolder out for the year and All-Pro linebacker Jack Campbell out indefinitely with a neck injury, suddenly linebacker seems like a pretty serious need. This week, the Lions have backfilled their depth chart with special teams pieces in KJ Britt and (reportedly) Owen Pappoe. But can they trust players like Derrick Barnes, Malcolm Rodriguez, and Trevor Nowaske to hold starting roles? Or do they need to make an aggressive move to raise the ceiling of the room and fortify the middle of the field? On this week’s Midweek Mailbag podcast, we discuss the Lions’ options at the NFL trade deadline, and outline a couple of names we’d like to see the Lions consider. At the top of that list is undoubtedly Eagles linebacker Zack Baun. The 29-year-old All-Pro linebacker is on a very manageable contract for Detroit (salaries of $1.215M, $1.345M, and $1.39M from 2026-28, plus a $14 million option bonus in 2027). It makes a little less sense for the Eagles (over $16M in dead cap), but if the Lions could make it worth it with draft compensation, they could get a deal done. And with the Eagles 2-6—losers of six straight—forced to play Tanner McKee at quarterback, it may make sense to acquire as much draft captial as possible. Other linebacker options discussed: Buccaneers’ Alex Anzalone and Dolphins’ Jordyn Brooks. We also talk about whether the Lions’ strategy should change considering how competitive the NFC North is this year. Does it make sense to get in an arms race with the Chicago Bears after their acquisition of Jeffrey Simmons? Or is that actually a reason to pull back this year and wait for a time in which things feel more open? And we talk about a lot of topics beyond the trade deadline, including: How the Lions’ “sidecar” formation was the perfect antidote to Brian Flores Why didn’t Ennis Rakestraw play much vs. Minnesota? What’s with the Lions’ short-yardage issues? Is it actually better to have the 5th or 6th seed in the NFC rather than the No. 2 seed? Should the Lions consider extending Christian Mahogany this offseason? How many carries for Sione Vaki is the sweet spot? Check out the show below, or find us on your favorite podcasting platform by searching “Pride of Detroit.” As always, you can also catch the podcast on our YouTube page and Twitch channel . On this week’s show, we went through some more Movember shenanigans, including eating something called earthworm jerky. All available on the video portion only.

title: Report: Detroit Lions to sign speedy linebacker to practice squad
summary: It appears the Detroit Lions will be adding even more linebacker depth to the team in the aftermath of serious injuries to Jack Campbell and Jimmy Rolder. In addition to reportedly signing KJ Britt from the Patriots’ practice squad, the Lions will also be signing linebacker Owen Pappoe (physical pending), according to a report from […]
full_text: Aug 22, 2026; Glendale, Arizona, USA; Arizona Cardinals linebacker Owen Pappoe (44) tackles Dallas Cowboys tight end Zack Kuntz (47)during the second half at State Farm Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Joe Camporeale-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect It appears the Detroit Lions will be adding even more linebacker depth to the team in the aftermath of serious injuries to Jack Campbell and Jimmy Rolder. In addition to reportedly signing KJ Britt from the Patriots’ practice squad, the Lions will also be signing linebacker Owen Pappoe (physical pending), according to a report from CBS Sports. Pappoe, who visited the Lions on Tuesday per the transaction wire, was a third-round pick of the Arizona Cardinals in 2023. Over the next three years, Pappoe played in nearly every game for Arizona (49 total), mostly on special teams—945 snaps on teams, 341 on defense. Pappoe was waived by the Cardinals as part of their roster cuts this year, but he was claimed by the Tennessee Titans the next day. He appeared in one game before the Titans released him a month ago. Pappoe gives the Lions extra depth on special teams, and he also has an intriguing athletic profile. Good lord https://t.co/LUawCoD6JJ pic.twitter.com/06trqaV1R3 — John Whiticar (@Whiticar) November 3, 2026 It will be interesting to see how the Lions’ linebacker room shakes out with Rolder out of the year and Campbell out indefinitely. On Monday, Lions coach Dan Campbell seemed to express confidence in three linebackers who will likely become the team’s starters: Derrick Barnes, Malcolm Rodriguez, and Trevor Nowaske. “Luckily we have some depth in there with Rodrigo and Nowaske and Barnes,” Campbell said. “Those three guys and Amen (Ogbongbemiga)’s been up for us, which is good. And then we have got (LB Joe) Bachie ready to roll.” Detroit has yet to make any of their new linebacker signings official, and there will be some roster maneuvering necessary. On Tuesday, they put Rolder on injured reserve and waived safety Bishop Fitzgerald , creating two spots on the 53-man roster. Britt will likely take up one of those spots, but the Lions will also have to create a spot on the practice squad for Pappoe. Therefore, it seems likely that Detroit will promote a player from the practice squad to fill the 53-man vacancy and create the spot for Pappoe. Seven-year veteran linebacker Joe Bachie is the most obvious choice, but we’ll have to wait until later Wednesday, when the Lions are likely to make these moves official.

title: Detroit Lions scouting report: Miami Dolphins searching for answers
summary: After back-to-back stressful divisional victories at home, the Detroit Lions get a bit of a break and head down to Florida to take on the Miami Dolphins. Detroit is on a three-game winning streak, and we’ve seen the defense take a step in the right direction to complement this offense. The Lions are finding their […]
full_text: MIAMI GARDENS, FLORIDA - NOVEMBER 01: Malik Willis #2 of the Miami Dolphins throws a pass against the New England Patriots during the first half of the game at Hard Rock Stadium on November 01, 2026 in Miami Gardens, Florida. (Photo by Megan Briggs/Getty Images) | Getty Images After back-to-back stressful divisional victories at home, the Detroit Lions get a bit of a break and head down to Florida to take on the Miami Dolphins. Detroit is on a three-game winning streak, and we’ve seen the defense take a step in the right direction to complement this offense. The Lions are finding their groove, it seems, and taking on a struggling team could be big for them. Miami is coming off another loss and aiming higher and higher at getting the top pick in the 2027 NFL Draft. The team hasn’t been strong on either side of the ball; the offense is missing playmakers because of injuries or skill set, and while the defense has talent, it hasn’t had enough impact on the field. Let’s take a deep look at the Dolphins’ season so far as they head into Week 9. Miami Dolphins 2026 season thus far (1-6) Week 1: Lost to Las Vegas Raiders 27-13 Week 2: Lost to San Francisco 49ers 35-13 Week 3: Lost to Kansas City Chiefs 24-10 Week 4: Lost to Minnesota Vikings 15-10 Week 5: Lost to Cincinnati Bengals 31-24 Week 6: BYE Week 7: Defeated New York Jets 28-25 Week 8: Lost to New England Patriots 24-19 Offensive stats: The offense has been the roughest part of the Dolphins team this season. Newly signed quarterback Malik Willis was given the keys to the starting job, but the supporting cast isn’t the same as it was in Green Bay. He’s thrown for six touchdowns, five interceptions, and is averaging 181.1 yards per game. His legs have helped a lot, as he’s averaging 6.3 yards per carry, amassing 225 yards, and three touchdowns. When he isn’t running the ball, second-year running back Ollie Gordon is. Gordon took over for De’Von Achane after Achane tore his ACL in Week 3, ending his season. Gordon is averaging 4.5 yards per carry, with 408 yards and a team-high four rushing touchdowns, sparking an offense that desperately needs help. Willis has struggled to pass as well; his top wide receiver, Malik Washington, has 31 catches for 329 yards, and tight end Greg Dulcich has 22 catches for 256 yards. Receivers Caleb Douglas and Kevin Coleman have found the end zone most often among the group, combining for four touchdowns (two each) with 21 catches for 308 yards. Willis’ offensive line has also struggled to give him time to throw. According to PFF, the line has the second-lowest pass-blocking grade (53.6). Willis has been sacked 21 times this season, the seventh-highest in the NFL. Run blocking is better, but not by much, ranking 27th with a 55.9 grade. Miami has had to rely on the ground game to stay alive, as Willis just doesn’t have the time or the weapons in the passing attack to make teams nervous. Defensive stats: On defense, there isn’t much to say on the positive side. While they aren’t the worst in the league, they’re near the lower end in a few areas. The Dolphins are tied for the fewest sacks in the NFL with nine, led by EDGE Chop Robinson’s four. The secondary has been struggling as well, with rookie safety Michael Taaffe leading the team with two interceptions. The Dolphins have allowed the highest completion percentage in the NFL (76.9 percent) and are tied for second-most 40+ yard passing plays with eight, according to Next Gen Stats. Once again, a safety leads the way in pass deflections with three by Dante Trader, as this unit can’t seem to get their hands on the ball often. While the secondary is struggling to make plays, the run defense hasn’t been up to par for the Dolphins either, ranked 31st by PFF with a grade of 51. They’ve allowed only three rushing plays of over 20 yards, the longest being 27, but could still improve by slowing down opposing offenses on the ground. Miami is ranked 26th in tackling with a grade of 48.2 and has 47 missed tackles this season, the eighth most in the league, per PFF. Injury notes Key players ruled out : RB De’Von Achane (IR) Key players to monitor : G/T Kadyn Proctor (concussion) When it comes to injuries, the Dolphins’ only major star who’s injured is Achane. Luckily for Miami, they have some good depth at the position. Rookie offensive lineman Kadyn Proctor is in concussion protocol, as he’s the only other key player currently dealing with a notable injury. Biggest strength: Running Backs When Achane went down, it looked like this struggling offense was about to take a giant step back. Not so fast, my friend, as Gordon would say. He’s helped give the ground game some life. While Achane never found the end zone this season, Gordon surged ahead of Willis in rushing touchdowns in his three starts. He’s become another solid running back for this team, and when Achane returns in 2027, this duo will be another stellar one-two punch. One of the best drives of the season for the Dolphins offense ends up in a TD from Ollie Gordon. 12-10 Vikings. pic.twitter.com/fTLQEN5sCu — Jake (@FinsCentral) October 4, 2026 Miami doesn’t have weapons in the passing game, and Willis is the only strength there. Willis also likes to run the ball, but he can’t do it all, and having Gordon with him gives this offense a better chance for success. If the running game struggles, this offense will collapse. For now, though, they are what is keeping them in these games offensively. Biggest weakness: Defense While the offense has started to figure some things out over the past three weeks, the defense is still struggling. It doesn’t matter if it’s on the ground or through the air; teams are having their way. Is it the worst defense in the NFL? No, but it’s in the bottom tier, and there aren’t many signs it’s heading in the right direction. They have created six turnovers this season, tied for the third-fewest in the NFL according to ESPN. Their run defense is a step above their passing defense, but against the Lions this week, that secondary will need to play the best game of their lives. Detroit’s offense will be one of the best offenses they’ve faced this year. They put up a fight with the Cincinnati Bengals and the Kansas City Chiefs, so the effort is there, but it will need to be better than those two matchups. The defense has very few playmakers on their side of the ball too, as Robinson is arguably one of the best players on this team. Former first-round pick defensive tackle Kenneth Grant hasn’t lived up to the hype, and the team can’t afford its top-end players to flail out. The best way this defense can improve is by forcing turnovers and keeping the field short so the offense has a better chance to put up points. Key matchup: Lions run defense vs. Dolphins run offense I’m not worried about this Lions offense putting up points against this Dolphins’ lackluster defense. The Lions defense has been inconsistent this season, especially against the run. While the secondary has garnered a lot of attention, rightfully so, the run defense hasn’t been quite up to the standard the team likes to be at. The Dolphins’ passing attack doesn’t scare me, even with the Lions’ secondary being their weakest link. Detroit lost a few players who can help stop the run against the Vikings—linebacker Jack Campbell is a big help in run defense, and fellow linebacker Jimmy Rolder was put in IR —leaving potential holes at the position. Co-sack leader D.J. Wonnum and safety Brian Branch left the game with concussions after they collided. While Branch helps the secondary, he does a solid job filling run fits to limit what running backs do at the next level. If Miami can run the ball well against Detroit, this game could be closer than people anticipate. This isn’t just about stopping Gordon; it’s also about containing Willis so he doesn’t damage you with his running ability. The Lions have faced off against quarterbacks who can use their legs, like Buffalo Bills quarterback Josh Allen,…
