title: Tuesday Tape: How close is the Chiefs’ pass rush?
summary: In the Kansas City Chiefs’ most recent loss, a 28-24 defeat to the Denver Broncos, the pass rush may have had its least impactful performance of the year. After the game, we wrote about the Chiefs’ pass rush that generated just two pressures over 34 dropbacks by Broncos quarterback Bo Nix, according to ESPN analytics. […]
full_text: (Photo by Matthew Stockman/Getty Images) | Getty Images In the Kansas City Chiefs ’ most recent loss, a 28-24 defeat to the Denver Broncos , the pass rush may have had its least impactful performance of the year. After the game, we wrote about the Chiefs’ pass rush that generated just two pressures over 34 dropbacks by Broncos quarterback Bo Nix, according to ESPN analytics. That comes roughly two months after Kansas City harassed Nix in a season-opening win with four sacks and two additional quarterback hits. The defense executed the game plan well without pressure through three quarters, but let’s take a closer look at the Chiefs’ pass rush overall from Week 8: Chris Jones rushing from inside When watching the game back, the Chiefs’ rush looked its best when defensive tackle Chris Jones lined up where he should most of the time: inside over the guard in a 3-technique or 4i alignment. On third-and-2 early on, linebacker Drue Tranquill blitzes and occupies the only player that can help right guard Quinn Meinerz on Jones. Getting a one-on-one, Jones flies off the line and through Meinerz’s outside shoulder to quickly enter the pocket. A quick pass negates the win by Jones, who ends up with hands on Nix. Jones lined up in the B-gap on 24 of the 48 plays he was on the field in Denver (50%). He typically lines up there on neutral downs (1st and 2nd down) or third-and-short. Needing four yards to convert this third down, Nix’s dropback is a little more drawn out than the previous third-and-short pass. This time, Jones and defensive end George Karlaftis bull rush the two right-side linemen and force Nix to feel them in the pocket — and Karlaftis finishes the rush by getting a hand on the pass. After the game, Chiefs Communications noted that Karlaftis took sole possession of the NFL lead in batted passes (7). He also earned the team’s only sack of the afternoon, although it came on a drawn-out play action where Denver left a tight end to block him on the back side. One of Jones’ biggest assets as a rusher is his size; he’s hard to see over when a quarterback is trying to scan the field, and his 6-foot-6 frame, even when blocked, can disrupt a dropback from the front of the pocket. When second and third downs get longer, Jones typically moves to line up either over or outside of the offensive tackle. Defensive end Felix Anudike-Uzomah becomes a key rusher from the inside in those scenarios; he blew up one screen pass in Denver by knifing in and getting to Nix quickly from an interior spot. However, I believe Jones is most impactful when rushing from the front of the pocket. Setting up one-on-ones After the game, Jones said the Chiefs needed to “win on one-on-ones.” He mentioned it being a big emphasis. He is included in that, but the pass rushers around him need to take advantage of Jones’s gravity. On this second-and-18, the Chiefs’ pass rush seems to run a stunt that invites Nix to move forward and to the right of the pocket. Jones flies down off the ball and occupies the right guard and center, setting up defensive end Ashton Gillotte to loop around behind him and meet Nix in the open space. However, Gillotte is either late to loop or simply forgot that was his assignment until Jones was in front of him. Suddenly, Nix had a wide-open platform to confidently fire a rocket over the middle. It’s hard to ask much more from the coverage on this one. On this third-and-10, Jones draws heavy attention from the three interior linemen of Denver after rushing over the center. The left guard helps and spins around before coming back to help the fullback — a key to the Broncos’ pass protection against blitzes — on linebacker Nick Bolton, who gets no penetration. However, look at the space Karlaftis gives left tackle Garrett Bolles to work into the pocket. Instead of gearing up for an inside move based on how the line came out, the Chiefs’ lead edge rusher takes himself out of the play by rushing upfield. On the other side, a sloppily executed stunt leaves Gillote and rookie R Mason Thomas useless. This gives Nix a platform to deliver a calm strike to move the chains that he simply misses. As the game wore on, the lack of wins from pass rushers not named Chris Jones became more evident. On this first-down play, up two scores in the fourth quarter, Nix buys himself enough time to eventually find a target over the middle for a huge gain (although Bolton slipped on his way to likely breaking up the pass). Jones draws two blockers, and most notably, Gillotte can’t get past the right tackle, leaving Nix the space to throw. With nose tackle Khyiris Tonga on the field, the team wasn’t built to get after the quarterback, so is it worth criticizing the coaching staff for not using edge rusher R Mason Thomas more in a full-time role once the Chiefs build such a late-game lead? The bottom line Kansas City’s pass rush wasn’t the biggest factor in blowing the game in Denver, but a few more splash plays would have gone a long way in a game the Chiefs led in the second half until the final minutes. One tweak is to keep Jones on the inside at all times when getting after the quarterback and give Thomas more run on the edge; he only played 17 snaps against the Broncos, less than 30% of the snaps. However, the main critique is of the players around Jones. He isn’t making plays himself this season, but he is still drawing a lot of attention; his teammates need to sharpen their pass-rush moves to take advantage of it more often.

title: Numbers Never Lie: 5 Chiefs stats to know from loss to Broncos
summary: Numbers never lie, right? There are so many statistics to parse through during the NFL season that some can be misleading. After each game, it’s a good exercise to review NFL “Next Gen Stats” and “Premium Stats” from Pro Football Focus and find the numbers that paint a picture not only of the game, but […]
full_text: (Photo by Dustin Bradford/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Numbers never lie, right? There are so many statistics to parse through during the NFL season that some can be misleading. After each game, it’s a good exercise to review NFL “Next Gen Stats” and “Premium Stats” from Pro Football Focus and find the numbers that paint a picture not only of the game, but of what to expect from the Kansas City Chiefs moving forward. 1. No Chiefs defender earned more than one QB pressure in Denver Five Chiefs players tied for the team lead in quarterback pressures against the Denver Broncos , according to PFF . All with just one. Defensive end R Mason Thomas Defensive end Ashton Gillotte Defensive end Felix Anudike-Uzomah Defensive end George Karlaftis Nose tackle Khyiris Tonga Karlaftis recorded one sack, but PFF’s metrics show no other hits on quarterback Bo Nix. Chiefs leaders in QB pressure rate through 7 games ( @NextGenStats ) R Mason Thomas (17%) George Karlaftis (12%) FAU (9.6%) Ashton Gillotte (7.5%) Khyiris Tonga (7.1%) Chris Jones (6.7%) Peter Woods (2.2%) — Ron Kopp Jr (@RonOnChiefs) November 2, 2026 The biggest absence on the list is defensive tackle Chris Jones, who has generated pressure at one of the lowest rates among Chiefs defenders this season. In the two losses, Jones recorded just one pressure and no tackles; PFF marked him with two missed tackles against the Seahawks. 2. Chiefs wideouts average 5 yards per target against Broncos On 17 passes thrown their way and 13 completions, Chiefs wideouts averaged just 5.2 yards per target against the Broncos, even with No. 1 receiver Rashee Rice (7 catches for 53 yards) back in the lineup. Over the last two weeks, Chiefs wideouts have averaged just 4.5 yards per pass. In the Week 1 beatdown of the Broncos, Chiefs wideouts gained just 37 yards on 10 targets. In the 3 games since Tyquan's injury, Chiefs WRs not named Rashee Rice have a combined stat line of 36 targets 24 catches (67% catch rate) 213 yards (8.9 ypc) No TDs Long completion of 23 yards — Ron Kopp Jr (@RonOnChiefs) November 2, 2026 As defenses have seen more tape on Kansas City’s offense this season, the receivers have become more necessary to maintain a rhythm and finish drives. Many of the unit’s shortcomings recently have fallen on the lack of consistency from the receiver position; specifically, Xavier Worthy. He has not stepped up in the way the team needed after losing the primary deep threat in the scheme, Tyquan Thornton. 3. Nohl Williams and Kristian Fulton allowed just 29 receiving yards in Denver Over six passes thrown at Chiefs’ starting cornerbacks Nohl Williams and Kristian Fulton, filling in for the injured Mansoor Delane (shoulder), they caught only three passes for 29 yards (only 9 yards gained after the catch). Fulton was called for defensive pass interference early on, but overall, the Chiefs shut down the perimeter against wide receivers Courtland Sutton and Jaylen Waddle. Denver found success through the air only by targeting the middle of the field, where safety Chamarri Conner and linebacker Nick Bolton allowed big-time catches in crucial spots. 4. Chiefs tie season-high mark with 28 under-center plays against Broncos A week after running just 12 plays from under center, a season-low mark, the Chiefs’ offense re-established its identity in Denver and tied the season-high number of 28 plays run from under center; the team matched it against the Miami Dolphins in Week 3. Patrick Mahomes also attempted the most passes from under center in any game this season, dropping back 14 times. However, Kansas City averaged just 4.5 yards per play from under center, the second-lowest rate of the year behind the poor showing in Seattle. It may not have been the most efficient game, but the offense looked much better than it did in Seattle, and getting back to what worked through the first five games of the year felt like a big factor in that. 5. Kenneth Walker has 105 rushing yards combined in two losses Over 35 rushing attempts against the Seattle Seahawks and Denver Broncos , lead back Kenneth Walker has averaged just three yards per carry, gained six first downs and only found room for one 10-yard run In the previous five games, Walker averaged 5.8 yards per carry, moved the chains 37 times and had 20 runs of 10 or more yards. Seattle and Denver certainly found a blueprint for limiting Walker on the ground, and the Chiefs looked better from week to week at countering that attention with an effective passing game. In Denver, there were good play designs to get the ball in the hands of running backs or tight ends off play-action or misdirection that didn’t show up against the Seahawks. However, is the emergence of running back Emmett Johnson as a pass-catching playmaker enough to overcome the next elite defense that shuts Walker down completely? That’s where the logic in a trade-deadline move comes from.
author: Ron Kopp Jr.

title: NFL Power Rankings Week 9 Roundup: Chiefs fall fast after two losses
summary: In Week 8 of the 2026 NFL regular season, the Kansas City Chiefs lost to the Denver Broncos in a pivotal game for the division and conference standings. Let’s see how the national media reacted to it in this week’s sampling of power rankings: ESPN: 6 (Down from 4) Best in-season trade acquisition ever: WR […]
full_text: (Photo by Matthew Stockman/Getty Images) | Getty Images In Week 8 of the 2026 NFL regular season, the Kansas City Chiefs lost to the Denver Broncos in a pivotal game for the division and conference standings. Let’s see how the national media reacted to it in this week’s sampling of power rankings: ESPN : 6 (Down from 4) Best in-season trade acquisition ever: WR Kadarius Toney in 2022 The Chiefs had one of the league’s best offenses in 2022 and still added Toney, acquiring him from the Giants for a 2023 third-round pick and a 2023 sixth-round pick. He wasn’t a major part of the offense, but he made contributing plays to help the Chiefs to the No. 1 seed in the postseason. The greatest game in Toney’s career was Super Bowl LVII, when he scored a touchdown and generated a pivotal 65-yard punt return in the second half to help the Chiefs complete their comeback victory. That punt return is the longest in Super Bowl history. — Nate Taylor The Athletic : 5 (Down from 3) Reality check: They’re bringing Justin Tucker back? It feels inevitable after Harrison Butker missed another kick Sunday, this one a 54-yarder with 2:36 remaining that might have changed the complexion of the game. Butker, 31, has now missed six field goals this year and 11 in the last two years, and the Chiefs just added Tucker to the practice squad. Tucker, 36, hasn’t played since 2024 and served a 10-game suspension last year following allegations of sexual misconduct. — Chad Graff and Josh Kendall Pro Football Talk : 7 (Down from 5) Can the Chiefs beat the best teams in the league? — Mike Florio CBSSports.com : 7 (Down from 4) The explosive running game of the 5-0 start has gone away the past two weeks, both losses. See the correlation? They have to get Kenneth Walker going again. — Pete Prisco Yahoo! Sports : 7 (Down from 4) Biggest need: Receiver, but don’t forget about offensive line This is no surprise: The Chiefs still need help at receiver. Their offense has been built around Kenneth Walker III to good results, but it’s an incomplete unit. Rashee Rice is productive but not a dominant No. 1, Xavier Worthy hasn’t broken out and there’s not much else to speak of. Among the Chiefs’ wideouts, Rice has 243 yards, Worthy has 230, Tyquan Thornton has 219 but he’s on injured reserve and nobody else has more than 65. It’s a team that is a perfect candidate to try to turn around Brian Thomas Jr.’s career. But the Chiefs also can’t ignore the offensive line. Guard Kingsley Suamataia was benched for the second time this season on Sunday. Offensive tackle Josh Simmons has been a problem and was put on IR. Receiver would be the more splashy move, but adding to the offensive line might be even more prudent. — Frank Schwab USA Today : 10 (Down from 6) Of QB Patrick Mahomes’ 321 passing yards on Sunday at Denver, 72% went to his running backs and tight ends. Here’s hoping K.C. can find him a difference-making wideout ahead of the Nov. 10 trade deadline. — Nate Davis Sports Illustrated : 12 (Down from 6) Guys. Guys. Guys. GUYS. Guys. It was a false start. — Conor Orr Sporting News : 6 (Down from 3) Patrick Mahomes got back on track with his passing in Denver, timed with the return of Rashee Rice as his top wide receiver. Andy Reid can point to one big reason why the Chiefs lost to the Broncos. They had a season-high 11 penalties go against them, after having only 41 in the previous six games, the second-lowest total in the NFL. — Vinnie Iyer FOX Sports : 5 (Down from 3) That was a decent bounce-back game from the Chiefs after they got pounded by the Seahawks. They were literally inches away from beating the Broncos. Two losses in a row isn’t great, nor is the fact that Kenneth Walker III and their rushing attack struggled again. But Patrick Mahomes is playing his best football since his 2022 MVP season. That’s going to be enough to keep the Chiefs in the Super Bowl hunt. And if they add a receiver before the trade deadline, they might be the AFC favorites. Next game: vs. Jets (Sunday, 1 p.m. ET) Stat To Know : The Chiefs are one of only two NFL teams to rank in the top five in both total offense and scoring defense. They rank fifth in both categories, averaging 383.1 yards per game and allowing 18.7 points per game. — Ralph Vacchiano
author: Ron Kopp Jr.

title: Los Angeles Chargers news: Bolts-Ravens cannot be flexed despite lackluster matchup

title: Rams try another change on special teams
summary: The Los Angeles Rams released Alex Bachman as they continue to try and figure out their special teams. They released Xavier Smith earlier this year. They’re currently using Brandon McManus for field goals and Joshua Karty for kickoffs. The Rams are trying to adjust their special teams. Are their changes working? Not yet because they […]
full_text: INGLEWOOD, CA - NOVEMBER 01: Los Angeles Rams wide receiver Alex Bachman (11) returns a kickoff during the NFL game between the Los Angeles Chargers and the Los Angeles Rams on November 01, 2026, at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, CA. | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Los Angeles Rams released Alex Bachman as they continue to try and figure out their special teams. They released Xavier Smith earlier this year. They’re currently using Brandon McManus for field goals and Joshua Karty for kickoffs. The Rams are trying to adjust their special teams. Are their changes working? Not yet because they keep making changes. So far, McManus has been perfect, but will he deliver in the clutch? How long will Karty be used for kickoffs? Who will be the next return man for L.A.? Will the Rams go with someone who will just catch or someone with upside on the return? So many questions for the special teams unit, but as of now, Bachman won’t be one of them, and the Rams are still trying to find answers. Rams Release Alex Bachman as Special Teams Overhaul Continues (si.com) “The Los Angeles Rams have made another change on special teams as they head into Week 9. On Tuesday, the Rams released wide receiver and kickoff/punt returner Alex Bachman. Over the past several weeks, the Rams have been working to make improvements to their special teams unit, and Bachman being released is the latest indication of that. Earlier this season, the Rams turned to Bachman after they released wide receiver Xavier Smith from the same role. While Bachman fielded punts without issue, he didn’t offer much as a returner. Among players with at least five punt returns this season, Bachman averaged just 5.2 yards per return, which ranked 31st. At some point, the Rams needed to raise the bar from ‘just fielding punts’. Bachman averaged just 22.9 yards per kick return, ranking 62nd out of 75 qualifying returners.“ A newly added name to the NFL trade deadline rumor mill is the perfect target for the Los Angeles Rams (sports.yahoo) “So allow me to throw a name out there. New England Patriots defensive tackle Christian Barmore makes a lot of sense as a potential addition for the Rams. Los Angeles lost defensive tackle Puna Ford for the rest of the season. Barmore could certainly help the Rams replace some of what they lost in the middle of their defense – and he’s reportedly available. Why Christian Barmore makes sense for the Los Angeles Rams Barmore is a disruptive presence up front, and he brings plenty of size to the position. We’ve seen the kind of impact a disruptive defensive interior group is capable of with Seattle’s deep playoff run last year. The Rams have Aaron Donald, Braden Fiske, and Kobie Turner (injured reserve) – but Barmore is built a little differently. At 6-foot-5, 315 pounds, Barmore still has disruptive twitch in his game to complement to others on the Rams’ front.“ Ian Rapoport shares update on Myles Garrett’s outlook for Week 9 (ramswire) “McVay stopped short of saying Garrett will play against the Washington Commanders on Sunday afternoon, but he isn’t ruling it out, either. On Tuesday, Ian Rapoport of NFL Network shared an update on Garrett and said that once he gets on the field, “it should all happen quick.” He added that “this week is in play” for Sunday’s game but the Rams will need to see how Garrett responds to the week of practice. Myles Garrett is an interesting one,” Rapoport said. “I thought he was coming back last week. Just didn’t get to a point where he could feel comfortable enough on the knee, so it was like, all right, don’t rush it, stretch run, be ready this week. What I don’t know – I was told when he gets on the field for practice that it should all happen quick, so I think this week is in play, but we need to see how he actually responds. I think it’s finally, after like two months, in a pretty good place.” ESPN analyst lays out hypothetical trade for Rams to acquire Colts WR (ramswire) “Josh Downs requested a trade from the Colts and could be dealt before next Tuesday’s deadline. ESPN’s Ben Solak predicted some trades that he thinks “might” happen based on fit and logic, not inside information. One of them was the Rams acquiring Downs and a 2027 fifth-round pick from the Colts for a 2028 third-rounder.“ Patriots Quietly Make Move for Ex-Rams Linebacker Before Packers Game (sports.yahoo) “The Patriots are signing linebacker Elias Neal to their practice squad, less than a week after the Los Angeles Rams released him. The move was reported, by ESPN reporter Mike Reiss, who cited Neal’s agent, Sean Stellato. The Patriots had not officially announced the addition as of Tuesday afternoon. New England’s linebacker room leans on starters Robert Spillane and Christian Elliss, and Neal arrives with a résumé built almost entirely on special teams.“ Rams Get Matthew Stafford Update Amid ‘Interesting’ Myles Garrett Situation (heavy.com) “Despite the bottom-line positivity, Rapoport’s update on Stafford adds to the nebulous nature of the situation. Rams head coach Sean McVay did not provide much clarity following the reports. “He’s had some soreness there,” McVay told reporters on November 2. “I think he’d be better equipped, once you guys talk to him, to answer that. I can’t attest to stuff that I’m not necessarily aware of.” Rams boast hidden gem as LA heats up ahead of Commanders matchup (nypost) “Corum has been an overlooked piece for some time now, but the 25-year-old made sure he was remembered against the Chargers. During the first half, the crosstown rivals both looked willing to give the other a victory. Then, everything changed for the Rams in the third quarter when Corum’s 23-yard touchdown extended the lead to 17-9. The Michigan product tallied 73 yards on 11 carries against the Chargers and routinely made defenders miss. While Kyren Williams is the Rams’ primary running back, Corum has looked just as efficient — and at times better. Corum led the team in rushing yards, despite logging five fewer carries than Williams on Sunday.“ BEST PHOTOS: Blake Corum’s 23-yard touchdown, Wesley Bailey’s strip-sack & more | Best of the Rams’ Week 8 victory over the Chargers (therams.com) “The Los Angeles Rams hosted the Chargers at SoFi Stadium for a crosstown battle in Week 8. Browse through photos from the Rams’ 24-9 victory, including running back Blake Corum’s 23-yard touchdown, outside linebacker Wesley Bailey’s strip-sack, and more.” Rams cut PR Alex Bachman, place RB on IR and make 3 other roster moves (ramswire) “Bachman replaced Xavier Smith after he was waived, but he hasn’t exactly been an upgrade as a return specialist. He’s returned nine punts for 47 yards and 13 kickoffs for 298 yards, struggling to make defenders miss and pick up yardage. To take his place on the active roster, the Rams signed Cam Lampkin from the practice squad. Lampkin has been promoted from the practice squad twice but will now be a member of the 53-man roster. Nyzier Fourqurean was signed back to the practice squad after being released last week and running back Dean Connors was placed on injured reserve.“ Matthew Stafford’s Wife Kelly Demands Answers From NFL Over Rams Situation (si.com) “Los Angeles visits the Arizona Cardinals on Sunday, Nov. 15, before its Week 11 bye. However, because the Rams host the Green Bay Packers on Wednesday, Nov. 25 — the NFL’s first-ever Thanksgiving Eve game — they’ll get just 10 days between games instead of the usual 14. Kelly Stafford is Not Happy With the NFL Scheduling On Tuesday, Kelly took to her Instagram story to call out the league for doing her husband’s team dirty with their bye week scheduling. “@NFL Just curious to hear the thought process behind making the Rams the only team in the NFL without a true bye week,” Kelly wrote. “Because damn, after 18 years around this league, even I need a week off during the season… and I have never played a single snap.” Comment of the day: Feed post(s) of the day:

title: Rams release returner Alex Bachman
summary: The Los Angeles Rams have decided to move on from Alex Bachman, waiving the special teams returner as the team looks for a more dynamic option in the return game. Bachman’s limitations in acceleration, top-end speed and elusiveness ultimately made it difficult for him to establish himself as a reliable long-term solution. Bachman had an […]
full_text: The Los Angeles Rams have decided to move on from Alex Bachman, waiving the special teams returner as the team looks for a more dynamic option in the return game. Bachman’s limitations in acceleration, top-end speed and elusiveness ultimately made it difficult for him to establish himself as a reliable long-term solution. Bachman had an opportunity to carve out a role with the Rams by contributing on special teams, but the return game demands more than simply securing the football. Bachman failed to hit openings quickly, make defenders miss in space, and turn promising blocking into explosive plays. Enough of the “Alex Bachman” experiment… pic.twitter.com/vHLuMgJrsr — Rams Tapes 🇵🇷 (@RamsTapes) November 3, 2026 For a Rams team looking to improve its special teams production, the decision to move on reflects the importance of finding a returner capable of changing field position. Los Angeles has struggled to consistently generate positive results in that phase, making the search for a more explosive option an important roster consideration. Alex Bachman gained 0 yards on this play, and the ball is in his hands in this screenshot. How? pic.twitter.com/QYDnMGkvYq — Sosa Kremenjas (@QBsMVP) November 2, 2026 Potential Replacements The Rams could look internally or explore the available market to find their next return specialist. Internal options: The coaching staff could turn to players already on the roster who have experience handling kickoffs or punts. Tutu Atwell’s speed makes him an intriguing possibility if the team wants to explore a more explosive option, although his past track record did not appear to yield much either. External options: Los Angeles could examine available free agents, recently released players or return specialists on other teams’ practice squads. Josh Downs of the Indianapolis Colts has return experience, quick acceleration and the ability to make defenders miss. Downs also provides a role as a depth wide receiver option as the Rams continue to mull WR3 options.

title: Rams’ best option isn’t trade, it’s C.J. Daniels
summary: Rams head coach Sean McVay had heavy praise for receiver CJ Daniels this week, noting that the rookie sixth-round pick has done “a hell of a job” and deserves “more opportunities”. Instead of a big trade, should L.A. just promote from within and give Daniels a starting role alongside Puka Nacua? McVay has been asked […]
full_text: Rams head coach Sean McVay had heavy praise for receiver CJ Daniels this week, noting that the rookie sixth-round pick has done “a hell of a job” and deserves “more opportunities”. Instead of a big trade, should L.A. just promote from within and give Daniels a starting role alongside Puka Nacua? McVay has been asked as the trade deadline approaches if the Rams are looking to add to their wide receiver room, and so far, the head coach publicly has leaned more towards a “No” than a “Yes” . Instead, verbally opting to see other players return from injury, and step up on the depth chart. Enter Daniels, a Day Three pick in the 2026 NFL Draft who the Rams traded up to acquire . Daniels hasn’t accumulated any stats at the NFL level, yet, but McVay hints that Daniels, rather than a trade , could be an answer for the Rams at their receiver position as they move forward. The Rams have Puka Nacua, Davante Adams is on IR, and after them there is second-year veteran Konta Mumpfield and veteran Ram Tutu Atwell, but no one has been able to fill the void left behind by Adams, and if Nacua goes down, who can Matthew Stafford reliably throw to? Said McVay on how the Rams can bolster their wide receiver room for the last half of the season, “I do think there’s some guys on the roster that are capable of being able to step-up if their number’s called. Whether you’re talking about Tutu, I think Mumpfield’s done a nice job with his opportunities. There’s a guy in CJ Daniels that’s really done a hell of a job that you’re gonna see get more opportunities.” What does more playing time for Daniels look like? Will he be featured in the offense in a meaningful way? McVay keeps his answer vague, which is fair as he doesn’t want to tell other teams what his plans are, but one telling aspect is that McVay does say that he’s not going to hand out chances that could hurt the team. So, it begs the question, is Daniels ready to help the Rams now, or does he need more time to develop? “I would never rule out opportunities to get better, but at what opportunity cost? And you gotta be able to figure out for what does that look like for the long and the short.” If Daniels is ready, and if he performs well-enough to prove McVay right, then the Rams were correct in standing pat at the trade deadline. If Daniels isn’t ready, and if Nacua misses time, then McVay may regret the decision not to trade for a wide receiver before the deadline, and or not adding more help through the draft . The Rams are taking a gamble if they don’t add more depth, and according to McVay, not adding more depth could mean they are betting on Daniels.
author: Danny Stone

full_text: JACKSONVILLE, FLORIDA - NOVEMBER 1: Cornerback Charvarius Ward #7 of the Indianapolis Colts breaks up the pass meant for wide receiver Brian Thomas Jr. #7 of the Jacksonville Jaguars in the first quarter at EverBank Stadium on November 1, 2026 in Jacksonville, Florida. (Photo by Parker S. Freedman/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Los Angeles Rams have two intriguing wide receiver trade targets to consider ahead of the NFL trade deadline: Jacksonville Jaguars wideout Brian Thomas Jr. and Indianapolis Colts receiver Josh Downs. Both could provide a boost to Sean McVay’s offense, but they offer different solutions to the Rams’ needs. Thomas represents the higher-upside investment , while Downs could be the more affordable option for a team looking to strengthen its receiving corps without sacrificing significant draft capital. The Jaguars are now open to trading Brian Thomas Jr., per @AdamSchefter . Jacksonville would still want a high price back in any potential deal involving Thomas. pic.twitter.com/LnoAWelkVC — Evan Sidery (@esidery) November 1, 2026 The case for Brian Thomas Jr. 1. Similarities between Liam Coen and Sean McVay’s offenses Thomas already operates in an offensive system influenced by McVay’s coaching tree. Jacksonville head coach Liam Coen previously worked under McVay in Los Angeles, giving Thomas experience in a scheme with familiar concepts , terminology and route combinations. That could help ease his transition to the Rams. 2. An X-type wide receiver At 6-foot-3, Thomas offers the size, length and athleticism to become a true outside receiver. Los Angeles could use him as an X receiver capable of winning against press or zone overage, stretching the field and creating mismatches on the perimeter. His presence would give Matthew Stafford another dangerous downfield option. 3. Future control with his contract Thomas is still on his rookie contract, giving the Rams multiple years of team control beyond the current season. Acquiring a young receiver with his physical tools and long-term upside could be more than a short-term rental, potentially allowing Los Angeles to build its receiving corps around him for years especially with Davante Adams on an expiring contract. The case for Josh Downs 1. Inexpensive acquisition Downs could be the more financially and draft-capital-friendly target. If Indianapolis is willing to move him, the Rams may be able to address their immediate needs without paying the premium likely associated with Thomas. 2. Separation ability Downs excels at creating space, particularly from the slot. title: Quentin Lake is the Rams’ Nick Emmanwori and nobody knows
summary: The most underrated player on the Los Angeles Rams could be Quentin Lake, the versatile defensive back who is deserving of far more All-Pro consideration than he gets. Not only has Lake intercepted three passes and broken up a total of 11 throws, but he has also moved around the field to play three different […]
full_text: The most underrated player on the Los Angeles Rams could be Quentin Lake, the versatile defensive back who is deserving of far more All-Pro consideration than he gets. Not only has Lake intercepted three passes and broken up a total of 11 throws, but he has also moved around the field to play three different positions like nobody else on the entire roster. After playing the majority of his snaps in the slot in 2025, Lake is now playing 44.5% of his snaps as a deep safety, 29.3% as a linebacker, and 18.7% as a slot. Despite defensive coordinator Chris Shula asking Lake to go from someone spending two-thirds of his time in the slot to 30% as a linebacker and 45% as a safety, the fifth-year vet is having an even better season in 2026 than he had in 2025. Shouldn’t Quentin Lake be getting as much recognition for his work as a versatile chess piece Nick Emmanwori, Kyle Hamilton, and Derwin James are getting in the league? Quentin Lake in the right place at the right time 👏 LACvsLAR on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/6PJJ0x3cpQ — NFL (@NFL) November 1, 2026 Lake’s 2026 After Lake had 61 tackles, one interception, 10 passes defensed, and one sack over 10 games in 2025, he’s on an even bigger pace this season: 56 tackles, three interceptions, 11 passes defensed, and a forced fumble. Over his last 18 regular season games, that adds up to: 117 tackles 4 interceptions 21 passes defensed Lake is tied for second in the NFL in interceptions this season, and second in passes defensed. He’s the only player to be top-two in both categories. The most passes defensed for a safety in 2025 was 13 by Tykee Smith. Lake already has 11 . According to Pro-Football-Reference, Lake has allowed 6.1 yards per target and 58.7% completions on throws to him as the closest defender. Perhaps his only negatives is that Lake has been blamed for five missed tackles and two touchdowns (and he was blamed for being the closest defender on three touchdowns in the playoffs last season—but he also had three passes defensed), but Shula would be lost without him. We could also call Lake the best veteran bargain on the team because the three-year, $38 million extension he signed on January 1 looks like a steal. Lake has an $8 million cap hit this season and is signed through 2028. Stout against the run and the pass, Quentin Lake is the most valuable piece on L.A.’s defense—especially while Myles Garrett is out and Trent McDuffie has been banged up. The twitter account “InsidetheSecondary” notes that “Lake’s pre snap movement creates uncertainty for (Justin) Herbert” because the Chargers’ quarterback could not predict where Lake would end up after the snap. Information Warfare: Quentin Lake Lake’s pre snap movement creates uncertainty for Herbert. Is he blitzing, dropping, or changing the coverage picture? Initial alignment: 2×10-12 yards off of #3 Before Snap alignment: 2×6 yards pic.twitter.com/CVqbCu7ohO — InsideTheSecondary (@HybridDBFilmz) November 3, 2026 Because Lake does it all. In 140 snaps as a linebacker, Lake has 9 “stops” (tackle for a negative play) In 14 snaps as a defensive tackle, Lake has 3 PRESSURES (that’s more than some of LA’s DTs) In 89 snaps out of the slot, Lake has two interceptions In 219 snaps as a safety, Lake has 20 tackles, proving an ability and willingness to cover the field Lake has also lined up as an EDGE, cornerback, and strong safety. Whereas Emmanwori and Hamilton are praised as two of the top young defensive players in football at any position, Lake gets practically none of the attention despite having arguably the best season and the exact same versatility. Quentin Lake is one of two safeties in the NFL with a defensive grade above 90.0 (min 100 snaps played), according to @PFF . He also has the highest coverage grade (91.6) and is tied for the most passes defended through 4 games with 7 (TruMedia). pic.twitter.com/tbxQRfjVkU — Los Angeles Rams PR (@TheLARamsPR) October 8, 2026 What would it take for Lake to get the same attention? Well, it’s probably a little too late for that on the same scale. Lake was a sixth-round pick, not highly-touted draft prospects like James, Emmanwori, and Hamilton. That always sets a player back, even if it’s a ridiculous reason. But at his current pace, if Lake finishes with 20 passes defensed (that’s more than any player had in 2025) and 5+ interceptions, he should be undeniable. Lake is on the right track. Now he just needs to stay on it.
author: Kenneth Arthur

Ashton Jeanty: The No. 6 overall draft pick saw his play time and work load decrease dramatically. He played a career low 40 percent of the snaps, but more importantly, the Boise State product had just two carries as he saw rookie fourth-round pick Mike Washington get a whopping 25 carries. Raiders coach Klint Kubiak said the decision had nothing to so with Jeanty’s disparaging words about the Jets’ defense. We will see if Jeanty gets more work against the 49ers. But this was a major development. Jack Bech: The second-round pick returned from spending four games on the injured reserve with a broken forearm. He played 40 percent of the snaps, but was not targeted as a wide receiver. Darien Porter: The third-round pick injured his groin on the first play from scrimmage. His availability for Sunday’s game is unknown. Caleb Rogers: The third-round pick was benched after he started two games at right guard, in favor of rookie Trey Zuhn. Kubiak indicated Zuhn will play against the 49ers. Rogers played two plays on offense and six on special teams. Charles Grant: The offensive lineman, taken in the third round, didn’t play on offense as usual, but he did log five snaps on special teams. Dont’e Thornton: The wide receiver, taken in the fourth round, was activated from the injured reserve, but he was a healthy scratch. So, that’s not overly encouraging. Tonka Hemingway: The fourth-round pick suffered a stinger for the second time since Week 5. His availability for Sunday in unknown. JJ Pegues: The defensive tackle, taken in the sixth round, was inactive for the fifth time this season. It was a bit of a surprise since he had a forced fumble in Week 7 and the team had just waived Jonah Laulu. Meanwhile, rookie Tim Keenan, elevated from the practice squad, has been getting quality playing time the past two weeks. It leads to speculation that a Keenan-for-Pegues roster move could potentially be in play at some point. Cody Lindenberg: The seventh-round pick played 18 snaps on special teams, which is his norm. He didn’t play on defense, a week after he had three defensive snaps, his first defensive action of his career.

title: Raiders make some changes and take down the Jets
summary: The Las Vegas Raiders, losers of four straight, rolled into MetLife Stadium and got back to their winning ways against the New York Jets. Besting last years win total (3) and getting win #4 on the year. All while scoring a season-high 38 points. Kirk Cousins silenced all talks about a change at quarterback, continuing […]
full_text: (Photo by Mitchell Leff/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Las Vegas Raiders, losers of four straight, rolled into MetLife Stadium and got back to their winning ways against the New York Jets. Besting last years win total (3) and getting win #4 on the year. All while scoring a season-high 38 points. Kirk Cousins silenced all talks about a change at quarterback, continuing to show why he is the starter, as he threw for three touchdowns and ran for another. ‘Kirko Chainz’ outdueled former Raiders quarterback Geno Smith and got it done for the silver and black. Finding tight end Brock Bowers for two touchdowns and welcomed wide receiver Jalen Nailor to the party. Through eight weeks, #Raiders QB Kirk Cousins is third in passing yards (2,124) and second in TD passes (19). He is on pace to finish with 4,514 yards, 40 touchdowns and 11 interceptions. Cousins has never recorded 40-plus touchdowns in a season in his career. — Ryan McFadden (@ryanmcfadden_) November 2, 2026 To top it off, Cousins even broke out his own old man dance, “The Wellness Celebration.” A tribute to …the training staff that gets him ready to play every week. After successfully executing a goal-line quarterback sneak, Cousins broke out what looked like it was equal parts funky chicken, armpit farts and my shoulder hurts. But all is well that ends well; after a performance like that, he could have Texas two-stepped all over East Rutherford, New Jersey. Switching things up Third-round draft pick Trey Zuhn made his debut at right guard, playing well enough to earn another start. Zuhn was neither seen nor heard from, so much so that Cousins said he didn’t realize he was there. Displaying great footwork, surprising amounts of awareness, balance and strength. His versatility lent stability to a position which has been in flux as of late. It appears that head coach Klint Kubiak has finally seen enough and recognizes the need for a change at running back. Ashton Jeanty was not his draft pick, and after six out of seven weeks of a lacking running game, he was ready to see something different. Mike Washington was a player he pounded the table for. Washington may not have broken 100 yards on 25 carries or scored a rushing touchdown, but his impact was definitely profound. Kubiak stated that the decision to make the switch was his own. Jeanty will continue to have a big role in the running game moving forward despite having only two rushing attempts. For all you “stats people” knocking Mike Washington’s 3.3 YPC… Goal-to-go: 6 carries for 0 yards Outside goal-to-go: 19 carries for 83 yards (4.4 YPC) The O-line can’t get a push at the goal line. Watch the game. Not the box score. — Richie Incognito (@68INCOGNITO) November 2, 2026 Running back by committee is a great idea as long as every role is filled correctly. Washington is the lead back and should be the bell cow receiving the majority of the carries. Jeanty has a much more well-rounded skill set; his pass-catching out of the backfield is putting up better receiving numbers than some of the marquee wide receiver #1s. Running back #3 is usually a special teamer; lo and behold, Dylan Laube was the first kick returner of 2026 to house a kickoff return.
author: Philip Robinson

title: Mike Washington Jr.-Ashton Jeanty leads Las Vegas Raiders talk in Week 9 NFL Power Rankings
summary: The Las Vegas Raiders managed to start November right by getting a win and ending a four-game losing streak, taking down the New York Jets 38-33. Meanwhile, a running back change where Mike Washington Jr. became the lead back and Ashton Jeanty was the third-down option in New York leads the discussion surrounding the Raiders […]
full_text: (Photo by Mitchell Leff/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Las Vegas Raiders managed to start November right by getting a win and ending a four-game losing streak, taking down the New York Jets 38-33 . Meanwhile, a running back change where Mike Washington Jr. became the lead back and Ashton Jeanty was the third-down option in New York leads the discussion surrounding the Raiders in the Week 9 NFL Power Rankings. Sports Illustrated 17. Las Vegas Raiders Last week: 22 I can’t be the only one who saw Klint Kubiak open the door just a smidge for Mike Washington Jr. and watched as Washington kicked the thing open, right? It’s a different feel when the rookie out of Arkansas is in the backfield. — Conor Orr Since I mentioned the stacked boxes (eight or more defenders) that each running back has faced in defense of Jeanty in the past, it’s only right that I circle back to it now that Washington has had a chance to be the RB1. Per Next Gen Stats , Jeanty still has faced the fifth-highest rate of stacked boxes among qualifying running backs at 29.6%. However, that figure has come down since the beginning of the season, sitting at or below 30% every game since Week 4. To be fair, Las Vegas playing from behind in the majority of those contests is a big factor. That being said, the Silver and Black were trailing in a good portion of the Jets game, and Washington faced a stacked box on 48.0% of his carries , tied for the fourth-highest rate in Week 8. According to Sumer Sports , Washington is averaging 2.9 ypc (27 carries for 78 yards) on such carries, while Jeanty is at 2.6 ypc (43 carries, 113 yards) . The biggest difference between the two is that the rookie has a slight advantage in rushing yards over expected (RYOE) per attempt: +0.4 to -0.3, according to NGS . That’s something to monitor as the former’s workload (presumptively) continues to increase over the coming weeks. NFL.com 20. Las Vegas Raiders Last week: 25 The aerial stylings of Kirk Cousins, Brock Bowers and the rest of the crew delivered again, ending the Raiders’ four-game losing skid in a wild, back-and-forth affair in MetLife Stadium. Like much of Las Vegas’ 2026 season, I certainly didn’t expect one development to emerge: rookie Mike Washington Jr. has taken over as the bell cow in Silver and Black, while Ashton Jeanty has become Klint Kubiak’s preferred third-down, pass-catching back — and is making a difference. He played a big part in the Raiders’ comeback win Sunday and at least adds a bit of dynamism to the unit. — Nick Shook The irony of Jeanty getting demoted to the third-down role is that he’s been one of the best receiving backs in the league. He leads the position with 37 catches, 376 yards (82 more than anyone else) and three receiving TDs (tied with Bhayshul Tuten). That’s on top of ranking fifth (minimum 50 total touches) in yards per reception (10.16) and ninth in EPA per target (0.16), according to Sumer . For the record, of the eight running backs that have a higher EPA/target than Jeanty, only Chuba Hubbard has at least 20 targets (26), while Jeanty is sitting at 48 to bring down his average. But, of course, the Raiders didn’t make the Boise State product the No. 6 pick in the draft to play a complementary role… The Athletic 19. Las Vegas Raiders Last week: 24 Reality check: Ashton Jeanty may not bounce back It was a tough week for Jeanty. After he made disparaging comments about the Jets, ESPN commentator and former Jets head coach Rex Ryan called him “soft as Charmin.” On Sunday, the No. 6 pick in the 2025 draft was essentially benched for rookie Mike Washington. Jeanty finished with two carries for 9 yards, while Washington had 25 for 83. — Josh Kendall, Chad Graff I have a hard time buying that Jeanty’s comments were the only reason why Kubiak reduced his role in what was a pivotal game for the team’s playoff hopes. But I also won’t deny that the remarks played a factor in the decision. If the 25-2 carry split/ratio continues against the San Francisco 49ers this weekend, that’s a strong sign Jeanty wasn’t just being punished or disciplined this past Sunday. Bleacher Report 17. Las Vegas Raiders Last week: 20 The Las Vegas Raiders were well-prepared for their second trip to the East Coast this season. They fell behind early, but Kirk Cousins showed why he still gives the Silver and Black the best chance to win, throwing for 247 yards and three touchdowns and scoring a touchdown on a quarterback sneak. For now, head coach Klint Kubiak is trying to stay in the playoff picture, so expect Cousins to keep the starting job for the foreseeable future. Rookie first-rounder Fernando Mendoza’s time will come, but the .500 Raiders should keep riding Cousins’ arm for now. The Raiders are a flawed team with an inefficient ground attack, averaging three yards per carry, and a leaky defense, but Cousins and the passing game give them a chance to pull off victories. — Moe Moton B/R starts to reverse course here, primarily focusing on last week’s theme with the “quarterback controversy” between Cousins and Mendoza . I mentioned this last week; beating the Jets likely keeps Cousins behind center for two more games since the Raiders will still be “in the hunt”. Additionally, there’s more momentum that Mendoza’s first start comes after the Week 13 bye. ESPN 20. Las Vegas Raiders Last week: 22 Best in-season trade acquisition ever: DB Mike Haynes in 1983 The Raiders bolstered their secondary by acquiring Haynes from the Patriots. The move was instrumental to winning a title that season, as he recorded an interception, two pass breakups and a tackle in Super Bowl XVIII against Washington. Haynes, who was elected to the Hall of Fame in 1997, went on to play seven seasons with the Silver and Black. In 87 games (72 starts), he totaled 18 interceptions. — Ryan McFadden ESPN took a very different approach to their Power Ranking analysis, choosing to play on the upcoming trade deadline and focus on nostalgia. McFadden hit the nail right on the head because Haynes is considered one of the best in-season trade acquisitions in NFL history, not just the Raiders’ history. Also, I can’t think of a better one off the top of my head because the organization has primarily been a seller, if anything, at the deadline during my lifetime. For what it’s worth, when I asked Google AI for the best Raiders in-season trade acquisition, Haynes came up first and Carson Palmer was second. Palmer is on the wrong end of two of the worst trades in franchise history, or at least the last 15 to 20 years. The Raiders gave up first- and second-round picks to get the quarterback out of retirement and away from the Cincinnati Bengals in a desperation move after starter Jason Campbell suffered an injury while the team was 4-2 in 2011. Palmer had a 4-5 record down the stretch, and the club missed the playoffs that year. The Silver and Black went 4-12 the following season and traded Palmer, along with a seventh-round pick, to the Arizona Cardinals for sixth- and seventh-round selections. He had a 38-21-1 record in Arizona , earning a second-team All-Pro bid and leading the Cardinals to the playoffs in 2015.

title: Mike Washington’s role greatly expands
summary: Here is a look at how the Las Vegas Raiders’ 2026 draft class (eight of the 10 picks are on the 53-man roster) fared in a 38-33 win at the New York Jets on Sunday and what to look for Sunday at the San Francisco 49ers. Fernando Mendoza:The No. 1 overall pick has only played […]
full_text: (Photo by Mitchell Leff/Getty Images) | Getty Images Here is a look at how the Las Vegas Raiders’ 2026 draft class (eight of the 10 picks are on the 53-man roster) fared in a 38-33 win at the New York Jets on Sunday and what to look for Sunday at the San Francisco 49ers. Fernando Mendoza: The No. 1 overall pick has only played in Week 5 in a mop-up role. Treydan Stukes: The Raiders’ second-round pick played all 64 defensive snaps and had a pass breakup. Trey Zuhn: The third-round pick made his starting debut, playing every offensive snap. He held up well and coach Klint Kubiak indicated he will remain in the lineup at right guard at San Francisco. Jermod McCoy: The fourth-round pick played extensively for the first time this season. He preciosuly only played on defense in two games. He played 53 percent of the defensive snaps (and 16 snaps on special teams) after starting outside cornerback Darien Porter was hurt with a groin injury. McCoy had his ups and downs, but Kubiak said he will get more chances in the future. Mike Washington: The fourth-round pick played played 60 percent of the snaps, a sea high and he had a season high 25 carries, for 83 yards. Ashton Jeanty had just two carries. It seems like, for now, Washington is the Raiders’ lead tailback, which is stunning considered Jeanty was the No. 6 overall pick last season Dalton Johnson: The fifth-round pick safety was inactive for the seventh time in eight games. Zeke Masses: The fifth-round pick played 45 defensive snaps after Porter was hurt. He rotated with McCoy and made a big paly late even though he gave up some plays. He will likely continue to compete with McCoy for playing time if Porter remains out. Malik Benson: The sixth-round pick was a healthy scratch for the first time. We might have to wonder if Benson’s roster spot is in jeopardy if he continues to sit on game days.

title: Raiders news: Rookie defenders making plays
summary: The Las Vegas Raiders’ defense has had its struggles this season and the rookie class, overall, has been somewhat quiet. But two Raiders’ rookie defenders have found a way to make an impact. According to the Raiders’ public relations department, rookie safety Treydan Stukes and cornerback Zeke Massses have combined for 10 passes defensed. Masses, […]
full_text: (Photo by Candice Ward/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Las Vegas Raiders’ defense has had its struggles this season and the rookie class, overall, has been somewhat quiet. But two Raiders’ rookie defenders have found a way to make an impact. According to the Raiders’ public relations department, rookie safety Treydan Stukes and cornerback Zeke Massses have combined for 10 passes defensed. Masses, a former starter and now backup, has seven pass breakups and Stukes, a season-long starter, has three. They each had one Sunday against the New York Jets. The nine passes defensed is the most by a Raiders’ rookie class through the first eight games of a season for the franchise since 2000. Also, the Raiders’ rookie class is the eighth NFL team since 2010 to have a draft class with four interception and 10 pass breakups since 2010. That’s solid work. title: Miami Dolphins: Deux et Machina, not for us!
summary: The Truths: The Miami Dolphins have played two “one-half” games the last two weeks. A “half-game” was good enough against the hapless New York Jets but a “half-game” was NOWHERE near good enough against the unspectacular New England Patriots. How they reached the Super Bowl last year just shows that lady luck and buffoonery still […]
full_text: MIAMI GARDENS, FLORIDA - NOVEMBER 01: DeMario Douglas #3 of the New England Patriots carries the ball for a touchdown against Juju Brents #8 of the Miami Dolphins during the fourth quarter of the game at Hard Rock Stadium on November 01, 2026 in Miami Gardens, Florida. (Photo by Megan Briggs/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Truths: The Miami Dolphins have played two “one-half” games the last two weeks. A “half-game” was good enough against the hapless New York Jets but a “half-game” was NOWHERE near good enough against the unspectacular New England Patriots. How they reached the Super Bowl last year just shows that lady luck and buffoonery still reign supreme in the NFL. Zebras gone wild – Courtesy of Greek and Latin writer s: And let us not forget how the Patriots are the recipient of every close call, especially against us. I literally think that on EVERY single non-procedural penalty, the refs call up to Goodell and Satan to ask permission to charge the Patriots with a penalty. I am not joking. A bunch of blind shamans from Mongolia would do a better job officiating. How in the name of God do the field refs rule the NE dude short and then go to commercial and then when we get back from the commercial we have a “Deux et Machina” moment where NE is GIVEN a first down AND Steve Ross is kicked in the groin to boot. For those of you who may not know “Deux et Machina” ….it is a Latin phrase written into plays/stories thousands of years ago to explain how a character can be in the Aegean Sea one moment and the very next scene the character is sitting on top of Mount Vesuvius. The term translates to God and Machine. It takes God and Machine to stop the Miami Dolphins. And the networks and the NFL trot out Gene Steratore (remember he is the Phins major Zerba enemy) to say how stupid Dolphins’ fans are for even questioning the infinite wisdom of the NFL. In the offseason, I will rack my own brain and re-watch games where the Fins were completely ruined by the refs. I will try to write a treatise on this. I HATE having to sound whiny about the officiating, but IT IS A NATIONWIDE STORY. Armando Salguero et al have discussed the garbage that masquerades as officiating. Like D’Attaglia in the Godfather , NE is not our real enemy; just an annoyance. Buffalo is our Barzini! On to the game itself: NE is NOT very much better than us. Don’t forget that. The announcers were fawning over the overrated Drake Maye. He isn’t that good. He throws a decent long ball but remember NE got the matchups they wanted. Not hard throws. He isn’t 1/100 th the QB that Tom Brady was. Know this: it is 10,000 times harder to thread a 3 rd and 18-yard deep-square-in under a withering pass rush (one of the routes that put Aikman and Irvin in the HOF) versus throwing a deep ball when he has 5 seconds to throw with very little pressure. Generally speaking, those throws aren’t there in the playoffs when it is freezing in Buffalo, Pittsburgh and Kansas City. This is one reason why the Phins haven’t won a playoff game, much less a road playoff game in 10,000 years since a dome playoff game against Seattle (going from memory). Yes, Seattle used to be in the AFC. Chuck Knox, Jim Zorn, Davie Krieg all come to mind. Moving on, I want to give out a simple sign if your team is good or not good. What I am about to say doesn’t guarantee a Super Bowl or a playoff win but it tells you if you have a chance. I didn’t see the sign – Not Ace of Base The sign is simply this: if you can run the ball for 2 yards when the opposing KNOWS it is coming, you have a chance to be good. The reverse: can you stop a team from getting 2 yards when everyone knows they are going to run. That is the sign. If you remember with all those McDaniel teams, we would pop 30, 40 and 50 yards runs BUT when we tried to run a for two yards with Ollie Gordon, he was BLOWN UP in the back field. Pathetic! We could not get the two yards when the other team KNOWS it is coming. I see improvement in this field with our OLINE. I see improvement in this team. There are so many good signs. EXCEPT special teams. Our kicker gets 1 pass. He used it up on the doink. He killed us on the bad miss. It didn’t cost us the game but imagine if it was close. Don’t forget, Borregales missed too and he kicked in the stadium for YEARS. Are we able to get a punt block or a kick return? And someone needs to look up Carlos Huerta (kicker for the Canes about 30 years ago). Huerta was/is the GREATEST ON-SIDE KICKER EVER. The Canes were losing to Univ of Michigan by 15 in the 4 th qtr in 1988. After a Canes score, he drove the ball straight into the ground and the ball shot up very high and then it was a free-for-all ( I passed up a Ted Nugent reference here, so there! )……the Canes recovered and Huerta kicked the FG to win 31-30. But no, the Dolphins tried the dribble and it failed. Special teams COULD be to our advantage BUT NO, Sullivan and Hafley are settling for mediocrity. BACK TO THE GAME Back to improvements: Before we jump down the Phins throat let’s remember there were many games against Pats where we led in the first half and Belichick made his half-time improvements and we lost. This happened while Jacoby was their QB. The way we lost to them yesterday is nothing new. Vrabel learned a lot from Belichick. Did you notice that on first down, many of Ollie’s runs went for 0 or 1 yard? Then on second down he would get 6-8 yards, still good, but we did not wear them down. This is good news, NE actively had to respect our run game but they didn’t wear down. We had some manageable 3 rd downs. On the flip side, we wore down while on defense. They found a weakness where the RB would seemingly head for the initial run read but then almost invariably cut back BEHIND the line and way from the initial run read. I haven’t looked at the film yet but that tells me the DEs and/or LBs (away from the ball) aren’t getting through and/or they are overcommitting aka racing to the ball but behind their own DL ( where the LBs are )not in the backfield (easier said than done). This will sound ludicrous based on our talent but back in the day, believe it or not, teams would run at Lawrence Taylor (LB Goat) so that they could try to get hats on him. If they ran away from him, he would simply run down the back from behind. He was virtually unblockable. We need to get that edge (who plays away from the ball to penetrate) A LITTLE( in the Goldilocks zone ) to take away the cutbacks that we saw yesterday. We don’t have that talent. Yet. Uche and Chop played decently but they have their limits. We all know TALENT always wins out. We are heading in the right direction, EXCEPT for special teams. Malik played well: he made two really bad throws and if he only makes two bad throws every game, I can live with that. Who is out there in college (outside of Mestemaker who gives you a thrill? All those current QB dudes(Chambliss, Leavitt, etc. are system QBs from the sissy 7-on-7 schools…just like Maye). The Pats made an obvious choice yesterday: funnel everything to the inside and set their DEs to keep outside to prevent the Malik runs. They dare us to run straight ahead and to throw. Their first half, we did. I have to watch the film but NE went to 9 on the intensity level and we simply didn’t match. Those little Malik runs weren’t there and we didn’t exploit the middle of the field like we should have. In closing, NE is a good team, not great. We need to set the organizational sights on surpassing NE and eventually Buffalo and to be able to fight against a fully charged Baltimore(with Lamar?) and KC(I fear 10 more years of Mahomes). And then to be able to fight the LA Rams, Seattle, San Francisco and the Bears(this is the team that scares me long term because Williams is young and they are improving). We shoot for the stars! Go Phins!

title: Patriots vs. Dolphins reactions and review: Tuesday Thoughts With The Earl
summary: The Miami Dolphins teased us with a 13-3 halftime lead over the New England Patriots in Week 8.  But then the real Dolphins showed up and ended up losing 24-19, despite drawing close late.  Here’s what I saw upon initial watch. THE OFFENSE WASN’T GREAT, BUT WASN’T THE CULPRIT I’m sure most of you are […]
full_text: The Miami Dolphins teased us with a 13-3 halftime lead over the New England Patriots in Week 8. But then the real Dolphins showed up and ended up losing 24-19, despite drawing close late. Here’s what I saw upon initial watch. THE OFFENSE WASN’T GREAT, BUT WASN’T THE CULPRIT I’m sure most of you are like “WHAT?!?!?” But hear me out on this. The Dolphins had a rough 3rd quarter in which they only gained 6 net yards. That is bad, but there are some circumstances behind that. There were some additional issues that need to be cleaned up. First would be the number of sacks. Willis was sacked 5 times, 3 of which occurred on the 1st 2 drives. Everyone will want to blame the new guy – Jarrett Kingston – but I saw All-Pro Aaron Brewer get blown up a few times also. The entire OL was an issue early on. They started to settle down later though. The run game was less effective than it has been, but as I pointed out Friday in Three Reasons Why , the Pats are good in run defense, limiting teams to under 4 yards per carry. BUT… I like that Willis spread the ball around with 9 different players getting a target. Overall, I thought Willis played with command of the offense and looked decent. His stats weren’t “elite” and there was the interception that doinked off the helmet of a Pats player, but he was not the problem in this game. Gordon got it going late and the WRs did well against a stingy Patriots secondary. They had their moments. However… THE DEFENSE IS MOVING IN THE WRONG DIRECTION Anytime there is a new coach and a new scheme, it takes some time for players to adjust. That is especially pronounced with a young roster like the Dolphins have. I was hoping to see some improvement to this point in the season. But alas, that just isn’t happening. The stats reveal the issues. Let’s start with pass defense. The Dolphins are allowing a completion percentage of 76.9%, which is on pace to be the worst in league history. Anyone and everyone can complete a pass against the Dolphins. I would argue that one of us could complete a pass against this defense. In 7 games this season, the Dolphins have allowed 195 pass attempts. Only 45 total have fallen incomplete. 4 of those INTs and the Dolphins are dead last in passes defensed at 13. They aren’t stopping anyone from catching the ball. They are allowing 8.3 yards per attempt, which is tied for 2nd worst. Teams are passing at will against the Dolphins, to the point it seems they don’t even have to try hard. Almost any time an opponent drops back to pass, their pass catchers are wide open; the Dolphins defenders aren’t around the ball. On the 2 TD passes for NE, the receivers were wide open. It’s just too easy. It is unacceptable. The run defense is another issue. If you look at YPC allowed, the Dolphins are actually respectable, tied for 7th at 3.8 YPA. But that is mostly due to volume. The Dolphins allow 29.7 attempts per game, which is 2.8 higher than the league average. Teams run a lot against the Dolphins. The Dolphins had 2 good games against opponents, where they limited them to under 100 rushing yards. But they have allowed 100+ rushing yards in the last four games, and have allowed at least one RB in each of the last 4 games to average over 4 yards per carry. They aren’t getting stops either. In Sunday’s game, they allowed the RBs to gain critical yards late to keep drives alive and ultimately finish off the Dolphins. It’s not a time of possession issue either. The Pats only had the ball about 2 minutes longer than the Dolphins. The Dolphins are also bad in terms of getting off the field. They are 2nd worst in the league at 3rd down conversion percentage at 50.6%; only the Cowboys are worse. In 7 games, the Dolphins have forced 18 punts, which is 2nd worst – Cincy has forced 17 punts. That’s an average of 2.6 per game. League average is 28.3 and 3.8 per game. The Dolphins have only produced 6 turnovers. The Dolphins allow 2.74 points per drive, which is second worst – Buffalo is at 2.76. Nothing exemplifies what the defense is more than the final sequence of events in this game. The Dolphins scored a late TD to make it a one score game. They didn’t get the onside kick, but had a timeout plus the 2 minute warning. It was a long shot, but a stop on 3rd down means the Dolphins would get the ball back for a slight chance to make a play. The play sequence: 2 yard pass – 2 minute warning, 3 yard run – timeout. Here is the chance for the stop. Get a stop and get about a 1 minute to do something… 5 yard run. 1st down. Game over. My entire point here is that the defense is a massive problem. We Dolphins fans tend fixate on the QB and OL. It’s always their fault for every loss and we even find issues in the victories. We all knew coming in that Malik Willis was going to need some refinement and is probably not the long-term answer. But we should stop worrying about him for the moment because that isn’t getting fixed in 2026. We’ve all heard the adage “defense wins championships”. Miami is barely fielding a defense that could reach a below-average status, let alone a defense worthy of being in the playoffs. This group is bad and what’s worse is there are only a handful of players that could be considered building blocks within the group. Right now, I would say Zach Sieler, Chop Robinson, Jordan Phillips, Jordyn Brooks, Jacob Rodriguez, and Chris Johnson are the only players deserving of a prominent role next season. And really, that all depends. Rodriguez started hot but has started falling off in recent games. Johnson is ok at this point. You may see those names and think that’s half of the starters. But teams need at least 3 pass rushers, 4 defensive tackles, 4 linebackers, 5 corners, and 3-4 safeties. Miami has 6 out of 20 for next season and one of them is over 30 years old. They need 2 additional edge rushers to have a solid trio. They need 2 additional DTs, particularly one that is a pass rusher. They have half of the needed LBs, though I’ll be somewhat lenient towards Trey Moore because he hasn’t played yet. But he’s a 4th round pick, so expectations should be limited accordingly. They have 1 CB out of 5 and 0 safeties out of 4. Not only is this not getting fixed in 2026, but it’s not getting fixed in 2027 either. Not completely. Even with the high draft pick and all the FA money, they’ll likely get 4 of those things fixed. Why only 4? Because counting on every draft pick to be a hit is foolish. FAs are hit or miss. I’ve warned everyone who will listen… this rebuild is going to take time. The Dolphins are on pace for 2-3 wins this season. They aren’t going from 2-3 wins to 10-11 wins in 2027. You can safely bet on 5-6 wins. Then MAYBE after 3 full drafts and 2 big offseasons in FA, they will have enough talent to be competitive. But they aren’t close right and the issue isn’t the man under center or his protection. But that’s what everyone wants to focus on. THIS AND THAT What about that pesky 3rd quarter? The Dolphins only gained 6 yards and that’s turrible. But let’s discuss it. The Dolphins defense got a rare 3-and out. The offense went 1 yard run, incomplete pass that wouldn’t have counted because of a penalty, and a pass to Greg Dulcich that he wasn’t even looking for . The Pats get the ball. 7 rushing yards on the 1st 2 plays, then a 4 yards pass with 3 to gain on 3rd down. Can’t get off the field. Then an 8 yard run followed by a TD pass where the WR was, to know one’s surprise, wide slap open. The next drive: incomplete pass, 5 yard run that ended up going backwards thanks to a penalty on Gordon. Then an incomplete pass to Wright that maybe wasn’t a great pass, but who cares? If Wright catches it, he wasn’t getting the 20 yards needed to get a 1st down. The Pats got the ball back with 8:35 left in the quarter. 13 plays. 8 runs. A fumbled snap that became a 26-yard pass play. One TD. The defense actually got a 3rd down stop, but allowed a close play that was overturned for a 4th down conversion. A completed…

title: 2026 NFL Week 9: Buffalo Bills at Minnesota Vikings
summary: The Minnesota Vikings, coming off of their first loss of the 2026 regular season, will make their first prime time appearance of the year against one of the National Football League’s best teams. U.S. Bank Stadium will host Monday Night Football to cap off Week 9, as the Vikings will play host to the Buffalo […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - NOVEMBER 13: Justin Jefferson #18 of the Minnesota Vikings catches a pass in front of Cam Lewis #39 of the Buffalo Bills during the fourth quarter at Highmark Stadium on November 13, 2022 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Isaiah Vazquez/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Minnesota Vikings, coming off of their first loss of the 2026 regular season, will make their first prime time appearance of the year against one of the National Football League’s best teams. U.S. Bank Stadium will host Monday Night Football to cap off Week 9, as the Vikings will play host to the Buffalo Bills. Both of these teams will come into this one with records of 6-1, but they’re getting it done in significantly different ways. The Vikings come into this one with one of the best defenses in the league, but they have struggled mightily on offense through their first eight games. They have only gone over the 20-point mark twice since their season opener, and their lack of punch contributed to their 19-15 loss to Detroit in Week 8 to knock them from the ranks of the NFL’s undefeated. The Vikings’ offense has been unable to sustain drives and has relied on their defense. . .too much, at times. . .to win games. They’re going to need to find some points in this one if they want to avoid a second consecutive loss. On the other side, the Bills, powered by quarterback Josh Allen, come in with one of the best offenses in the NFL. Their 33.3 points/game average is the best in the league, and they haven’t been held under 24 points in any game they’ve played this season. Buffalo comes into this one riding a three-game winning streak, including a 36-10 blowout victory over the Baltimore Ravens in Week 8. The last game between these two teams was one of the most memorable regular season games in recent years. In 2022 at Orchard Park, the Bills took a 27-10 lead late in the third quarter, but an 81-yard touchdown run by Dalvin Cook and a touchdown run by C.J. Ham got the Vikings to within 27-23. The Vikings then drove down the field and got a miracle conversion on a 4th-and-18 on an amazing catch by Justin Jefferson, but appeared to have their efforts fall short when the Bills’ defense stoned Kirk Cousins at the goal line on 4th-and-goal on a sneak attempt. Amazingly, Allen fumbled the exchange from center on the very next play, with Eric Kendricks falling on the loose ball for an improbable Minnesota touchdown to give them the lead. Allen then led the Bills to a tying field goal as the gun sounded to force overtime. Minnesota took the lead in OT on a Greg Joseph field goal, and Patrick Peterson ended things by intercepting an Allen pass in the end zone to seal a crazy 33-30 victory for the Vikings. Because this is Monday Night Football, the game will be broadcast on ESPN, with kickoff slated for 7:15 PM Central time. We’ll be putting everything about this one right here in our stream for the week, so keep checking back here for all the latest. Vikings vs. Bills odds: Opening lines for Week 9 matchup

title: Is Kyler Murray Fixable? Breaking Down the Vikings’ Offensive Struggles
summary: The Minnesota Vikings suffered their first loss of the season, falling 19-15 to the Detroit Lions, and the Kyler Murray conundrum has fans searching for answers. On The Real Forno Show, host Tyler Forness and Producer Dave Stefano broke down the All-22 film, advanced data, and the difficult truth: the eye test screams panic, but […]
full_text: DETROIT, MI - NOVEMBER 01: Minnesota Vikings quarterback Kyler Murray (1) walks off of the field heading to the locker room at the conclusion of a regular season NFL football game between the Minnesota Vikings and the Detroit Lions on November 1, 2026 at Ford Field in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Scott W. Grau/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Minnesota Vikings suffered their first loss of the season, falling 19-15 to the Detroit Lions, and the Kyler Murray conundrum has fans searching for answers. On The Real Forno Show , host Tyler Forness and Producer Dave Stefano broke down the All-22 film, advanced data, and the difficult truth: the eye test screams panic, but the numbers say Murray is “bang average.” “We’re gonna tackle the Kyler Murray conundrum that the Vikings have,” Forness said. After reviewing the tape, he admitted: “Everything that he can do that we’ve seen over the course of this season, especially with the accuracy element, it just wasn’t there.” Yet the data tells a different story — Murray ranks 17th in EPA per play (.089) and 16th in success rate (49.3%) among 30 qualifying quarterbacks. “The data tells you that Kyler Murray is pretty average. The eye test sends you wanting to hit the panic button ,” Forness explained. Stefano cited NFL Next Gen Stats: “Murray threw for a season high 115 yards despite only completing four of his 13 attempts for a 30.8% rating, the lowest downfield completion rate in a game since 2023.” Forness pointed to Kevin O’Connell’s complex offense as a potential culprit, comparing it to a brilliant but inaccessible AP Physics teacher. “I think there might be a little too much of this PhD element within the Kevin O’Connell offense,” he said, suggesting simplification could unlock Murray. He also questioned Justin Jefferson’s usage: “Why is Jefferson only getting about six [targets]? Why are we not giving him the ball a lot more?” Key Points: Murray’s accuracy has no clear fix: “There is no through line to where we can point to this and say, ‘Hey, we fix this, we’ll fix some of those accuracy concerns.'” Jefferson underutilized: Only 40 targets through seven games while Jaxon Smith-Njigba, Puka Nacua, CeeDee Lamb, and Ja’Marr Chase each receive 10-12 per game. Offensive line played well: PFF registered just two pressures all game. Carson Wentz is not the answer: “He’s less accurate than Kyler Murray. He’s a statue in the pocket. He reads defenses worse.” Run defense collapsed: 153 Lions rushing yards in the second half and 18 missed tackles. “They got their asses handed to them.” Defensive line depth concerns: Caleb Banks and Domonique Orange aren’t ready for major snaps; Tyrion Ingram-Dawkins played 57 snaps. “Why in the world is Tyrion Ingram-Dawkins playing 57 snaps?” Trade deadline targets: Jonathan Taylor or Breece Hall could transform the offense. “Those guys would elevate your team to a different stratosphere.” Lions bullied the Vikings: Detroit made Jared Goff a “handoff merchant” — “They should feel insulted by that.” Jack Campbell injury concern: “This isn’t even about football anymore. This is just about I just want the person to be okay.” Bills preview: Priority is containing Josh Allen — “You need to contain that golden retriever in the pocket.” Listen: View Link Or on your favorite podcast aggregator. Watch: The Vikings still sit at 6-1 with a defense Forness believes is “good enough to win a title.” But the offensive questions are mounting, and with the trade deadline looming, the next eight days could define the season.
