title: Scouting Jets quarterback Will Levis
summary: The Jets recently signed former Titans quarterback Will Levis to their practice squad. Today, we break him down in detail. The 27-year old Levis is listed at 6’4” and 229 pounds and was a second round pick out of Kentucky in 2023. He has started 21 games in his NFL career, winning just five, and […]
full_text: NASHVILLE, TENNESSEE - AUGUST 29: Will Levis #8 of the Tennessee Titans looks on before the preseason game against the Chicago Bears at Nissan Stadium on August 29, 2026 in Nashville, Tennessee. (Photo by Justin Ford/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Jets recently signed former Titans quarterback Will Levis to their practice squad. Today, we break him down in detail. The 27-year old Levis is listed at 6’4” and 229 pounds and was a second round pick out of Kentucky in 2023. He has started 21 games in his NFL career, winning just five, and did not play last season due to injury. Background Levis was a three-star high school recruit, whose college career began at Penn State, where he redshirted his first season in 2018. He got a chance to start his first game in the following season but after two years with the Nittany Lions, he had attempted just 102 passes, completing 61 for 644 yards with three touchdowns. He had also rushed for 473 yards and six touchdowns. Levis decided to transfer to Kentucky in 2021 and passed for 367 yards in his first start – a sign of how far he had come since his first start with Penn State where he carried the ball 17 times and only passed in 15 times. In 13 starts, Levis completed 66 percent of his passes for 2,827 yards and 24 touchdowns while also rushing for 376 yards and nine scores. However, he led the SEC with 13 interceptions. Levis’ second season with the Wildcats saw him start 11 games and he passed for over 2,400 yards and 19 touchdowns with another two touchdowns on the ground. However, he threw another 10 interceptions. Heading into the 2023 NFL draft, Levis’ stock seemed to be rising, with some reports indicating he was under consideration to be selected first overall. However, he ended up dropping out of the first round altogether with the Titans moving up to select him with the first pick of day two. Levis struggled in camp and preseason, and began the year as the number three quarterback. However, he got a chance to start his first game in late October and threw four touchdown passes in a win over the Falcons. Several weeks later he passed for 327 yards and two late touchdowns in a comeback win over the Dolphins. Overall, though, he was just 3-6 as a starter, completing 58 percent of his passes for 1,808 yards and eight touchdowns with four interceptions. He did also rush for one touchdown. Levis began his second season as the starter but got off to a bad start as the Titans lost four of their first five with Levis leading the league in turnovers. He would miss time due to injury in the middle part of the season and then after a couple of good performances, his play took a downturn and he was benched down the stretch. He ended the season with just two wins and 12 interceptions in 12 starts. He had just over 2,000 passing yards and 13 touchdowns. Ahead of the 2025 season, the Titans drafted Cam Ward first overall and then it was announced that Levis needed shoulder surgery and would miss the entire year. After an underwhelming camp this year, indications are that Levis asked to be released at the end of preseason and the Jets picked him up after he cleared waivers. Let’s move onto some more in-depth analysis of what Levis brings to the table, based on in-depth research and film study. Measurables/Athleticism Levis has good size and big hands, displaying athleticism, toughness and power as a runner. He posted a 34-inch vertical and 124-inch broad jump during his combine workout. Arm Strength Levis’ arm strength is regarded as one of his best attributes and he is not afraid to rip passes into a tight window. He can also be effective on deep throws, and puts a lot of air under the ball, throwing both from the pocket and on the move. Accuracy Levis’ completion percentage in college was in the mid-60’s which is acceptable, but largely a product of the fact he threw a lot of dump-offs. To his credit, he improved his completion percentage from 58 to 63 in his second NFL season. His ball placement has been inconsistent throughout his college and pro career, but the bigger issue seems to be that he’s often late on throws. With that said, from time to time he will throw a bullseye on a tight window throw. Under pressure Levis’ pocket presence is another area that holds him back. He doesn’t seem to have a good feel for pressure and will often try to escape rather than throw the ball away. He has been sacked 69 times in his 21 career starts but some of them came as he held the ball too long or ran himself into trouble. The bigger issue for Levis is that when pressure comes, he will often panic and try to make something happen rather than cutting his losses, which can lead to some catastrophic mistakes. He has had nine passes batted down or deflected at the line and has fumbled 17 times in his career, losing 10. He does at least show some toughness in terms of being prepared to stay in the pocket and get a throw off under heavy pressure. Footwork/Technique Levis has a quick, compact release and throws a tight spiral, but he can struggle to put touch on the ball and needs to tighten up his mechanics. He doesn’t seem to trust his footwork, instead being over-reliant on off-platform throws. While he is capable of making these at times, he can sometimes be erratic as a result. Decision Making With 23 interceptions in his two years as a full-time starter in college, and 16 in 21 starts at the pro level, it’s evident that Levis isn’t afraid to take risks. However, this can lead to him being burned when he tries to force throws or is inaccurate. Moreover, he can make some really reckless decisions with the ball. In assessing his potential to become a more reliable quarterback, you have to be concerned over Levis’ inability to read the field at times. On this play, he threw to a receiver who was covered on fourth down even though another receiver was all alone on the same side of the field. His overall mindset in terms of a refusal to take sacks or throw the ball away rather than take a risk of a fumble, interception or injury can be problematic. Mobility Levis was really a run-first quarterback when he started his college career and even had a game where he rushed for 113 yards and four touchdowns after transferring to Kentucky. However, he was obviously keen to establish himself as more of a traditional passer ahead of the 2023 draft, because he hardly ran the ball at all in his final season. Levis is capable of moving around the pocket to get throws off, but ultimately lacks feel and poise in these situations. At the pro level, he’s used his legs at times but has just one touchdown and a longest gain of 21. He does display toughness and will battle for yardage as a ball carrier. However, there should also be concerns about ball security and keeping himself healthy because he can be reckless at times. Special teams Levis has not played a role on special teams at any level and would not be expected to in the NFL. Scheme Fit As noted, Levis ran the ball a lot when he was with Penn State, but did get a chance to operate in a pro style system when Liam Coen was his offensive coordinator during his first season with the Wildcats. He has been a teammate of current Jets Trevin Wallace, T’Vondre Sweat, Brant Banks, Samuel Womack, Nate Lynn and Jarvis Brownlee Jr. during his career. Injuries Levis missed the entire 2025 season after requiring shoulder surgery. He had originally suffered an injury to his AC joint in week four of the 2024 season and then aggravated that injury in the following game, causing him to be out for three weeks. In his final season in college, Levis missed a few games when he suffered a dislocated finger and an ankle injury that left him in a walking boot in the same game. He also had a hamstring issue during his rookie preseason. title: Some Long-Term Thoughts on the Jets at 2-6
summary: It may certainly be “Same Old Jets” vibes at 2-6, with another season seemingly over before we’ve even gotten through most of November. But while this team isn’t good, I do think it’s quite a bit different than the majority of the Jets teams we’ve seen over the last several years. Some previous Jets teams […]
full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NEW JERSEY - NOVEMBER 01: Braelon Allen #0 of the New York Jets runs against Hezekiah Masses #35 of the Las Vegas Raiders during their game at MetLife Stadium on November 01, 2026 in East Rutherford, New Jersey. (Photo by Al Bello/Getty Images) | Getty Images It may certainly be “Same Old Jets” vibes at 2-6, with another season seemingly over before we’ve even gotten through most of November. But while this team isn’t good, I do think it’s quite a bit different than the majority of the Jets teams we’ve seen over the last several years. Some previous Jets teams have outright sucked and actually managed to win a few games they probably shouldn’t have. This one is losing games they likely should be winning based on how they played on the field. It doesn’t make it any less frustrating, but to me, there’s been a slight difference. Here are some broader takeaways I now have after nearly half the season is complete: The Offense Has a Bright Future Through nearly half the season, as crazy as it is to say about a 2-win team, this Jets offense is probably pacing to be one of the better Jets offenses of the last 15 years or so. Let’s take a look at where some prior Jets offenses ranked through eight weeks: 29th, 17th, 32nd, 30th, 26th, and 32nd. Being 12th in EPA/Play and 10th in Success Rate is an extreme upgrade over what we’ve become accustomed to watching. Nearly any metric you choose to utilize paints this offense as, at worst, average. Even more depressingly, put this offense on some of the Jets teams in recent memory (in particular, the Saleh ones), and this Jets team would have been a legit playoff contender. Sometimes teams in small samples can have misleading metrics or stats that aren’t indicative of future performance. In this offense’s case, I don’t think that’s true. I think there’s a pretty legitimate reason to be optimistic about the offense going forward. Outside of Geno Smith yesterday, everyone who started on that offense is under contract next year. The average age of those guys was 23.8. That’s crazy young. And the majority of these guys, whether at the skill positions or on the offensive line, were early picks. This is the type of continuity the Jets have never really been able to establish on that side of the ball. At least not in recent memory. Offenses are historically proven to be way more consistent than defenses year over year. Normally, it’s much more difficult to improve upon your offense than your defense, as Jets fans unfortunately know. There’s reason to believe what we’re seeing isn’t just some random stretch of good performances, either. To me, it’s very believable that guys like Adonai Mitchell, Omar Cooper, Braelon Allen, Mason Taylor, and Kenyon Sadiq continue to improve. None of these guys have played a ton of football, and all had various traits that made them enticing as prospects. Armand Membou, Joe Tippmann, and Olu Fashanu I’d consider all to be, at the very worst, average NFL starting offensive linemen. Membou in particular has been lights out since his struggles to start the year. To me, there’s enough glimpses, whether on tape or statistically, to show that almost all these guys are NFL-caliber starters. The red-zone struggles are another story entirely, and to me, you need to look long and hard at the staff on this. It’s honestly hard to grasp how an offense can move the ball as consistently as this one does between the 20s and then struggle so much once it gets inside the red zone. Is it Reich? Is it Geno? Is it luck? I’m not quite sure. I’d love to see the correlation, but I have to think it’s pretty uncommon for an offense to perform this well between the 20s and be this bad once the field gets shorter. Regardless, due to the long-term makeup of this roster, I think it’s very plausible that the supporting cast around the quarterback just gets better and better over these next few years. A lot of this will depend on who the young future QB is going to be, but overall, there’s a lot to like here. The Record Might Be Slightly Misleading I expect to get some blowback here. And to be fair, I would fully understand it. No one wants to hear it, especially when the team just let two games against mediocre to bad teams slip away, but the Jets are probably slightly unlucky to be 2-6 right now. Looking at Net EPA/Play, the Jets are in an extremely similar tier to the Raiders, Texans, Giants, Panthers, and Ravens. All of those teams have better records than the Jets. The main problem for the Jets? They’ve been losing almost every close game they’ve been in. They’ve now blown multiple fourth-quarter leads. They have lost a whopping four games this year in which they outperformed their opponent on a Success Rate basis. This shows up in their record in one-score games. For example, The Jets are now 1-5 in one-score games. A team like the Giants? 1 loss in 5 one-score games. A 3-1-1 record. That’s a major difference. Now, I don’t want to sit here and say the players and staff deserve ZERO blame for this. They obviously do, especially when we watch them fail to execute in critical situations, both in regard to clock management and on-field performance. But simply put, most metrics show this team probably should have a win or two more than they do based on how they’ve performed. Some of it is simply bad luck. The Defense Needs Serious Attention We talked positively about the offense. I think it’s a unit where we’re beginning to see high-pick investments start to turn things around. The defense, on the other hand, is a completely different story. This defense is a mess. Top to bottom, I’m not sure this unit does one thing well. The secondary has now really begun to struggle after a strong start. The linebackers are inconsistent week over week. And the defensive front is reliant on a rookie to be a game-breaking talent despite playing only seven career games. Many, if not most, of the free agent signings have been marginal upgrades at best, and looking forward, there are very, very few long-term pieces here. How many of these guys can you feel confident will be starters for the Jets 2-3 years from now on defense? I think David Bailey is someone you can be confident about. T’Vondre Sweat also showed enough flashes where I think he’s going to be a nice long-term piece. AZ Thomas is young and has flashed a bit, but he’s been very up and down. Dane Belton has played really well, but his contract is expiring. Bottom line is, there’s not much here at all. And not only are they bad overall, they’re particularly bad on 3rd down as well as in the red zone, another major contributor to them losing games. One interception in the last 24 games tells it all, to be honest. This entire side of the ball needs serious attention in the offseason. There are a lot of assets and there will be a lot of opportunities to address it, but right now there are very few reasons to feel good about where this defense is headed. Similar to last year, I think it’s pretty much over for this unit. I would be very surprised if this unit finishes anything better than a bottom-5 unit by year’s end. The level of competition is about to increase, and they simply do not have the talent currently to compete. Special Teams Is an Underrated Problem Special teams deserves some attention here, too. This unit stinks. After finishing #1 in DVOA last year, this unit has quickly joined the bottom tier of the league. It continued yesterday with them giving up a kickoff return for a touchdown. When you consistently lose close games, special teams has to be part of the conversation. It’s an underrated reason why this team has the record it does. Braelon Allen Is Becoming the Future And then there’s Braelon Allen. I think it’s getting more and more difficult to ignore how good he’s turning into. He’s 22 years old and is already 4th in Rushing Yards Over Expected (+133), 1st in percentage of runs over expected (53.2%), and 7th in Yards Per Carry. He’s also 11th in…

title: Film Review: Eagles need their best defenders to start playing like their best defenders
summary: I wanted to see a response from the Eagles’ defense after last week. I don’t think we got much. The Commanders finished with 339 yards and averaged 5.9 yards per play. I didn’t come away from the film thinking this defense had improved significantly. Washington still had too many easy pockets and too many running […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - OCTOBER 26: Jordan Davis #90 of the Philadelphia Eagles walks off the field for halftime during the second quarter against the Dallas Cowboys at Lincoln Financial Field on October 26, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Kathryn Riley/Getty Images) | Getty Images I wanted to see a response from the Eagles’ defense after last week. I don’t think we got much. The Commanders finished with 339 yards and averaged 5.9 yards per play. I didn’t come away from the film thinking this defense had improved significantly. Washington still had too many easy pockets and too many running lanes to exploit. In fact, I think the Eagles were fortunate the Commanders didn’t have a more explosive running back. The rushing numbers could have been worse. I know that sounds strange after allowing 135 yards at 5.2 yards per carry, but some of these gaps were enormous. A better back could have turned more of those opportunities into explosive plays. Unlike the offense, I can at least see Vic Fangio trying different things. There were heavier fronts, more man coverage, and more pressure. The problem is that the changes aren’t working consistently, either. And when even Quinyon Mitchell isn’t playing well, you know this defense is in serious trouble. Let’s get into it. Defense I don’t think the run defense bounced back. That is the starting point here. The Eagles used five-man fronts and sometimes put six defenders on the line, but the Commanders still created some huge rushing lanes. Jalen Carter had an inconsistent game, which we will get to, but Jordan Davis was disappointing again. When Davis is playing well, he can occupy space and keep the linebackers clean. When he isn’t, the whole run defense looks much more vulnerable. That has been the case for a while, and it is why his recent performances bother me so much. I know he’s likely hurt, but he is still out there, so I’m only judging what’s on the field. Eagles' Defense All22 Thread vs. Washington. 1) I don't think the run defense bounced back, and I think a good running back may have had some explosive runs against this front. Even with a 5-man front (and sometimes 6!), Washington seemed to create a lot of openings in the run… pic.twitter.com/SWtYnA7Qsc — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) November 3, 2026 This is third-and-1. Look at the space the Eagles create for the offense. Both defensive tackles slant in opposite directions, and the middle of the defense opens up. You are making a short-yardage conversion far easier than it needs to be. I don’t know whether these are called slants or whether the tackles have the freedom to react to the blocks in front of them. I don’t know the answer. But whatever the rule is, the result cannot be acceptable. If the movement is called, someone has to account for the space it creates. If players choose to go around blocks, they have to understand what they are leaving behind. Linebackers can’t do anything when offensive linemen climb directly onto them. Getting around a double team is only useful if you can affect the run. If you swim away from the point of attack and allow a blocker to climb cleanly, you have made life easier for the offense. Some of the up-front movement in this game was maddening. The Eagles’ slants are so hit-and-miss. If they slant the right way, it can work. But it feels so boom/bust. 2) This is on 3rd and 1! The double slant with both DTs going in opposite directions happened again, and it opened up these huge lanes in the middle of the defense. Are the players being coached to slant in opposite directions, or are they just allowed the freedom to choose… pic.twitter.com/4mubPYuqWo — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) November 3, 2026 I have criticized Andrew Mukuba plenty, and he made more poor plays in this game. But I want to give him credit for the way he kept playing. Some defenders on this team look passive right now. Mukuba was still flying toward the football and trying to make something happen. That matters to me when things are going badly. You can question the tackling technique here, but the forced fumble is all about effort. He flies downhill and knocks the ball out of Chig Okonkwo’s hands, and Zack Baun recovers it. The turnover gave the offense possession at the Commanders’ 26-yard line and set up the Eagles’ only touchdown. Whatever else I say about Mukuba, he helped create an opportunity to win this game. 3) I think Mukuba made a number of poor plays once again in this game, but I will give him credit for how he played. Some players on this defense are going through the motions and playing very passively. Whatever you think of Mukuba (and his tackle technique here!), he is… pic.twitter.com/ZcS3bp4LUE — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) November 3, 2026 This might be the worst slant of the game. Byron Young is already aligned with a significant gap between himself and Nolan Smith. He then slants inside and makes that space even bigger. Look at the right guard and right tackle. They can head straight to the second level without dealing with a defensive lineman first. How is this supposed to work? The Eagles end up with four defenders accounting for three gaps on one side of the formation, while the run goes the other way. With a better block from the right guard, this could have been a very long gain. Jeremiah Trotter Jr. makes an excellent play to limit the damage. Asking your linebacker to rescue a rep like this is a terrible way to live. This is also why I am reluctant to judge the linebackers purely by whether they get off blocks. Trotter has limitations when a big lineman gets into his frame, but look at how easily those linemen are reaching him. The defensive front has to give him a chance. 4) This has to be the worst slant of the game. Someone, explain what is going on. Byron Young is already lined up with a huge gap between himself and Nolan Smith. Then he makes it even wider by slanting inside. Look at the size of the gap! Look at the RG and RT! They can just… pic.twitter.com/HkbqCL0rRX — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) November 3, 2026 The run defense was bad, but the pass rush was equally frustrating. Fangio cannot consistently affect the quarterback with four rushers, and it is killing his defense. Here, the Eagles drop both edge defenders and bring a linebacker, changing where the rush comes from. It makes very little difference. Jayden Daniels gets a pocket that most quarterbacks would happily take all night. Daniels can easily see the field and deliver the football. You can ask the secondary to cover well, but you cannot keep giving an NFL quarterback this much comfort. The Eagles generated pressure on only 30.3% of dropbacks despite the higher blitz rate. At some point, someone has to beat a block. 5) The run defense was not good, but the pass rush was equally bad. Vic Fangio just can't win with 4, and it's killing his scheme. They drop both edge defenders here and send a LB, but nothing comes. You will not see many better pockets in the NFL. Look how easy this is for… pic.twitter.com/K8Sce69myq — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) November 3, 2026 The Commanders’ under-center outside zone caused problems, too. They used motion away from the run to pull Cooper DeJean out of the box and change the numbers for the run fit. That is a straightforward way to make a defender move before attacking the space he leaves, and the Eagles didn’t handle it well enough. Once again, watch the defensive line. All three interior defenders move left, and the run goes right. Look at the gap between Moro Ojomo and Arnold Ebiketie. The back has far too much room to work with. I know I sound like a broken record, but this looks like a fundamentally poor run defense. The Commanders ran outside successfully, especially from under center. Across all concepts, they gained 106 yards on 17 carries from under center, compared with 29 yards on nine shotgun runs. That difference fits what we are seeing here. 6) The Eagles had a real issue with under-center outside…

title: Eagles on pace for worst offense since 1998: How did it get to this point?
summary: There’s no argument the Philadelphia Eagles offense is bad. The 2026 unit is historically bad. The Eagles are 29th in the NFL in points per game (17.1) and 30th in points per drive (1.61). They’re 32nd in yards per game (265.3) and yards per play (4.4), far from the offensive juggernauts the franchise has posted […]
full_text: LANDOVER, MARYLAND - NOVEMBER 01: Head coach Nick Sirianni of the Philadelphia Eagles reacts during the fourth quarter against the Washington Commanders at Northwest Stadium on November 01, 2026 in Landover, Maryland. (Photo by Patrick Smith/Getty Images) | Getty Images There’s no argument the Philadelphia Eagles offense is bad. The 2026 unit is historically bad. The Eagles are 29th in the NFL in points per game (17.1) and 30th in points per drive (1.61). They’re 32nd in yards per game (265.3) and yards per play (4.4), far from the offensive juggernauts the franchise has posted this century — whether that would be from Andy Reid, Chip Kelly, Doug Pederson, or even Nick Sirianni. There has only been one Eagles team that has put up fewer points than the 2026 squad this century. The 2012 Eagles averaged just 16.6 points per game, and they ended up with a 4-12 record in what would be Reid’s last season. The 1.61 points per possession is also the lowest since 2012. The 265.3 yards per game is the lowest through eight games since 1999 (244.0), and that Eagles team started 1-7 before rallying to finish 5-11 (year one under Reid). The 4.42 yards per play is the lowest since 1999 (3.92), and only the 1998 offense was worse than those two (3.73). Those 1998 Eagles were an abomination. They were 30th out of 30 teams in points per game (10.1) and yards per game (261.7). That was the only time in franchise history the Eagles finished in the 30s in points and yards per game. If points per possession and yards per possession were measured in 1998, the Eagles would have been last in those categories too. The 2026 Eagles have the worst offense this century, and is the worst Eagles offense since 1998. That unit had Bobby Hoying start the seaosn before a rotating carousel of quarterbacks that included Rodney Peete and Koy Detmer. The Eagles went from Hoying to Peete before returning to Hoying and eventually Detmer. So how did the 2026 Eagles get to this point? How did they go from a top-10 offense, to middle of the back, to what they are now — all over the past year? There were quite a few contributing factors towards the Eagles offense reaching historically bad levels for the franchise. 1. Jeff Stoutland deciding not to return The Eagles offensive line was middle of the pack last season, the first time in the Nick Sirianni era the offensive line wasn’t a top-10 unit. Outside of Lane Johnson, all the other starters on the offensive line started 14+ games — so injuries didn’t play a factor in the mediocrity. Stoutland’s role as run-game coordinator also regressed, as Nick Sirianni and former offensive coordinator Kevin Patullo began incorporating different run designs to the offense. With these changes in place, Stoutland reportedly wasn’t consulted about them as his title was in name only. With Stoutland not having a prominent voice as in years past, he decided to step aside after the 2025 season. Chris Kuper was hired as the offensive line coach, despite the Minnesota Vikings ranking 31st in sack rate (11.0%) and 27th in pressure rate allowed per dropback (39.8%) last season. The Vikings were 26th in sack rate (8.0%) and 29th in pressure rate (37.8%) from 2022 to 2025 under Kuper. The Eagles offensive line under Kuper this year? They are 24th in sack rate (7.9%) and 28th in pressure rate (42.7%). They were 19th in sack rate (6.7%) and 20th in pressure rate (35.4%) last year. 2. The Kevin Patullo hire, followed by Sean Mannion hire The Eagles were coming off a Super Bowl victory in the 2024 season, but offensive coordinator Kellen Moore was leaving after one season to take the New Orleans Saints head coaching job. Philadelphia didn’t have a deep opol of candidates for the offensive coordinator role since the Eagles played into February, so Patullo was promoted from passing game coordinator to offensive coordinator. Patullo was passing game coordinator for four seasons, and came over from the Indianapolis Colts with Nick Sirianni. His lone season as offensive coordinator was a disaster, as the scoring dropped from 27.2 points per game to 22.3 (seventh to 19th) and points per possession from 2.50 to 2.00 (eighth to 21st). Yards per game dropped from 367.2 to 3111.2 (seventh to 24th) and yards per play from 5.6 to 5.2 (11th to 19th). The Eagles went from 24.7% in three-and-out rate to 36.0% (21st to fourth). The offense got worse with Sean Mannion hired to replace Patullo, as the changes to the offensive scheme has made the unit worst. Injuries to the offense haven’t helped (Jordan Mailata is the only player to start every game), but the Eagles are historically bad on offense. To showcase Mannion’s struggles, look at the second half of games.The Eagles average 4.6 points per game and 3.9 yards per play (both 32nd in the NFL). The third quarter is even worse, ranking 32nd in points per game (1.6), yards per game (43.0), yards per carry (2.5), yards per play (3.1), and yards per attempt (4.0). The offense went from bad to worse. 3. Lane Johnson retiring Johnson’s sudden retirement played a factor in how this offense has performed, as the Eagles haven’t won a game since his sudden retirement after Week 4. The Eagles are 0-3 since Johnson retired, and 3-8 in games he’s missed since last season (including playoffs). The Eagles were 122-63-1 with Johnson in the lineup, a .659 win percentage (including postseason). They are 18-30 without him, a .375 win percentage. Johnson’s replacement at right tackle, Markel Bell, has had a rough start to his career. Bell has allowed five sacks in his three starts, and is tied for second amongst right tackles in most sacks allowed. He has allowed a 7.3% pressure rate per dropback this season — seventh-worst amongst right tackles in the NFL. Right tackle is a new position for Bell, and he wasn’t expected to play this year. Bell was expected to take over for Johnson after this season, just three years after moving up to FBS from Holmes Community College. The Eagles were going to have to adjust to life without Johnson at some point. This wasn’t expected to happen this season. 4. Jalen Hurts out for the season Any time a team loses their franchise quarterback hurts. What Jalen Hurts over the past month is way bigge rthan football. Hurts was discovered to have a having a superficial blood clot in his leg following the team’s trip to London, which was discovered before he played in the team’s Week 5 game against the Jaguars. An ultrasound in the middle of that week found the blood clot had moved to his lungs, which put Hurts on blood thinners and ruled him out for the season. The Eagles are 58-25 in games Hurts has started since he became the full-time starting quarterback in 2021, a .699 win percentage. Without Hurts, the Eagles are 3-7 in 10 games — a .300 win percentage. The Eagles passing game has struggled with Hurts, but he has found ways to win football games. They just aren’t getting that when Hurts isn’t on the field. In the three games Tanner McKee has started, the Eagles are 32nd in yards per play (4.2), 31st in yards per attempt (5.6), and 29th in offensive points per game (15.0). McKee has completed 63.2% of his passes for 638 yards with 2 TD, 2 INT, and a 76.6 passer rating. He is 31st out of 32 qualified quarterbacks in yards per attempt (5.6) and 26th in passer rating. There is a massive drop off from Hurts to McKee, who couldn’t beat out Andy Dalton for the QB2 job this summer. 5. Failure to address TE position The Eagles didn’t have the depth at tight end in the 2025 season, despite Dallas Goedert having 11 touchdown catches. Goedert had 591 receiving yards and the rest of the tight ends had a combined 116. While the Eagles ranked 22nd in tight end receiving yards, they also had a significant hole in blocking at the position. The Eagles addressed the position by signing Johnny Mundt to a one-year contract as the blocking tight end and drafting Eli Stowers in the second round to be the TE2 behind Goedert. Stowers struggled to…

title: NFL Power Rankings: Week 9 Edition
summary: Now that Week 8 of the 2026 NFL season is in the books, it’s time for an incredibly meaningful and serious exercise: NFL Power Rankings! What differentiates these rankings from all others is that they’re THE only truly accurate ones in the entire universe. Hard to believe, I know. But it’s true. Let’s take a […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - OCTOBER 26: Philadelphia Eagles head coach Nick Sirianni looks on before a game against the Dallas Cowboys at Lincoln Financial Field on October 26, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Emilee Chinn/Getty Images) | Getty Images Now that Week 8 of the 2026 NFL season is in the books, it’s time for an incredibly meaningful and serious exercise: NFL Power Rankings ! What differentiates these rankings from all others is that they’re THE only truly accurate ones in the entire universe. Hard to believe, I know. But it’s true. Let’s take a look at how all 32 teams stack up. BLG’S WEEK 9 POWER RANKINGS 1 – Chicago Bears (LW: 5) – The Bears going into Seattle and dominating the reigning Super Bowl champions was really impressive. This team looks like a force to be reckoned with, especially after adding Jeffery Simmons to their defense. Overall strong combination of talent and coaching. Feels like there are NFL teams mastering 4D chess while the Eagles are struggling with tic-tac-toe. https://t.co/kGjci7JymF — Brandon Lee Gowton (@BrandonGowton) November 3, 2026 2 – San Francisco 49ers (LW: 2) – The 49ers had a solid bye with Seattle (NFC West threat) and Minnesota (No. 1 seed threat) losing. They’ll host a spunky Raiders team in Week 9. 3 – Buffalo Bills (Last Week: 3) – The Bills have lost one game this season and it was by three points to a division rival. As their conference’s only one-loss team, they have a navigable path to the No. 1 seed in the AFC playoff picture. 4 – Kansas City Chiefs (LW: 1) – Make that two straight losses for the Chiefs. This team needs some help ahead of the NFL trade deadline and they’ll probably make some moves to get it. 5 – Detroit Lions (LW: 7) – The Lions are the only NFC North team yet to lose a game in their very competitive division. They continue to be ravaged by injuries but they shouldn’t be slept on. 6 – Minnesota Vikings (LW: 4) – The Vikings weren’t going to stay undefeated with how inept their offense has been. Their defense is going to make teams really earn wins over them, though. 7 – Jacksonville Jaguars (LW: 9) – The Jags own the NFL’s best point differential at +85. The next closest team is the 49ers at +58. Jacksonville also ranks second in DVOA. They’re a real title contender. 8 – Seattle Seahawks (LW: 6) – If the season ended today, which it doesn’t, the Seahawks would actually be on the outside looking in with seven teams ahead of them in the NFC playoff picture. This is still a good team but they’re not an elite team like they were last year. 9 – Cincinnati Bengals (LW: 8) – Despite being 12.5-point home favorites, the Bengals needed overtime to beat the lowly Titans. Not really ideal to allow Cam Ward to log the third-best passer rating of his career against your defense. 10 – New England Patriots (LW: 11) – It has not been a great vibes season for the Pats but they’re 4-1 in their last five games. Drake Maye has thrown 14 touchdowns to two interceptions for a 122.2 passer rating during that stretch. 11 – Los Angeles Rams (LW: 12) – The Rams are benefiting from a softer part of their schedule. It also sounds like Myles Garrett could be back soon. Maybe they’ll make a run. 12 – Denver Broncos (LW: 13) – Unfortunately, Sean Payton is a pretty good coach. The Broncos are tied for the NFL’s best record against the spread this season, a sign that this team is outperforming their expectations. 13 – Las Vegas Raiders (LW: 15) – The Raiders broke their four-game losing streak with a thrilling win over the Jets. Very interested to see how they fare over their next three games: at San Francisco, vs. Seattle, at Denver. That stretch will be a litmus test for just how real this team is. 14 – Green Bay Packers (LW: 16) – The Packers are lacking a signature win over a good team this season. They’ve beaten lesser competition but have yet to come out on top against a big dog. (I’m not counting the Bears game that Tyson Bagent started.) 15 – Pittsburgh Steelers (LW: 20) – Do we have to take the Steelers seriously? They’re currently the top team in the AFC North, though Cincy’s ceiling appears to be higher. 16 – Baltimore Ravens (LW: 10) – Oof. The Ravens are taking a big fall here after losing both Lamar Jackson and Tyler Huntley to injury. Undrafted rookie Joe Fagnano might start in Week 9 even though he’s banged up as well. Not looking good. 17 – Dallas Cowboys (LW: 14) – The Dallas defense is a joke and Brian Schottenheimer is doing a bad job. That being said, Dak Prescott deserves more blame than he’s getting. The Cowboys actually got a stop in overtime after the Cardinals got the ball first. Only needing to move into Brandon Aubrey’s long field goal range while playing at home, Prescott oversaw a drive that netted -5 yards in three plays and resulted in a punt. That’s a gotta have it moment for the highest paid quarterback in the NFL and he came up extremely small in a huge spot. Hardly the first time! 18 – New York Giants (LW: 18) – The G-Men are returning from their bye as road betting favorites in Philly for the first time since 2009. New York is also looking to boost their roster with more talent ahead of the NFL trade deadline. They just might win the NFC East. 19 – Cleveland Browns (LW: 17) – The Browns had a chance to make people take them more seriously by beating the Steelers in Pittsburgh. They did not come close to making it happen. 20 – Tampa Bay Buccaneers (LW: 22) – Obligatory mention of the Bucs winning in Week 8 despite not completing a pass. The Bucs are perhaps following the 2024 Eagles script of just running the hell out of the ball. Not a bad strategy if teams can’t stop it! 21 – Carolina Panthers (LW: 19) – Two of the three Panthers’ win this season have come against depth quarterbacks (Cooper Rush and Tanner McKee). They’re not scaring anybody. 22 – Atlanta Falcons (LW: 21) – I continue to maintain that the Falcons are the NFL’s most unpredictable team on a weekly basis. They followed up an impressive Week 7 over the 49ers by losing to a team that couldn’t even complete a single pass against them. 23 – Arizona Cardinals (LW: 27) – Minshew Mania is running wild on you, brother! The Cards are one win away from surpassing their 2026 projected win total (3.5 games) with nine games left to play. Props to Mike LaFleur for helping his team overachieve expectations. 24 – New Orleans Saints (LW: 23) – The Saints are returning from their bye to host the Sheuder Sanders-led Browns. We’ll see if Kellen Moore can make a run in a weak NFC South. 25 – Houston Texans (LW: 24) – The Texans are returning from their bye to play the Bolts in California. If Houston can’t win this game, stick a fork in them. 26 – Washington Commanders (LW: 28) – The Commanders didn’t exactly look amazing in a win over the Eagles but, hey, they bought some time to keep their season alive in a weak division. We’ll see if they can build on this victory with the Rams, Giants (massive game in the NFC East), and Bengals up next. 27 – Miami Dolphins (LW 29) – After losing their first three games by double digits, the Dolphins’ last four games have been decided by one possession (1-3 in that stretch). title: Eagles News: Moro Ojomo is drawing “real interest” ahead of the NFL trade deadline
summary: Welcome to The Linc, the daily Philadelphia Eagles links roundup at Bleeding Green Nation! I just don’t believe the Eagles are seriously interested in paying Moro Ojomo after signing Jalen Carter and Jordan Davis to big-money contract extensions. Unless they move on from Carter or Davis … or plan to do so in the offseason. […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PA - OCTOBER 04: Philadelphia Eagles defensive tackle Moro Ojomo #97 waves to the fans during the game between the Los Angeles Rams and the Philadelphia Eagles on October 4, 2026 at Lincoln Financial Field in Philadelphia, PA.(Photo by Andy Lewis/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Welcome to The Linc, the daily Philadelphia Eagles links roundup at Bleeding Green Nation! I just don’t believe the Eagles are seriously interested in paying Moro Ojomo after signing Jalen Carter and Jordan Davis to big-money contract extensions. Unless they move on from Carter or Davis … or plan to do so in the offseason. Seems to me like they’ll trade Ojomo ahead of the deadline. If there isn’t a great offer, they can just keep him and hope he factors in to their compensatory pick formula. Now, what can they get for him? Hard to say for sure. I think some might overstate his value considering he has zero sacks this season and only six in his career. But he’s better than those numbers would indicate. Maybe a third-round pick? Let’s get to the Philadelphia Eagles news and links … NFL Week 9 latest intel, buzz questions, fantasy tips and trade deadline news – ESPN This could be for edge or interior help, in part because the Jaguars have versatile players such as Travon Walker who can play multiple spots up front. Eagles defensive tackle Moro Ojomo is a person of interest here, though Philly is inclined to keep and potentially extend him. […] Speaking of Philadelphia, my sense is the Eagles could be trading some players but likely won’t engage in a rebuild. As one source pointed out, that’s not in the Eagles’ organizational DNA. We already know they aren’t trading running back Saquon Barkley. Look, let’s not be naive — general manager Howie Roseman will take advantage of good value if it’s there, and supporting players are surely on the radar. But dealing big names would be a mild surprise. Ojomo will be a test of the Eagles’ transitional state. There’s real interest in him (from Jacksonville and others). Whether Philly acts on that interest will tell a lot. Eagles thoughts: Nick Sirianni’s staff stays put, questions at QB and Moro Ojomo’s trade value – The Athletic Moro Ojomo is a fascinating player to watch during the next week leading up to the trade deadline. The Eagles don’t like letting talented homegrown defensive linemen out the door — and they’re feeling the pain of seeing Milton Williams and Josh Sweat go elsewhere — but it’s hard to see a scenario where Ojomo returns next season with Jalen Carter and Jordan Davis still on the roster. Sports Illustrated reported last week that the Eagles are telling teams they’re not interested in trading Ojomo and want to keep him, but will they pay three defensive tackles top-of-the-league money (assuming that’s what Ojomo commands on the open market)? They seem to have made their choice when they signed Carter and Davis. “Howie (Roseman) and (Jeffrey) Lurie mean so much to me for giving me this opportunity to play for this team,” Roseman said. “I think I was the 23rd DT picked up? If we could make it work, I love playing for the city; I love working hard for the city. I want to produce results for the city. I hate letting them down and being 2-5 like we are. … I mean, I don’t think any door is shut. I wouldn’t say that. You don’t know what the future holds.” It’s a nice thought. It doesn’t seem realistic. The Eagles would be smart to get compensation for Ojomo now, especially in what could be a seller’s market at defensive tackle. If they can land a third-round pick, it would be better than any potential compensatory pick in 2028. Perhaps they can find a way to get a second-round pick. Ojomo said he doesn’t know what will happen — “I just work here,” he said — but he has the talent to help a contending team down the stretch. It hasn’t shown in his statistics this year. I believe in the player, and he’s also a value-add in the locker room. The Eagles will miss him if he’s gone. It’s the reality of the NFL. “I like the way I started the season a little bit,” Ojomo said. “The last couple games being banged up and all that, I want to get back to kind of playing confident, fast. I think that ‘get off’ is one of the things I do at a really high level. That’s one of the things I want to kind of lock in on these next however many games.” Eagles-Commanders Film Review: The idea that Jalen Hurts was holding this offense back should be finished by now – BGN I’m struggling to get particularly angry about this offense anymore. There were times when watching the Eagles lose 27-10 to the Commanders bored me. We keep seeing players asked to do things that don’t suit them. Every week, I sit down hoping to see something different, and every week, it feels like I’m writing about the same problems. The Eagles scored their final points with 4:27 remaining in the first quarter. There was an awful lot of football left to sit through after that. The idea that Jalen Hurts was holding this offense back, and that everything would look dramatically different with a quarterback who preferred playing under center and throwing over the middle, should be finished by now. Tanner McKee hasn’t transformed anything. It’s the same offense, with the same limitations, and very little downfield passing game. That doesn’t mean Hurts was playing perfectly or that McKee has played well. He hasn’t. It means changing the quarterback was never going to solve all of this. Bowen: As the Eagles lurch further into the throes of disaster, shouldn’t somebody down there get at least a little upset about this?- PHLY Eagles I would not make a good NFL head coach or coordinator for many reasons. High on that list would be, I can’t imagine being at ground level of a disaster like we currently are experiencing with the Eagles, and not reacting with urgency, frustration, and alarm. The Eagles’ coordinators held their weekly media briefings Tuesday. I’m smart enough to know that the manner they convey to reporters doesn’t necessarily mirror their private reactions. They don’t want their players to think they are panicking. Even so, the matter-of-fact, “we just need to tweak this or that” patter at this point in the season is jarring to the ear. Six losses in a row? The last three by double figures? All to teams that currently have losing records? Defensive coordinator Vic Fangio has been known to get acerbic when his players aren’t performing to his standards. Not this season, which is shaping up as the worst by far in Fangio’s three years with the Eagles. Vic seems a bit distant these days, almost sedated. When asked to comment on specific players, he either praises them, as he has done repeatedly when asked about Cooper DeJean’s uncharacteristic struggles, or refers to injuries they are working through. 2026 NFL offensive line rankings: Lions retain top spot, Colts fall without Quenton Nelson – PFF 22) EAGLES — Left guard Landon Dickerson had his best game of the season, amassing a 72.8 PFF grade in the Eagles’ loss to the Washington Commanders on Sunday night. Having permitted nine pressures from 75 pass-blocking snaps in his previous two starts, he allowed just two on 44 snaps this week. However, the right side of the line was ineffective, with Tyler Steen and Markel Bell combining to give up eight pressures. In Roob’s Eagles Stats: A big pile of misery broken up by tiny encouraging blips – NBCSP The Eagles have had fewer than 350 yards of offense in all eight games so far this year, with a high of 341 at Tennessee. This is the first time in more than half a century they’ve opened a season with eight games under 350 net yards. Last time it happened was the first 11 games of the 1971 season, when their yardage high was 315 yards in a 37-14 loss to the Bengals in the season opener at Riverfront Stadium. Going back to last year, the Eagles have gone 10 straight games with fewer than 350 yards, their longest streak since an 11-gamer over…

title: Eagles waive player they traded for last year
summary: The Philadelphia Eagles are waiving Jakorian Bennett, as noted by the NFL’s November 3 personnel notice. The Eagles previously opened Bennett’s 21-day practice window to return from injured reserve on October 14. The team was coming up on the deadline to either 1) activate him to the roster or 2) shut him down for the […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - JANUARY 04: Jakorian Bennett #23 of the Philadelphia Eagles looks on against the Washington Commanders at Lincoln Financial Field on January 04, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Mitchell Leff/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Philadelphia Eagles are waiving Jakorian Bennett, as noted by the NFL’s November 3 personnel notice. The Eagles previously opened Bennett’s 21-day practice window to return from injured reserve on October 14. The team was coming up on the deadline to either 1) activate him to the roster or 2) shut him down for the remainder of the 2026 season. Instead, the Eagles chose door No. 3 and waived him from IR to apparently allow him to catch on with a new team. Or perhaps he could return to Philly on the practice squad if he does land elsewhere? Finding themselves in need of corner help, the Eagles originally acquired Bennett in a trade with the Las Vegas Raiders last summer. There was hope the 2023 fourth-round pick might be able to contribute but he ended up logging just 98 defensive snaps (69 of which came in Week 18 last year with the Eagles resting starters) and 58 defensive snaps in 2025. Bennett began the 2026 season on IR after getting injured in the preseason. Had he stayed healthy, he might’ve pushed for the top backup outside cornerback role that has instead been claimed by veteran Jonathan Jones. But with Jones recently getting hurt and being a 33-year-old playing on a one-year deal, it could’ve made sense to put Bennett in that role instead. He could’ve even been in line to see starting snaps with the Eagles potentially set to move Riq Woolen ahead of the NFL trade deadline. Instead, Bennett is gone. Meanwhile, the Raiders are still utilizing Thomas Booker IV, whom the Eagles gave up to get Bennett. Booker logged the third-most defensive tackle snaps for Las Vegas last year and the fourth-most so far this season. OTHER NEWS: The Eagles also released wide receiver Quentin Skinner from the practice squad after originally signing him last week .

title: Vic Fangio on Jonathan Greenard: ‘Practice is important. He’s had next to none.’
summary: The Eagles defense has been inconsistent throughout the season, something defensive coordinator Vic Fangio highlighted when he spoke to reporters on Tuesday. He talked about self-scouting, what he saw from different players, and why Jonathan Greenard’s lack of practice has been so impactful. The DC also provided a short recap for their Sunday night loss […]
full_text: Photo by Mitchell Leff/Getty Images | Getty Images The Eagles defense has been inconsistent throughout the season, something defensive coordinator Vic Fangio highlighted when he spoke to reporters on Tuesday. He talked about self-scouting, what he saw from different players, and why Jonathan Greenard’s lack of practice has been so impactful. The DC also provided a short recap for their Sunday night loss to the Commanders. “Tough loss. We have to find a way to win those low-scoring games. We’ve done it here in the past. We’ve gotta be able to do it.” Here’s what else the DC had to say: On Jonathan Greenard “What I see, is a guy that’s had very, very little practice. I mean, when I say very little, miniscule. He missed all of training camp, missed the first two weeks of the season — no practice. Started practicing, was on a pitch count, played 19 plays, was gonna increase the next week, he got hurt early in that game. Didn’t finish that game. Didn’t play the next game. And, he’s been limited in practice. Contrary to some people’s popular belief, practice is important. He’s had next to none.” The only way to overcome that is with practice, explained Fangio. He noted that there was no magic pill or portion to catch up, no amount of watching tape or walkthroughs will make up for practice reps. Even for a veteran like Greenard, the DC was clear that practice matter. “Practice is important for everybody.” He went on to talk about Greenard is still finding his groove, and those practice reps are what will allow him to feel more comfortable in the system. It’s not for a lack of want to, or lack of effort, it’s just something that takes time executing what they’re asking of him and then carrying that over into games. Fangio also said that the bye week won’t offer any kind of catch-up period, noting that most teams don’t practice during the bye week, but that time might help Greenard get healthier. On Jordan Davis “He’s been not quite as good as he had been in the past, these last couple weeks. Think he’s got a little problem with his hand there, but he can be better. But we love Jordan [Davis] and he can get there.” On their self-scouting process Fangio said that they’re constantly evaluating things, and that it wouldn’t make sense to wait for the bye week to self-scout. It’s something they do every week. As for how he feels about their run defense to this point in the season, the DC said it’s been inconsistent. He thought it was okay, borderline good, but then at the end of the game gave up that 33-yarder. Fangio said that he needs to do a better job of coaching it and calling it, and then the players need to execute. On the Giants’ offense “They’ve got a really good offense They’ve got skill at the receiving position. They did a nice job raiding the Ravens, not just for John [Harbuagh], but with [Isaiah] Likely and [Patrick] Ricard. They got a lot of the Ravens-type offense that they had when Greg [Roman], and they’ve intermixed Kansas City-type passing in there with Matt [Nagy], and they’ve got it going right now. They got good wide outs, good tight ends, two good backs, and the quarterback is commanding in a short amount of time, and has really done a nice job,. For them to get [J.J. McCarthy] for a sixth round pick is a steal.” Other notables He said that Andrew Mukuba overall has had a good season, and that there were some plays he’d like back, but the safety is a good young player who he expects to be a good player for a long time. Jeremiah Trotter Jr. will continue to get playing time, and Fangio noted they’ll have to see about Jihaad Campbell ’s health moving forward. The DC admitted that there might be some wavering in the confidence of the defense, while asking what comes first, winning or confidence. As we get closer to the trade deadline, Fangio said that he doesn’t feel the need to talk to any players about rumors circulating, but he would if he felt any were catching steam that was not true.

title: Eagles News: Chris Kuper could be in trouble
summary: Welcome to The Linc, the daily Philadelphia Eagles links roundup at Bleeding Green Nation! Speaking on Monday, Nick Sirianni said the Eagles aren’t going to make any changes. But just because he said that publicly doesn’t mean things could be happening behind the scenes. Something’s gotta give with the team losing six straight and not […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PA - JULY 30: Philadelphia Eagles offensive line coach Chris Kuper is shown during the Philadelphia Eagles training camp on July 30th, 2026 at Jefferson Health Training Complex in Philadelphia, PA. (Photo by Terence Lewis/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Welcome to The Linc, the daily Philadelphia Eagles links roundup at Bleeding Green Nation! Speaking on Monday, Nick Sirianni said the Eagles aren’t going to make any changes. But just because he said that publicly doesn’t mean things could be happening behind the scenes. Something’s gotta give with the team losing six straight and not showing signs of getting better. The Eagles’ offensive line looks like they don’t know what they’re doing. Let’s get to the Philadelphia Eagles news and links … Short Term Stuff – Iggles Blitz It really is hard to judge Sean Mannion accurately. He’s had to deal with an insane amount of injuries. The players all speak highly of him. There haven’t been guys ripping him to the media on the record and we aren’t hearing complaints from anonymous sources. At the same time, the offense is historically bad. They can’t be ignored. I would leave Mannion in place for now. The bye week is coming up soon. That will give them a chance to really focus on self-scouting and try to find some fixes. Chris Kuper has also been dealt a tough hand. He thought he was getting 4/5ths of the OL that led the team to a SB win in 2024. Oops. Two of them are no longer with the team. He has already had multiple starters at LG, C, and RG. Jeff Stoutland had injuries last year and the OL wasn’t good so this is not all on Kuper. Still, the confusion and blown blocking assignments is something new. And that is on Kuper. Which offenses are allowing the most free runners? Percentage of pass plays with an unblocked pressure in 2026, through November 1. Highest allowed first: Eagles: 18.2% Dolphins: 15.8% Panthers: 13.9% Colts: 13.5% Commanders: 13.3% Patriots: 12.1% Ravens: 11.9% Texans: 11.9%… — Ryan Paganetti (@RyanPaganetti) November 2, 2026 Eagles-Commanders what we learned: Offensive line miscues should build pressure on Chris Kuper – PHLY Eagles During his Monday news conference, Sirianni said he won’t make changes to the coaching staff roles. He also defended Kuper’s effort behind the scenes. “We’re not coaching well enough right now and we’re not playing well enough right now,” Sirianni said Monday. “I know we’re speaking offensively. Right now we’re not doing all the things we need to do to win football games. And that falls on everyone’s shoulders. … Chris is coaching his ass off. He’s fighting his ass off. He’s coaching his ass off on a daily basis. You guys don’t get to see that on a daily basis. You get to see it for three hours on Sunday. … I know he’s giving players good tools to use fundamentally and helping them become the best players they possibly can be.” It might make more sense to wait until after this Sunday’s matchup against the New York Giants to take advantage of the following bye week before making changes, but there’s a legitimate argument that the Eagles pass protection calls are currently limiting the team from actually evaluating the group for the future. Eagles vs. Commanders: The good, the bad, and the ugly – BGN It was revealed last week that numerous sources in and around the Eagles told Bleeding Green Nation that they still trusted and believed in head coach Nick Sirianni and Fangio. That Sirianni still had the locker room. They still somehow believed that Sirianni could turn around this disaster, because he proved he could win. But where there was once unbending support for learning-on-the-job offensive coordinator Sean Mannion and offensive line coach Chris Kuper, that was bending. It has changed to doubt as the Eagles kept sinking. Mannion simply seems overwhelmed. Kuper can’t foresee where unblocked pressures could come from. That was last week. Let’s make a very strong—but very correct assumption—Mannion and Kuper will not be here next season. Maybe sooner than that. Maybe. 13 young Eagles worth watching in what’s left of a lost season – NBCSP QB Joe Milton: Maybe the Eagles really do just ride it out with backup quarterback Tanner McKee in place of Jalen Hurts. But there’s some definite intrigue with Milton. The Eagles signed him off the Cowboys’ practice squad on Oct. 16 and it didn’t take long for Milton to supplant Cole Payton as the new backup. The 26-year-old Milton (6-5, 236) has played in just five career games but the former sixth-round pick has plenty of arm talent. His highlight reel from his 2023 season at Tennessee is littered with highlight plays. Milton has a big arm and can elude pressure. He just wasn’t very consistent. But in this lost season, if McKee continues to struggle, it would be fun to see Milton get a chance. NFC Hierarchy/Obituary: Week 9 edition – PhillyVoice In Week 5, the Eagles probably played their best game of the season in a loss to the Jaguars, but it was also the week where they may have failed spectacularly as an organization, allowing Jalen Hurts to board two intercontinental flights to and from London and play in a game despite knowing that he had a superficial blood clot in his leg. He would eventually be diagnosed with deep vein thrombosis (“DVT”) and bilateral pulmonary emboli (blood clots in the lungs). His season was over at that point. Investigations into what exactly happened from a medical perspective are most certainly not over. And then the last three games, without Hurts, the Eagles got their teeth kicked in by a trio of teams that have a combined 5-12-1 record this season when they don’t get to play the Eagles. Against those three teams, the Eagles got outscored by 43 points and outgained by 343 yards. Seven things Solak thinks for NFL Week 9: Bucs atop NFC South? RB trades coming? – ESPN This trade would be a massive win for the Eagles. Eagles trade TE Johnny Mundt and a 2027 seventh-round pick to the Vikings for a 2027 sixth-round pick. The Vikings might be a headliner for Jonathan Taylor-trade hype, but my sense is that they’re really looking for a strong blocking tight end after the season-ending injury to Josh Oliver in Week 3. Mundt was in Minnesota from 2022 to 2024 with coach Kevin O’Connell and is currently losing his TE2 job in Philadelphia, as rookie Eli Stowers and veteran Grant Calcaterra return from injured reserve. Mundt played 13 snaps in the Eagles’ loss to the Commanders on Sunday night, his season low. He’ll give the Vikings more reliable point-of-attack blocking for a nominal price. Eagles’ odds to pick No. 1 overall in the NFL draft are stronger than you think. That makes QB the only question. – Inquirer The reality of the Eagles’ present moment is one that can define their next 5 to 10 years. After another listless performance in a 27-10 loss to the Commanders, the Eagles are almost surely going to end up with a draft pick in the realm where franchise quarterbacks are most often selected. They have a very real chance at landing the No. 1 overall pick. If they don’t earn it outright, they could have an opportunity to trade for it. If they don’t have an opportunity to trade for the pick itself, they could have an opportunity to trade for the incumbent quarterback of the team that does wind up with the pick. Right now, pole position belongs to the Chargers, who also happen to have a 28-year-old quarterback who has received MVP votes. This is not an argument that Justin Herbert is a better quarterback than Hurts. It certainly isn’t an argument that his resume is better. Likewise for Drew Mestemaker, or CJ Carr, or Arch Manning, or any of the other college quarterbacks who mock drafts have targeted as potential first-round picks. The argument is that the Eagles must decide where they stand in each of these individual cases. It’s not even an argument. It’s just the way an organization must handle its business, same as every year. Except, this year,…

title: Eagles-Commanders Film Review: The idea that Jalen Hurts was holding this offense back should be finished by now
summary: I’m struggling to get particularly angry about this offense anymore. There were times when watching the Eagles lose 27-10 to the Commanders bored me. We keep seeing players asked to do things that don’t suit them. Every week, I sit down hoping to see something different, and every week, it feels like I’m writing about […]
full_text: Aug 7, 2025; Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, USA; Philadelphia Eagles head coach Nick Sirianni talks with quarterback Tanner McKee (16) in a game against the Cincinnati Bengals at Lincoln Financial Field. Mandatory Credit: Bill Streicher-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect I’m struggling to get particularly angry about this offense anymore. There were times when watching the Eagles lose 27-10 to the Commanders bored me. We keep seeing players asked to do things that don’t suit them. Every week, I sit down hoping to see something different, and every week, it feels like I’m writing about the same problems. The Eagles scored their final points with 4:27 remaining in the first quarter. There was an awful lot of football left to sit through after that. The idea that Jalen Hurts was holding this offense back, and that everything would look dramatically different with a quarterback who preferred playing under center and throwing over the middle, should be finished by now. Tanner McKee hasn’t transformed anything. It’s the same offense, with the same limitations, and very little downfield passing game. That doesn’t mean Hurts was playing perfectly or that McKee has played well. He hasn’t. It means changing the quarterback was never going to solve all of this. The Eagles finished with 268 yards at 3.9 yards per play, and 69 of those yards came on the final possession with the game already gone. Their only touchdown followed a takeaway that gave them the ball at the Commanders’ 26-yard line. Injuries matter, obviously, but Sean Mannion and Nick Sirianni still have to put a functioning offense on the field. Right now, I don’t see the staff finding enough answers or showing much willingness to move away from what keeps failing. With that in mind, I’m going to spend more time looking closely at the younger players over the rest of the season. Their development is becoming a really important part of this year. There are still individual reps worth watching, even when the offense as a whole makes it difficult to stay interested. Let’s get into it. Offense Before this gets too miserable, let’s start with a good McKee throw! This is the sort of middle-of-the-field completion we heard about all offseason, and he deserves credit. He can make these throws. I don’t think McKee is a good player right now. His play has been pretty dull, and there is almost no vertical passing game to make watching this offense worthwhile. However, I’ve maintained all season that no quarterback would look good consistently in this situation, and I stand by that. I would absolutely expect McKee to look better in a proper scheme with protection that could handle pressure. The Eagles produced +0.30 EPA per pass play from a clean pocket in this game and -0.95 under pressure. You still have to evaluate the quarterback, but you can’t ignore the conditions around him. Eagles' Offense All22 Thread vs. Washington. 1) Hey, it's going to get rough, so shall we look at a good McKee throw before it gets negative?! Here is the classic middle-of-the-field throw that we promised all offseason! McKee has not looked good at all. However, I've… pic.twitter.com/ZqpvXsQkUb — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) November 2, 2026 Right, normal service has resumed. It’s been a while since I had to write at length about Grant Calcaterra being used incorrectly, so apparently the Eagles decided to give me some fresh material. I simply do not understand what on earth the coaching staff sees on film when they watch him. It’s not even fair to him! This isn’t how he should be used. Here he is lined up as a fullback, failing to block anyone. Calcaterra came out of college as a receiving tight end. Across this season and last season, he has nine catches for 76 yards. The Eagles kept him, cut Cameron Latu and EJ Jenkins, who are better blockers, and have ended up using Calcaterra like this. Latu wasn’t a great player, but he could at least be used in this role. If you are going to keep a receiving tight end who offers very little as a blocker, you need a plan to use him as a receiver. Instead, we’re back to watching him struggle with blocking assignments. Again. This is not a serious way to use your personnel. 2) Right, normal service has resumed. Buckle up. It's been a year since I got to moan about the Eagles' use of Grant Calcaterra, so the team decided I needed new film to chew on. Seriously, I can't believe the Eagles kept him after last year, and I can't believe how they used… pic.twitter.com/v8TMU9dZi6 — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) November 2, 2026 The protection plan still doesn’t give the quarterback enough help against these looks. The Commanders show seven potential rushers, and the Eagles have six players to protect. That doesn’t automatically make the play impossible, but the offense needs an answer for the defender it cannot block. The condensed formation makes a quick throw underneath more awkward because linebackers can drop out of the pressure look and sit in those throwing lanes. The Eagles run their standard crash concept, but McKee has an unblocked rusher in his face and releases the ball before the concept is ready. At least they’re blocking the interior rushers and leaving the edge free this week! Progress, I suppose. The Eagles have allowed pressure on 57.7% of blitzes, the highest rate in the NFL. They cannot figure this out. 3) The Eagles still have no answer for the blitz. Washington shows 7 potential rushers, and the Eagles only have 6 to protect. They remain condensed, so they can't throw quick slants or anything underneath because they will throw into linebackers dropping out. So, they just run… pic.twitter.com/uZA4WUdS3c — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) November 2, 2026 There were a couple of calls I really liked, so we may as well look at them! This little spinner play-fake in the backfield causes the linebacker to hesitate, and Saquon Barkley releases on the wheel route. The backfield action gives the defender something else to process before he can commit to covering Barkley, creating the opportunity to get the ball to an excellent player in space. Barkley’s release through the B-gap is a nice little detail. It makes him harder for the linebacker to pick up than if he simply released straight outside. This is a good example of the design helping the player win his matchup, and it produces a 24-yard gain. More detail like this would be nice! The Eagles can manufacture opportunities with scheme by doing things like this. It would be great if the Eagles used this successful play to build something else off of it. Maybe run the same look but actually give it to the WR next time. They don’t build on the success they have (which isn’t much, so it’s even more important!). 4) A positive play! This is a beautiful play call. They run this little spinner play fake in the backfield, causing the linebacker to hesitate, and then hit Saquon Barkley on the wheel route. Barkley also releases through the B-Gap to make it harder for the linebacker to pick… pic.twitter.com/ZN2HidEOxr — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) November 2, 2026 Another good play! I would love to see more of Willie Lampkin as an extra blocker. He is exactly the sort of player a creative offensive coordinator should enjoy finding uses for, especially when the alternative is repeatedly asking tight ends to make blocks they can’t make. The direct snap to Barkley is clever, and he does the rest by beating the defense to the edge for the touchdown. I still have no idea why he’s playing when he clearly doesn’t look 100%. I respect him enormously for doing it, and the ability is still obvious on individual plays like this, but it remains a strange situation to watch. 5) What is this, another positive play? I would love the Eagles to use Willie Lampkin more as an extra blocker, rather than use heavy personnel. Lampkin would be someone a creative OC would love to have. Pittsburgh’s defense has been the star of the show this season and has continued to trend in the right direction. The defensive line is ferocious, and the defense is filled with veterans and young stars. The trade of Joey Porter, Jr. looks better with each game as Daylen Everette has been excellent at cornerback. Speaking of the coverage, what coverages has Pittsburgh leaned into in 2026? Pittsburgh is a zone coverage defense with 35.3% of coverages in Cover 3 and 23.7% in Cover 4. Cover 2 is run 14.2% of the time, with Cover 6 having the lowest total at 9.5%.
