title: Steelers’ offensive line is one of the best units in the league
summary: After trouncing the Cleveland Browns 27-6 at Acrisure Stadium on Sunday, the Pittsburgh Steelers are one of the hottest teams in the NFL. Heading into their bye, the team is riding a four-game winning streak and starting to generate some national buzz after pundits mostly wrote them off as irrelevant over the summer and first […]
full_text: Mandatory Credit: Barry Reeger-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect After trouncing the Cleveland Browns 27-6 at Acrisure Stadium on Sunday, the Pittsburgh Steelers are one of the hottest teams in the NFL. Heading into their bye, the team is riding a four-game winning streak and starting to generate some national buzz after pundits mostly wrote them off as irrelevant over the summer and first quarter of the season. Whether it’s talking to fellow fans or listening to the players conduct interviews, there’s an unmistakable energy and optimism surrounding this team that hasn’t been felt in quite some time. The vibes are thriving in Pittsburgh right now. But it wasn’t that long ago that the exact opposite was true. Following the Steelers October 1 loss to the Browns on Thursday Night Football, the Steelers felt lost. With a 2-2 record and both sides of the ball struggling to find any semblance of an identity, the fanbase was dejected. And judging by how players and coaches alike spoke this week about the trip home from Cleveland, they were doing some soul-searching of their own. Steelers DC Patrick Graham said the turning point for both the defense overall & himself in his role was the bus ride after the loss in CLE Oct 1 He reflected while listening to Amy Winehouse "She's depressed in the song; I'm depressed on that day" Steelers haven't lost since — Chris Adamski (@C_AdamskiTrib) November 2, 2026 @byjoeybray TJ Watt practically name dropped the “day of reflection” in postgame interviews yesterday after the game. pic.twitter.com/HnPlV296ob — Bob Nutting Burner (@nuttingsburner) November 3, 2026 T.J. Watt and the defense’s performance since that game are, of course, a crucial element in the winning streak the Steelers find themselves in. But what I want to examine further today is something that first began to emerge when the Steelers were overseas in Paris: the return of Pittsburgh’s formations utilizing six offensive linemen. Starting in Week 7 against the Saints, the Steelers have reintroduced their jumbo, 6 OL packages in earnest. This has been a welcome development since it was so effective for PIT a year ago. With these 6 OL packages, PIT is averaging +0.11 EPA/play — Ryan Parish (@ArmchairScout21) November 2, 2026 In 2025, the Steelers and then-offensive coordinator Arthur Smith began experimenting with jumbo packages that brought guard Spencer Anderson onto the field for some extra heft in the trenches. Not to disimilarly from the NBA, Anderson began to fill a “Sixth Man” role for the team, frequently joining the starting five linemen and tight end Darnell Washington up front. The strategy was easy enough to follow; in a league where defenses are trying to match up with high-flying passing attacks by using lighter linebackers and getting five or more defensive backs on the field, countering with bigger bodies presents an offensive the opportunity to overpower their opponents on the ground. With a coaching staff shakeup and Anderson initially opening the season as the starting right guard, the Steelers abandoned their trendy 2025 formation during the first month of the season. However, given how successful it was last year and how running the ball is clearly still their biggest strength, it shouldn’t be that surprising to see the Steelers re-exploring this wrinkle in their offense. Since Week 7, the Steelers have called 29 plays with Anderson on the field as a sixth lineman. Turns out, it’s not unlike riding a bike, because the team has picked it up right where they left it. Pittsburgh has used four different personnel groupings with jumbo, but they have heavily leaned into one grouping: 11 personnel (one running back, one tight end, two wide receivers) — 21 plays 12 personnel (one running back, two tight ends, one receiver) – four plays 20 personnel (two running backs, zero tight ends, two wide receivers — three plays 22 personnel (two running backs, two tight ends, zero wide receivers) – one play The most effective and most used of these 6OL personnel packages has been 11P. PIT has 21 such plays. Per Sumer Sports, they are averaging: +0.12 EPA/pass (4 attempts) +0.25 EPA/rush. +0.22 EPA/play average. NFL average is +0.05 EPA/play — Ryan Parish (@ArmchairScout21) November 2, 2026 When you look at the stats above, you may be wondering what this exactly tells us. For those of you less familiar with the Expected Points Added (EPA) metric, it’s a stat that takes into account field position, as well as down and distance, and how many points years and years of historical data tell us we can expect from a given play based on those factors. Outperforming those expectations gets you a positive EPA, and underperforming generates negative EPA. Running plays, historically, are less likely to generate explosive plays than passing. Likewise, an offense is considered less likely to pick up a first down with a rushing attempt from second-and-long or third-and-long. That makes generating positive EPA on the ground much more difficult overall. Through eight weeks, only five offenses average a positive EPA per rush: Buffalo (+0.11), Kansas City (+0.11), Pittsburgh (+0.07), San Francisco (+0.07), and Jacksonville (+0.01). Consider that further. On 17 attempts, the Steelers are averaging more than three times as much EPA per rush from their jumbo 11 personnel package than they are this season overall. That highlights just how explosive they’ve been from these looks. Explosive gain for 29 yards against the Saints pic.twitter.com/ZFOXWfVGcf — Ryan Parish (@ArmchairScout21) November 2, 2026 Put in simpler terms, the Steelers have run the ball 24 times with six linemen on the field, whether that be with 11, 12, 20, or 22 personnel. Nine of those rushing attempts (37.5%) converted a first down or scored a touchdown. Nine of those plays also generated gains of at least five yards. Four runs (16.6%) went for 10 or more yards. Steelers left side obliterates the Saints, and PIT gets rookie RT Max Iheanachor on the move to clear out the LB in the middle. Anderson does a great job sealing off his man, and Washington and Bernard make the edge and CB freeze long enough for Warren to explode through the hole pic.twitter.com/8EvthOhXko — Ryan Parish (@ArmchairScout21) November 2, 2026 And it hasn’t mattered which player the Steelers have had in the backfield; both Jaylen Warren and Rico Dowdle have been productive. Warren has 16 carries for 95 yards (5.9 YPC) and a score. Dowdle has turned eight carries into 35 yards (4.4 YPC) and a touchdown. PIT fans, remember when we dreaded any toss plays being called? No more. Here, three sets of double teams set the table, and Fautanu used a nifty move to box out his defender like it was basketball to open the lane for Dowdle to burst through for 16 yards pic.twitter.com/czQWAEkyfc — Ryan Parish (@ArmchairScout21) November 2, 2026 Another toss, this time for 5 yds Washington/Anderson with a double team that takes out a second defender with his own guy. Fautanu/Frazier climbing to the 2nd level. McCormick initially looks like he overshoots, but that was either a great sell job or an amazing recovery pic.twitter.com/K0au7tjrAA — Ryan Parish (@ArmchairScout21) November 2, 2026 This play was a fun one that saw Rodgers manipulate the defense with the threat of a pass, even though the Steelers have only a handful of passing attempts from these looks. A Rodgers pump fake gets the Saints' right side and LB (20) to react. Iheanachor makes the LB pay for the misstep, Anderson moves his man just enough, Washington sets an edge, & rookie WR Germie Bernard with a marvelous bit of blocking on the S to let Warren do the rest for 5 yds pic.twitter.com/5pMSX7REFw — Ryan Parish (@ArmchairScout21) November 2, 2026 Against the Saints in Paris, the Steelers ran the ball 12 times against one passing attempt out of these looks. In Week 8 against the Browns, they once again ran it 12 times. Here were five of the highlights: 1. Dowdle 9-yard TD Dowdle…

full_text: (Photo by Scott Taetsch/Getty Images) | Getty Images Former Pittsburgh Steelers quarterback Russell Wilson interviewed for the head coach opening at North Carolina State, per Adam Schefter. “Former Super Bowl champion QB Russell Wilson interviewed today for the head coaching job at North Carolina State, where he played three seasons,” Schefter reports . “NC State now has two former NFL greats who starred there, Wilson and Philip Rivers, as prominent head-coaching candidates.” Wilson is currently an analyst for CBS Sports on The NFL Today. He joined the Steelers in 2024 after two less-than-memorable years with the Denver Broncos. In one season with the Steelers, Wilson threw 16 touchdowns to five interceptions in 11 games for the Steelers, going 6-5 as a starter before the Steelers lost to the Baltimore Ravens in the wild card round. He then signed with the New York Giants, where he started three games before being benched for Jaxson Dart. Wilson was a 10-time Pro Bowl selection, nine of which came from 2012-21 with the Seattle Seahawks, where he won a Super Bowl and went to another. title: Adam Schefter shuts down Garrett Wilson to Steelers trade rumor
summary: The Pittsburgh Steelers have been connected to several wide receiver possibilities as the NFL trade deadline approaches, but one prominent name appears to be off the table. ESPN NFL insider Adam Schefter poured cold water on speculation surrounding a potential trade for New York Jets wide receiver Garrett Wilson, making it clear that he does […]
full_text: (Photo by Evan Bernstein/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Pittsburgh Steelers have been connected to several wide receiver possibilities as the NFL trade deadline approaches, but one prominent name appears to be off the table. ESPN NFL insider Adam Schefter poured cold water on speculation surrounding a potential trade for New York Jets wide receiver Garrett Wilson, making it clear that he does not expect the former first-round pick to land in Pittsburgh. The speculation gained traction after NFL insider Jason La Canfora suggested Pittsburgh could be ambitious ahead of the Nov. 10 trade deadline and potentially pursue another playmaker. Wilson was among the names mentioned as a possible fit alongside DK Metcalf, giving the Steelers another weapon in their passing game. However, Schefter made it clear that the connection between Wilson and Steelers quarterback Aaron Rodgers should not be viewed as a reason to expect a reunion. “I was told last week; no way they trade him.” Schefter said on his podcast Tuesday. Wilson and Rodgers spent two seasons together with the Jets in 2023 and 2024, but reports have indicated that their relationship was not particularly strong toward the end of their time together. Schefter suggested that people speculating about the reunion might not understand the full dynamic between the two. “I don’t think people know that full relationship there. I don’t know that that would work. That’s not happening. Garrett Wilson’s not being traded to Pittsburgh.” There are also significant reasons New York would be reluctant to move on from Wilson. The 26-year-old signed a four-year, $130 million contract extension in 2025 and remains a central piece of the Jets’ long-term plans. He also has not requested a trade, despite the team’s struggles this season. Pittsburgh, meanwhile, enters its bye week with a 6-2 record and sits in a strong position in the AFC North. With the trade deadline approaching, the Steelers could still explore ways to strengthen their receiving corps as they look to make a legitimate postseason run. For now, though, Steelers fans may need to look elsewhere for a potential trade target. Let us know what you think in the comments . title: Steelers Week 8 grades in win over Browns
summary: The Pittsburgh Steelers are coming off their most dominant performance of the season in a 27-6 clobbering of the Cleveland Browns. The win puts Pittsburgh at 6-2 going into the bye and just a half game back of the top seed in the AFC. As we do every week, Joey Bray and I are here […]
full_text: (Photo by Justin K. Aller/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Pittsburgh Steelers are coming off their most dominant performance of the season in a 27-6 clobbering of the Cleveland Browns. The win puts Pittsburgh at 6-2 going into the bye and just a half game back of the top seed in the AFC. As we do every week, Joey Bray and I are here to give you our grades from the Steelers’ biggest win of the year. QB Aaron Rodgers Jarrett Bailey: Rodgers didn’t light up the stat sheet, but he didn’t have to when the Steelers ran for 200 yards. He did, however, lead a 44 second touchdown drive at the end of the first half that served as the dagger into the Browns’ chances of winning, and he hit Darnell Washington on multiple chunk passes downfield. If DK Metcalf holds onto a ball that hits him in the chest, Rodgers’ stat line looks better and doesn’t have an interception. Grade: B- Joey Bray: Aaron Rodgers was just along for the ride in this one, and that’s not a bad thing at all. His 13-25, 172 yards, and an interception stat line is easily one of the worst we will see this season from Rodgers. However, you never watched this game and thought Rodgers was playing poorly. With the Steelers up multiple possessions for most of the game, and running the ball as well as they were, it was a low stress game for the veteran quarterback. He stayed clean and moved well, taking only one sack, which matters as the Steelers will undoubtedly have to rely on Rodgers more and more down the stretch. Grade: C RBs Jaylen Warren & Rico Dowdle Jarrett Bailey: The Steelers’ running back duo had their best game as a tandem, racking up a combined 199 yards and two touchdowns. Jaylen Warren tied his career high of 143 rushing yards, while Rico Dowdle had his best game as a Steeler with 56 yards and the game’s first score. This is the Steelers’ offensive identity – pound the rock with these two backs and dare you to stop them. Grade: A+ Joey Bray: The Steelers have an identity offensively, and it’s running the damn football. Jaylen Warren has the second most scrimmage yards in the NFL through eight weeks, and is the most efficient running back in the NFL on a per-touch basis. Warren’s breakout season coupled with Rico Dowdle’s emergence over the last few weeks has given the Steelers a true two-headed monster in their backfield. Both backs got in the end zone and controlled the pace of the game as the Steelers cruised to an easy victory. Grade: A+ WR DK Metcalf Jarrett Bailey: This is just unfortunately who Metcalf is. He isn’t a No. 1 receiver. One catch for four yards is beyond unacceptable for the money he is making. Grade: F Joey Bray: It’s simply impossible for anyone to defend Metcalf anymore. It’s not just that the receiver isn’t making an impact, but he’s actively costing the team. Rodgers hit Metcalf right in the chest as the receiver bobbled the ball, which eventually led to an interception. With the Steelers up multiple possessions, it didn’t end up mattering much in terms of the outcome of the game. However, drops and frustrating plays have been the theme of the Steelers’ most expensive offensive player. The team almost certainly needs to add a weapon at the deadline so they don’t have to rely on Metcalf down the stretch. Grade: F Offensive line Jarrett Bailey: The Steelers led the NFL in EPA per rush in Week 8. They’ve led the NFL in that stat since Week 3. Aaron Rodgers also faced the third-lowest pressure percentage in Week 8. The offensive line has become one of the game’s best. Can’t say enough about how tremendous this group is. Grade: A+ Joey Bray: Tell a friend to tell a friend the Steelers have an elite offensive line. It is something to behold seeing just how far this offensive line has come along since they slid rookie Max Iheanachor and veteran Brock Hoffman into starting spots. Pittsburgh ran for 200 yards and only allowed one sack. The offensive line has suddenly become one of the strongest units on the Steelers roster. Grade: A Red zone offense Jarrett Bailey: If I see another fade to DK Metcalf after Aaron Rodgers clearly checked out of a called run, I’m going to launch a brick through my TV. Run. The. Ball. Pittsburgh still scored three red zone touchdowns, but this should have been a 38-6 win. Grade: C- Joey Bray: Stop throwing the goal line fades to Metcalf. It was especially curious to me that for as well as the Steelers were running the ball, they refused to run in goal to go situations. Whether it’s McCarthys playcalling, or Rodgers choice to throw the fades, they need to have a better collective plan moving forward. It’s hard to complain about much considering they won by multiple scores. But they will have to turn those field goals into touchdowns if they want to establish themselves as a serious contender in the AFC. Grade: D EDGE T.J. Watt Jarrett Bailey: Watt has officially returned to elite form. He had two sacks against the Browns, giving him 7.5 on the season – he had seven all of last season. He leads the NFL in sacks, and his pressure to sack percentage is fourth in the league (min. 100 pass rush snaps). Grade: A+ Joey Bray: At the midway point of the Steelers season, TJ Watt is on pace for 15 sacks. Watt added two to his total on Sunday as the Pittsburgh pass rush feasted on the Browns’ offensive line. The veteran edge rusher is defying all odds by having a career rejuvenation in 2026. Watt has once again become a player who can change the game in an instant. Grade: A+ Pass rush Jarrett Bailey: Eight sacks is an absurd number. It was great to see Alex Highsmith register five pressures. Highsmith, T.J. Watt, Cam Heyward, Patrick Queen, Kevin Jobity, and Keeanu Benton all registered at least half a sack, and the Steelers had a combined 31 pressures. Just tremendous work. Grade: A+ Joey Bray: Whenever you can sack the opposing quarterback eight times, you have a good chance of winning the game. The Browns were not able to handle the Steelers’ pass rush whatsoever on Sunday. The blitzing even got creative, as linebacker Patrick Queen recorded a sack and a half in the contest. This was a display of just how lethal the Steelers’ pass rush can be down the stretch for Pittsburgh. Grade: A+ Defense Jarrett Bailey: The Steelers were fifth in the NFL in EPA per play in Week 8, and they didn’t allow the Browns to reach the end zone. Overall, they’ve allowed just one second half touchdown this season, which is an insane stat. This unit has turned into one of the NFL’s best. Grade: A+ Joey Bray: You cannot ask for much more than holding your opponent to season lows in points and rushing yards, and that is exactly what the Steelers did on Sunday to Cleveland. The pass rush and linebacker play were immaculate and a large part of why the Steelers dominated this game from start to finish. Patrick Graham deserves all of the credit for the way he has this defensive playing with a secondary that still has some question marks. Grade: A+ Let us know what you think in the comments . title: Steelers Week 9 power rankings roundup: Heading into the bye atop the AFC North
summary: The Pittsburgh Steelers dominated the Cleveland Browns 27-6 from start to finish on Sunday, earning sole possession of first place in the AFC North heading into the bye week. Pittsburgh rushed for 200 yards while holding Cleveland to season lows in points and rushing yards. As always, let’s take our weekly look around the internet […]
full_text: Mandatory Credit: Charles LeClaire-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The Pittsburgh Steelers dominated the Cleveland Browns 27-6 from start to finish on Sunday, earning sole possession of first place in the AFC North heading into the bye week. Pittsburgh rushed for 200 yards while holding Cleveland to season lows in points and rushing yards. As always, let’s take our weekly look around the internet to see where the national media has the Steelers ranked in the power rankings roundup. FOX Sports: No.13 (No. 13 Last Week) “RB Jaylen Warren has just exploded in recent weeks, and he added another 157 rushing yards in a rout of the Browns on Sunday. And it’s a good thing, too, because the Steelers are really not getting much out of Aaron Rodgers and the passing attack. The Steelers can win a lot of games like that, though, especially with a defense that sacked Browns QB Deshaun Watson eight times on Sunday. It’s not a typical Mike McCarthy team, to be sure. But it’s working and it might be good enough to get them to the playoffs.” – Ralph Vacchiano The Athletic: No.12 (Last Week No.13) “This is Jaylen Warren’s team now. The fifth-year running back is first in the league in rushing EPA (19.0), third in yards per carry after contact (4.14) and sixth in rushing yards (704). He tied his career high with 143 yards on 17 carries Sunday, which was also his 28th birthday. Five of Warren’s top nine career rushing games have come this season.” – Chad Graff and Josh Kendall CBS Sports: No.10 (Last Week No. 15) “They are 6-2 as they go to their bye, which has them in first place in their division. The pass rush and run game have really keyed their fast start.” – Pete Prisco Pro Football Talk: No.8 (Last Week No. 10) “The schedule is lining up favorably; a 12-win season isn’t out of the question.” – Mike Florio NFL.com: No.12 (Last Week No.14) “Don’t look now, but the Steelers are turning into a bully fit for an AFC North crown. Pittsburgh’s defense suffocated Deshaun Watson and the Browns’ offense, while Jaylen Warren and Rico Dowdle tore through Cleveland’s defense in an emphatic win to grab hold of the top spot in the division. This one felt like big brother shoving little brother back into his place — and giving him a noogie for good measure.” – Nick Shook Yahoo! Sports: No.13 (Last Week No. 14) “A team that has among the oldest rosters in the NFL and is 6-2 before the deadline might generally be a big buyer to make a push with an aging team. Yet, it doesn’t seem like there’s one move that can put the Steelers on the same level as some of the NFL’s elite teams.” “Another receiver would be nice, but there’s a lot of money tied up in DK Metcalf, and someone like Josh Downs would be redundant with the skill set of intriguing rookie Germie Bernard. Perhaps adding Jacksonville’s Brian Thomas Jr. would make sense. Cornerback could help after trading away Joey Porter Jr., but the Steelers have been good at that position without him. An old team trading away valuable picks seems bad for the future. And a 6-2 team trading someone like edge rusher Alex Highsmith seems like the wrong move too. We might see Pittsburgh make a minor move or two but little else.” – Frank Schwab USA Today: No.13 (Last Week No.16) “The AFC North leaders have a league-high 26 sacks, yet rank 26th in the league with a 32.6% pressure rate. Go figure.” – Nate Davis ESPN: No.13 (Last Week No. 14) “Though the Steelers have been more active at the trade deadline under GM Omar Khan, the team doesn’t have a long history of impactful in-season trades. Still, the Steelers broke precedent in a major way when they acquired Fitzpatrick for a first-round pick early in the 2019 season. Though his production was inconsistent during his six seasons in Pittsburgh as his role in the defense shifted and morphed, he was undeniably a cerebral and impactful player. Fitzpatrick’s best season came in 2022, when he recorded a career-high six interceptions, including a pick-six.” – Brooke Pryor Despite four straight wins and currently holding the three seed in the AFC playoff picture, only one major media outlet places the Steelers inside the top 10 of their power rankings. Considering the fact that the Steelers need another wide receiver on the outside to supplement their passing attack, and a corner to sure up their secondary, this is reasonable. With that being said, it will be interesting to see if the Steelers see any movement in their rankings over their bye week should they make an addition prior to the NFL trade deadline on November 10th. Heading into the bye, the Steelers are exactly where they need to be to have a chance to repeat as the AFC North champions. Let us know what you think in the comments . CBS Sports ranked the NFL’s best new coordinators at midseason , and Graham earned the number two spot overall on the list. “The Pittsburgh Steelers’ defense has come back to life under new defensive coordinator Patrick Graham,” Garrett Podell writes. “They’re the league’s No. 3 scoring defense (18.0 points per game allowed), No. 6 total defense (305.6 total yards per game allowed), No. 3 run defense (83.9 rushing yards per game allowed), No. 8 third down defense (34.3% third down conversion rate allowed), No. 2 red zone defense (37.5% third down conversion rate allowed), and tied for No. 3 in takeaways (13).” “Having All-Pro edge rusher T.J. Watt turning back the clock also helps. After he had just 7.0 sacks in 14 games last season, Watt has 7.5 in eight games this season, which is tied for the league lead with Houston Texans All-Pro edge rusher Will Anderson Jr. No team has more sacks in the NFL than Graham’s unit’s 26, one more than the Brian Flores blitzkrieg Minnesota Vikings attack. ” “The Browns were flying high entering Week 8 with a 5-2 record, but they left Pittsburgh 5-3 after a 27-6 defeat in which the Steelers held them to both season-lows in points (6) and rushing yards (34). Graham is crushing it.” Graham was behind only Packers defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon on the list. Graham joined the Steelers staff after spending the previous four seasons as the defensive coordinator of the Las Vegas Raiders. Graham’s zone-heavy defense has done wonders for the unit. Take this past weekend, for example, as the team recorded eight sacks against Cleveland. The Steelers can finally say they once again have an elite defense to help them in their playoff push as they enter the second half of their 2026 campaign. With Graham in charge and the abundance of talent on the unit, it seems like the Steelers are destined to have their first top-10 scoring defense since the 2023 season. Graham deserves all of the praise he is getting from the media. Let us know what you think in the comments . title: Former Seahawks draft pick has become one of the NFL’s unlikely sack leaders
summary: One of the few bright spots on yet another very bad Tennessee Titans team is a former Seattle Seahawks pass rusher. Jacob Martin, a 2018 sixth-round pick who was famously part of the Jadeveon Clowney trade just prior to the 2019 regular season, has hung around in the NFL for nearly a decade. He’s been […]
full_text: One of the few bright spots on yet another very bad Tennessee Titans team is a former Seattle Seahawks pass rusher. Jacob Martin, a 2018 sixth-round pick who was famously part of the Jadeveon Clowney trade just prior to the 2019 regular season, has hung around in the NFL for nearly a decade. He’s been a rotational pass rusher with the Seahawks, Houston Texans, New York Jets, Denver Broncos, Indianapolis Colts, Washington Commanders, and now he finds himself in Nashville for his ninth season. It’s also his best season to date; one that has him as one of the NFL’s best at sacking the quarterback. After taking Joe Burrow down not once, not twice, but three times in Tennessee’s wild 43-36 overtime loss against the Cincinnati Bengals, Martin has already reached a career-high 6.5 sacks through eight games. Only T.J. Watt, Will Anderson, Chase Young, and Greg Rousseau have more sacks than Martin. So, the @Titans ' pass rush was going to fall off a cliff without Jeffery Simmons, right? Not if Jacob Martin had anything to say about it (and he had a LOT to say about it). pic.twitter.com/eWEZMryfp2 — Doug Farrar ✍ (@NFL_DougFarrar) November 2, 2026 Titans pass rusher Jacob Martin was incredible today with 11 pressures, 6 pass rush wins and 3 sacks. He was destroying the left side of the Bengals offensive line, especially on blitzes On the 11 dropbacks Martin had a pressure the Bengals offense had a -0.60 EPA/dropback and a… pic.twitter.com/KM89hDoSSw — Tej Seth (@tejfbanalytics) November 2, 2026 At 30 years old, Martin appears to be the definition of a late bloomer. He had 5.5 sacks last season with the Commanders, and as a starter on the Titans he’s putting up very impressive numbers under Robert Saleh. Martin leads the Titans with 21 pressures, his 7 quick pressures (which is a pressure within 2.5 seconds) puts him on pace to match if not surpass his previous career high of 16. He already has 14 QB hits, which is only four fewer than all of last season, and his tackles for loss is already at a career high. The only thing to note is his pressure rate of 11.4% is modest, but he’s turning his pressures into sacks, and his one-year, $9 million contract looks like it’ll parlay into a bigger deal next offseason … an offseason in which Seattle will likely be overhauling its edge rush unit. Meanwhile, fellow former Seahawk Boye Mafe recorded a strip-sack of Cam Ward in the same game, bringing his total to 5.5 on the season for the Bengals. His first season in Cincinnati is looking like one of the best of his career, and the Bengals should be in good shape to return to the playoffs given their remaining schedule. Good for both of them!

title: Seahawks Reacts Survey: Is Sam Darnold Seattle’s starting quarterback in 2027?
summary: Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NFL. Throughout the year we ask questions of the most plugged-in Seahawks fans and fans across the country. It’s crazy to be talking about an important part of a Super Bowl champion being off the team completely just a short time later, but we […]
full_text: Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NFL. Throughout the year we ask questions of the most plugged-in Seahawks fans and fans across the country. It’s crazy to be talking about an important part of a Super Bowl champion being off the team completely just a short time later, but we might be at that point with Seattle Seahawks quarterback Sam Darnold. The NFC Championship Game brilliance seems like a distant memory given the horror show to start the 2026 season. Seattle’s offensive woes are not exclusively Darnold’s fault, but he certainly has a helping hand in this mess . We aren’t running another poll on benching Darnold this season. Heck, if Drew Lock is going to remain sidelined with his elbow injury, then you can shelve any fantasy about giving Lock any run. But we’re absolutely at the point where barring an amazing second half of the season, Darnold’s future as Seahawks starter should be called into question. The franchise QB he looked like for about 10 weeks last year and the playoff run has regressed back to something close to the worst version of himself, and that volatility doesn’t sound like a recipe for a massive contract extension. Darnold’s contract is up in 2027 , so he could play out the rest of his deal and have another “prove-it” moment, possibly with a different offensive coordinator (again). Alternatively, John Schneider pivots and starts looking for his next guy, whether that’s believing in Year 3 Jalen Milroe, re-signing Lock to essentially recreate the Darnold magic with someone else, trading for a quarterback, or drafting one. So what say you? Is Sam the starting QB for Seattle next season? Vote in the surveys below! The confidence poll is the other question and I don’t need to explain that to regular Reacts participants. full_text: The Seattle Seahawks had a few free agents brought in for a tryout this week, with one name standing out given his three years as a starting guard for the Cincinnati Bengals. Cordell Volson was drafted by Cincinnati in 2022, starting 48 games at left guard over three seasons. A difficult 2024 led to a contract restructure before last season . He was waived/injured by the Bengals in 2025 after suffering a shoulder injury in preseason, and ultimately signed with the Tennessee Titans as a free agent this offseason. Oh that’s why Cordell Volson is now with the backups pic.twitter.com/5ZrfGHGfdC — Jordan Dajani (@JordanDajani) August 14, 2026 Volson was most recently with the Green Bay Packers practice squad in September before being released. On the 53-man roster, Seattle has Anthony Bradford and Beau Stephens as the backup guards to Grey Zabel and Quenton Nelson. There are no guards on the practice squad. As for the two tight end tryouts: Chase Curtis spent eight years in college between baseball and football, making him a 26-year-old rookie. He was unable to crack the New York Jets 53-man roster after five seasons at TCU. Kenny Fletcher went undrafted out of Rutgers and has spent time with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers and Indianapolis Colts. Ben Sims is the lone TE on Seattle’s practice squad.

full_text: The first year of Russell Wilson’s retirement has taken him to the NFL on CBS desk, but year two could see him back on the sideline. The long-time Seattle Seahawks quarterback interviewed for the North Carolina State head coaching job on Tuesday, ESPN’s Adam Schefter reported. This comes just a few days after it was reported another former NC State quarterback, Philip Rivers, would be pursued for the opening. Sources: former Super Bowl champion QB Russell Wilson interviewed today for the head coaching job at North Carolina State, where he played three seasons. NC State now has two former NFL greats who starred there, Wilson and Philip Rivers, as prominent head-coaching candidates. pic.twitter.com/sMYuHHKA2o — Adam Schefter (@AdamSchefter) November 4, 2026 Though either one of the former passers would be unconventional hires by the Wolfpack, Rivers at least has some coaching experience, having spent five seasons as the head coach at St. Michael Catholic High School in Alabama after his first retirement. He’s also soon to have ties to the current roster with his son, Gunner, committed to play for the Wolfpack. Wilson, meanwhile, has spent the entirety of his brief post-playing career as a part of CBS’ Sunday pregame show. But, as an NC State alum and a prominent figure in the football landscape, he could be an attractive head coaching candidate in the NIL era of college football. In three seasons with the Wolfpack, Wilson threw for 8,545 yards and 76 touchdowns across 36 games, and ended his career by leading them to a win over West Virginia in the Champs Sports Bowl. He transferred to Wisconsin in 2011 before being drafted by Seattle in 2012.

title: Snap Reactions: Jadarian Price & Zach Charbonnet return, can’t wake Seahawks offense
summary: It’s going to be a long week of debate about what exactly ails the Seattle Seahawks after the team was demolished on both sides of the ball against the Chicago Bears on Monday Night Football. On offense, Zach Charbonnet and Jadarian Price returned to action, while Quenton Nelson took to the field in a Seahawks […]
full_text: It’s going to be a long week of debate about what exactly ails the Seattle Seahawks after the team was demolished on both sides of the ball against the Chicago Bears on Monday Night Football. On offense, Zach Charbonnet and Jadarian Price returned to action, while Quenton Nelson took to the field in a Seahawks uniform for the first time since coming over from the Indianapolis Colts. None of that meant anything, and the offense continued to look like trash under first year offensive coordinator Brian Fleury. At receiver Tory Horton set a career high by playing 43 snaps, but with the ineffectiveness of the offense for most of the game, he did not have much of an impact as he pulled in just three receptions for 26 yards on a half dozen targets. On defense both Mike Morris and Rylie Mills set or tied their personal career high in defensive snaps played. Morris did so by playing 26 defensive snaps, matching the number of snaps he played against the Los Angeles Rams in the 30-13 to open the 2023 season in his regular season NFL debut. Meanwhile, the 23 snaps played by Mills marked the most of his career, topping the 20 snaps of action he saw in the Week 4 victory over the Los Angeles Chargers. Drake Thomas also returned to the field for the first time since the Week 5 loss to the San Francisco 49ers, playing 59 snaps, and Dante Fowler continued his unimpressive 2026 performance with just eight defensive snaps. On special teams Morris once again led the way with 23 snaps, with Brady Russell and Rodney Thomas right behind at 22. At the same time, former starters Emanuel Wilson and Anthony Bradford saw their only action of the night on special teams, as Wilson logged seven snaps and Bradford just three. And now it’s on to the Arizona Cardinals in Week 9, with last place in the NFC West potentially on the line.

full_text: Seattle Seahawks quarterback Sam Darnold is a Super Bowl champion who played an important part in bringing another Lombardi Trophy to Seattle, and that can never be taken away. Sam Darnold is also playing bad football. You can blame the offensive coordinator, you can blame the offensive line, you can blame the lack of a running game, but Sam Darnold is playing bottom-tier football. His worst throw from Monday night’s blowout loss against the Chicago Bears didn’t even count, but it’s emblematic of his incomprehensible decision-making. Sam's worst throw of the night was on a play that didn't count because of a defensive hold. This is not viable quarterback play. pic.twitter.com/ntueC8TChD — Mookie Alexander (@mookiealexander) November 3, 2026 Incidentally, the play design is pretty much DOA but there is no need to turn 2nd and 1 into a double coverage gamble. Darnold’s touchdown-to-interception ratio is barely 1:1 over his last 16 regular season starts. His mostly great playoff run is the break-up in what is otherwise a prolonged stretch of play that is far removed from much of his 2024 Minnesota Vikings season and the first 10-ish games of his Seahawks career. Sam Darnold in the second half of last season with Klint Kubiak calling plays: 19th in air yards per attempt 19th in comp % over expected Dead last in EPA per play This is not new. He's been figured out. — Seahawk Nerd (@SeahawkNerd) November 3, 2026 Sam Darnold from last year's Rams loss until now: 334/551 for 3,936 yards, 23 TDs, 17 INTs, and a sub-6.0 ANY/A. His ANY/A plummeted toward the back-end of last season. Darnold's downturn didn't start with Fleury. There's a clear inflection point. No run game crutch this time. — Mookie Alexander (@mookiealexander) November 3, 2026 (Editor’s note: It’s 344/551 and not 334) There are no advanced stats that can positively spin Darnold as an above-average starter at the moment. He really wasn’t playing particularly well for most of the back-end of 2025, but the running game finally sprung to life and Seattle’s defense and special teams repeatedly either scored or gave the Seahawks extremely short fields. The 2026 Seahawks are 4-4, which is not the end of the world, but how they’ve gotten to 4-4 is pretty much the worst case scenario in the short- and long-term. If Mike Macdonald’s defense hypothetically had curiously dropped off to be a middling group and the Seahawks were losing shootouts while Darnold was putting up impressive numbers, I think we could live with that and acknowledge that defenses can be more volatile year-to-year than offenses. Darnold is heavily culpable for at least three of the four defeats, and even his best game against the Washington Commanders is significantly impacted by what was effectively a game-losing pick-six. Darnold’s contract is a great mid-level contract for someone with his track record and roughly two seasons worth of good productivity. It’s also a contract that expires in 2027 , and the current version of Darnold does not look like someone who should be Seattle’s Week 1 starter, much less the starter in 2028. Barring substantial improvement over the second half of the season, John Schneider has a major decision to make on Darnold, regardless of whether or not Brian Fleury is still the offensive coordinator. We’ve seen Darnold be very good when paired with the right play-caller, and I am not going to put the failures of this offense exclusively at his feet. But Darnold is in that tier of quarterback who needs way more help to be functional than the likes of Josh Allen or Joe Burrow or Patrick Mahomes. Every quarterback needs at least some semblance of foundational support to succeed, but Sam needs way more stuff than, say, prime Russell Wilson. That includes, seemingly above all else, having an experienced and effective play-caller who can play to his strengths and minimize his worst habits. Brian Fleury does not seem to fit the bill. Darnold also needs play-action to work like we need air to breathe. When it’s not working, Darnold has consistently been anywhere from average to ruinous in pure dropback situations. He needs an offensive line to protect him so well that his pressure rate is low, otherwise this is what you get. Per ESPN Research, Sam Darnold was pressured on 14 of 39 dropbacks against Chicago. While pressured, he went just 1 of 11 for 13 yards and an interception. Here was Darnold postgame: pic.twitter.com/aeAYKUP4FP — Brady Henderson (@BradyHenderson) November 3, 2026 Darnold with a clean pocket and/or the ability to get the ball out of his hands quickly can sling it with the best of them. When he is dealing with pressure in his face, he is barely a starting caliber quarterback. We have two years of evidence in a Seahawks uniform. Sam Darnold was 30th out of 33 qualifying QBs in EPA/dropback when pressured, but he was also one of the least pressured QBs in the NFL last year. He's 31st out of 31 QBs in EPA/dropback when pressured in 2026, and he's top 12 in pressure rate. — Mookie Alexander (@mookiealexander) November 3, 2026 In effect, Sam Darnold needs: Play-action to be so insanely efficient that it overrides the lack of non-PA success. Favorable game scripts such that his team is almost never trailing . Related : A top-5 caliber defense such that his team is rarely trailing. An offensive coordinator/play-caller who can scheme up easy-button throws for fun. Related : A cheat code for a WR1. An offensive line that can pass protect competently. An explosive running game in case none of the above works out or is figured out by NFL defenses. To which I echo the thoughts of Carter: A good QB doesn’t need this much insulation. — Carter (@carso0onnn) November 3, 2026 There’s nothing wrong with building a great environment around a competent but limited quarterback, but that also means a crevice turns into the Grand Canyon when said environment is even marginally worse. You can live with Darnold’s turnovers if he’s as efficient as he was in 2024 and 2025. That is not even close to what we’re seeing in 2026. The possibility also cannot be discounted that two years of film effectively exhausted all of the routes that the likes of Kevin O’Connell and Klint Kubiak could make Darnold thrive. As I wrote not too long ago , “With non-elite quarterbacks there are only so many levers you can pull before competent defenses respond.” If Seattle sticks with Sam then it will likely need an(other) offensive coordinator to get him back on track, all while not being an immediate head coach candidate. This is the downside of having a defensive minded coach and your OC hires are either bad (see: Grubb, Ryan) or are so good that NFL teams take notice (see: Kubiak, Klint). The churn truly never stops unless you find that unicorn who can be a stable part of your organization while being no threat to hold a head coaching job. Seattle’s roster as a whole is a very good one; most of the players from last year’s Super Bowl squad are still here. Any premise of Seattle having a sustained window of playoff and Super Bowl contention was contingent upon Darnold sustaining his success and mercifully giving us all a break from debating Seattle’s next franchise quarterback. If Darnold cannot recapture even half of what made him go from draft bust to unlikely Super Bowl champion—this includes the rest of this year and (if applicable) his contract year in 2027—the Seahawks’ long-term vision is suddenly a lot more complicated. Drew Lock is a free agent and frankly I don’t want to bank on the QB revival thing yet again for a career backup entering Year 9. It’s not like Drew himself hasn’t had a history of being turnover prone with volatile week-to-week performances when he was a starter elsewhere. Jalen Milroe is a great unknown outside of preseason, and 2027 is a pivotal year for him to see if he’s even ready to be an NFL starter. Other than that? Seattle might find itself once again dealing with major uncertainty at the most important…
author: Mookie Alexander

title: Words of Prey, Seahawks-Bears: Gotta be better if you’re not going to catch any breaks
summary: For the first time all year, the Seattle Seahawks defense lost a game. In their, uh, defense, the other phases helped, several bang-bang calls broke the wrong way, the Chicago Bears proved far more formidable than expected, and thus came about the franchise’s most lopsided loss in two years. Stunning, but when you perform poorly […]
full_text: For the first time all year, the Seattle Seahawks defense lost a game. In their, uh, defense, the other phases helped, several bang-bang calls broke the wrong way, the Chicago Bears proved far more formidable than expected, and thus came about the franchise’s most lopsided loss in two years. Stunning, but when you perform poorly across the roster for most the game, against a well-coached contender, these are the setbacks that happen. Yeah, it happens. Although, man, it sure felt for a very specific and very brief moment that it didn’t have to. I speak, of course, of a portion of the fourth quarter, of those tantalizing four minutes and 13 seconds the Seahawks actually looked like themselves. (Which isn’t enough to win a game that lasts 60 minutes, they’re telling me. Now they tell me!) The good times began with Seattle’s lone takeaway. Praise be again to DeMarcus Lawrence, who is never allowed to retire. Tank’s exquisitely timed fumble recovery came on the heels of Seattle’s lone sack, via Mike Morris, filling in for Uchenna Nwosu on the edge. There’s that word again — lone. And mark the time: 13:14 of the final quarter. Everything should go right until 9:01, the second of pumpkinning. Therefore, Jadarian Price turned in his longest run of the night, a nine-yard burst; defensive holding gave the Seahawks a new set of downs; Price fought for four more tough yards inside the 10; and Sam Darnold found Cooper Kupp in the end zone for — you guessed it — his lone catch. Tory Horton caught the conversion, 20-17. Game on, right? If the Seahawks were to do anything, it would have to be now, with time running short. And wouldn’t you know it, the Dark Side came ready on Chicago’s next possession, bottling them up on 3rd and four with a beautiful Nick Emmanwori-Ernest Jones collaboration behind the line of scrimmage. It was gonna be 4th and six, and the Bears were gonna send the ball Seattle’s way inside of nine minutes remaining, just when Sam Darnold and his offensive line were starting to show some juice. But none of that happened. Lots of things didn’t happen. The game-changing TFL in question, for one. For once in their striped lives, the officiating crew got a delay of game right. Bless Mike Macdonald’s little heart, he tried to finagle a way to decline it, but you can’t accept a play that never occurred. Cheathawks only goes so far, after all. No matter. The Bears are still in third and long, stop ‘em anyway, no harm, no foul. Except the witching hour, 9:01 left on the clock, means the team’s 4:13 of competency (we mentioned this three clips ago for a reason!) has expired. So instead, all possible harm and foul break loose. A cute little lateral to Kalif Raymond outside the hashmarks turns into an uncute 39-yard gain as he slips tackle after tackle and splits defender after defender. D’Andre Swift punches it in on a hurry-up snap before you could even see a replay. Bam, 27-17, and the Seahawks never score again. Instead, Darnold’s eyes bugged out at how open A.J. Barner was, he threw it right into a defender’s hand, the ball ricocheted into James’ Lynch totally undeserving breadbasket, and voila, the Bears were set up with first and goal. A spot of stout red zone defense would keep the Hawks in it momentarily, but Emmanwori took an unnecessary pot shot in the end zone after a play, third down turned into first and goal, and Swift scored the knockout punch on the next snap. After all, the 4:13 of competency had run its course. Dang. It’s believable, albeit atypical, that special teams put the Seahawks in a hard place all night. Two bad kicks, two personal fouls, too much sloppy on a night you couldn’t afford it. It’s hard to believe the same team that *last week* dealt Patrick Mahomes one of his worst day at the office ever, and stymied OPOY candidate Kenneth Walker, couldn’t get to Caleb Williams and let D’Andre Swift score three times on the ground. It’s almost impossible to believe the return of RB1 and RB2, running behind a line bolstered by Quenton Nelson, made no difference at all. Seattle’s running backs carried the ball 17 times for 61 yards, combined. Sparklers are more explosive. It’s straight-up unbelievable this next clip isn’t a personal foul/ejection, and the one below is worthy of OPI in the fourth quarter of a National Football Game in the year 2026. The Bears were better Monday night, it’s difficult to argue otherwise. Maybe the rest game unfolds in the same general manner with those two bang-bang-plays reversed. Still, I’d like to visit the universe where they went the other way, wouldn’t you? A collection of bottom lines is, the Seahawks did not play good enough red zone defense (a pattern), did not play good enough red zone offense (a pattern) and rolled out disjointed offensive playcall after disjointed offensive playcall (layman’s opinion). The last drive lacked all urgency and ended with a Cooper Kupp drop on fourth down, when you needed either seven or a field goal. Exactly as dominant as the Seahawks looked to the national audience on SNF is how much they got their own asses kicked in primetime again a week later. Say anything you want about the officiating (it was weird at best and unlucky at worst). However: the refs didn’t go 1-11 on third downs. The refs didn’t stop throwing it to JSN in favor of off tackle runs behind a LG playing his very first game at RG. (Smith-Njigba hauled in one catch between halftime and garbage time.) The refs didn’t mess with Uchenna Nwosu’s ankle this week and knock Leonard Williams out of the game on Monday. The refs didn’t keep the Bears offense on the field for a 17-play TD drive in the first quarter. The refs didn’t run 17 times for 61 yards, with one explosive only. The refs didn’t save their first sack of Caleb Williams for the fourth quarter. The refs didn’t miss two kicks. The team that’s not as good as last year’s edition did all that, to themselves. Some of it not for the first time this year. Q1: Bears 7, Seahawks 0 Predator : It’s hard to not give it to Ben Johnson for formulating the longest touchdown drive against Seattle this year, 17 plays. Jeffery Simmons gets the nod, though, for this quarter of work. Prey : Sam Darnold Hey look, I have another angle of the play that wasn’t a personal foul, on a night the crew was unafraid to throw flags for this kind of thing. Literal definition of being headhunted, right here: The Seahawks would end the quarter on a high note, pinning the Bears deep then forcing a punt from inside the end zone and receiving it near midfield. I’d say they needed to turn that field position into more than three points but they lost by 17, so it’s not clear another handful of points would’ve mattered. Q2: Bears 13, Seahawks 9 Predator : Rome Odunze Look at the former Husky making the most of his return to Seattle, on the Bears’ second field goal drive of the quarter. Soft hands and a keen awareness of the soft spot in the zone. Odunze hasn’t seen the end zone yet this season but all his other stats increase, including yards per target, up to 10.0 now. This Bears offense really is something to behold. On back to back pass plays in the second: Seattle’s fifth offensive options is… not that. No matter what other trouble they’re having, though, the Seahawks offense can be counted to to furnish random fireworks, where they look like world-beaters, until immediately forgetting everything that worked. For example, it took them 38 seconds to travel 71 yards in the two minute drill: DPI, incompletion, quick sideline dozen to JSN, incompletion, throwaway, touchdown to, who else? I mention it in the linked post but Chicago shows an eight-man front, backs off to seven, leaving four in coverage. All JSN has to do is choose to break to the outside, where no safeties live, trust that Darnold is thinking the same thing, and await the ball. And that’s exactly how it unfolded. They can be so good. Q3: Bears 20, Seahawks 9 Predator : Fate, probability, the state of being due Prey :…
author: John Fraley

title: What does ‘going for broke’ look like for the 49ers?
summary: ESPN went through each team in the NFL to determine what their trade deadline goal is, who could be on the move ahead of the deadline, and which player each team should target. The San Francisco 49ers have a 99.1% chance of making the playoffs. For the deadline portion, the theme discussed the Niners “going […]
full_text: Photo by Ian Maule/Getty Images) | Getty Images ESPN went through each team in the NFL to determine what their trade deadline goal is, who could be on the move ahead of the deadline, and which player each team should target. The San Francisco 49ers have a 99.1% chance of making the playoffs. For the deadline portion, the theme discussed the Niners “going all in” for this season: What is the deadline goal? Go for it. The 49ers have been hearing for years that their Super Bowl window is closing, yet they remain in the mix. This season, the Niners established it early with a winning start, but injuries along the defensive line and at receiver have made their needs obvious. They already acquired DT DeForest Buckner , but it would be a surprise if San Francisco didn’t, as OT Trent Williams told ESPN, “go for broke” with another meaningful addition (or two). — Nick Wagoner What does going for broke look like? Giving up a first-rounder for Maxx Crosby? He’s been elite, hasn’t missed a game, and would give the Niners an embarrassing amount of riches along the defensive line. Per Sumer Sports, only Will Anderson has more impact plays than Crosby at edge rusher this season. Going for broke means using future assets to win a chip this season. Fans, in my mind, have long overvalued draft picks. Before the season began, we were told the 2027 class is loaded with a handful of franchise quarterbacks. The college season is almost over, and none of those players have lived up to the hype. That might encourage the 49ers, or make it easier, to part ways with their picks this season. If you’re getting a player who other teams have to game plan for, then it’s a no-brainer. If that player helps you win today and is a part of your nucleus for the next few seasons, then what’s the hold up? No surprises for who ESPN selected as the player on the 49ers roster who could be traded over the next week: Who could be on the move? Wide receiver Brandon Aiyuk . Be honest. You forgot he was still there, right? A ton of issues would need to be worked out, but it’s hard to imagine he just never plays again — especially because he just hired an agent . — Graziano Does including Aiyuk in a trade help you get a player you covet, or is all of Aiyuk’s value gone after he’s missed so much time? The 49ers getting a draft pick would feel like a win for them, but I’d use Aiyuk as a substitute for losing a potential pick, perhaps for the next player ESPN said the Niners should trade for: Who should they target? Jets WR Adonai Mitchell . It’s no secret that the 49ers are down bad at wide receiver. Mitchell has long flashed more promise than results, though we saw that promise Sunday when he recorded seven receptions for 142 yards and a touchdown. The Jets might be reluctant to part with Mitchell. But because they have Garrett Wilson, Omar Cooper Jr . and Kenyon Sadiq , it’s worth making a call. — Walder Adonai Mitchell was my favorite wide receiver in the 2024 NFL Draft. I had the Niners selecting him in just about every mock draft we did . I even said Mitchell was one of the top players in that draft . After a disappointing rookie campaign, the Colts shipped Mitchell to the Jets as part of a throw-in when they traded for Sauce Gardner. Michell has started to look the part. He missed a month, but he’s fresh off a game where he had 142 yards. Mitchell went over 60 receiving yards in the first two games. He’s a big body who can run and separate downfield. Mitchell is a walking big play. A quarter of his receptions are explosive plays. The Jets use him in the slot a little over 26% of the time, so he can move around the formation. He’s at his best on in-breaking routes. Best of all, he’s under contract for two more seasons and is only 24. We don’t know whether the wide receiver the 49ers drafted will ever play a full season. It might feel like the Niners are buying high after a big game, but Mitchell has always been talented. What does going for broke look like to you? Let us know in the comments below.
author: Kyle Posey

title: Why the 49ers roster construction has been a level above the rest of the NFL
summary: The San Francisco 49ers have not been the best drafters in the NFL during the Kyle Shanahan and John Lynch era, at least in recent years. And yet, they’ve found a way to remain perennial contenders, making a pair of Super Bowls and four NFC Championship Games over a nine-year run, and are currently Super […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - OCTOBER 19: Head coach Kyle Shanahan of the San Francisco 49ers leaves the field after a win against the Washington Commanders at Levi's Stadium on October 19, 2026 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Lachlan Cunningham/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers have not been the best drafters in the NFL during the Kyle Shanahan and John Lynch era, at least in recent years. And yet, they’ve found a way to remain perennial contenders, making a pair of Super Bowls and four NFC Championship Games over a nine-year run, and are currently Super Bowl favorites midway through the 2026 season. Overall, the 49ers have found a way to compete with top-loaded rosters, while also drafting well in certain years to keep good youth on the team. They’ve also made requisite trade deadline moves, been aggressive when the situation has called for it, and also benefitted from elite level coaching. In the NFL, we’ve seen some teams reach the top, but struggle to return. We’ve seen others remain in the playoff race year after year, but fail to reach that next level. The 49ers, though, have bounced back through hard years and have made the playoffs in five of the last seven years, with four of those appearances being to the NFC Championship Game and further. What’s been the secret to their success and roster construction? With the trade deadline coming up and another potential chance for the 49ers to improve their roster, I wanted to look at their past history under Lynch and Shanahan to see what separates them from the rest of the NFL. Initial foundation While many can fault the 49ers for some of their recent draft mistakes this decade, the 49ers built a very strong foundation of stars from their early draft successes. San Francisco got George Kittle and D.J. Jones in the fifth and sixth rounds of Kyle Shanahan’s first draft with the franchise back in 2017. In 2018, they added Fred Warner in the third round. And in 2019, they added Nick Bosa, Deebo Samuel, and Dre Greenlaw to the mix in the first, second, and fifth rounds. Right there, that’s a core of star players that help set the foundation for the 49ers, not only in the early years of the Shanahan era, but all the way to 2026. Kittle, Warner, Bosa, and Samuel ended up earning All-Pro awards. Greenlaw was a regular starter since his rookie year, forming one of the best linebacker tandems in the NFL. You follow up the strong drafting with quality trades from John Lynch for Jimmy Garoppolo and Trent Williams and even Emmanuel Sanders, and that’s what led to the 49ers’ first two NFC Championship Game appearances in 2019 and 2021. It’s rare that teams see that level of success, especially outside the first round, in the draft. Now, the 49ers weren’t close to perfect. They took Solomon Thomas and Reuben Foster in the first round in 2017, while Akhello Witherspoon, C.J. Beathard, and Joe Williams were their next three picks in the draft. In 2018, they took Dante Pettis in the second round and Tarvarius Moore in the third round. In 2019, they took Jalen Hurd in the third round and Mitch Wishnowsky in the fourth. There were a fair share of poor evals or draft misses, but the 49ers started their rebuild with a good foundation through the draft that set them straight going forward. Contract management Perhaps the biggest factor that sets the 49ers apart from other teams in the NFL is their contract strategy. The 49ers have dished out a ton of contracts near or at the top of position markets, like ones to Brock Purdy, Christian McCaffrey, George Kittle, Trent Williams, Nick Bosa, Arik Armstead, Charvarius Ward, and Fred Warner. They’ve been willing to pay up for their star talents, and those contracts have aged quite well for them, for the most part. Their mid-level extensions have also panned out well for the most part. Colton McKivitz’s three-year, $45 million deal is looking great already. When the 49ers initially signed Dre Greenlaw to a two-year deal worth under $10 million annually a few years back, that was a huge win. The biggest key is that the 49ers haven’t really been hurt as much by the contracts they’ve handed out. There have been a few poor contracts, such as Dee Ford and Brandon Aiyuk, but the 49ers have gotten out of those deals early. You could even loop Deebo Samuel, Javon Hargrave, or Jimmy Garoppolo’s contract into the mix as ones that were beneficial for the 49ers early on, but were ones they moved on from when they needed to. And the hits have been really good hits. Each of their extensions mentioned above has paid off. And their free-agent splashes have done really well as well. The Niners were early with Charvarius Ward and got high-level play out of him. Same with Richard Sherman a few years back. And this year, Mike Evans is looking like a huge hit. This has been where other teams have really struggled, be it to move off prior contracts or handing out bad ones in the first place. Nearly every team in the NFL has at least one of those on the books. The 49ers, on the other hand, have done a really good job of getting deals done early, while also getting out of them when they need to. Trades This is another key area that has separated the 49ers and led to a ton of their success. San Francisco has always been willing to flip capital for star players. They sent two draft picks for Trent Williams back in 2020. They traded for Christian McCaffrey at the deadline in 2022. They went after Chase Young the year after. San Francisco has made some major moves, as well as a ton of minor moves to position themselves well. They’ve also usually looked for multi-year value from their trades, which has worked wonders from a value perspective. Whether it was a small deadline move for Charles Omenihu or even the recent splash for DeForest Buckner, the 49ers have generally navigated the trade deadline well without overpaying with draft capital. Then, in the offseason, they’ve also been willing to make moves as well. These other avenues of improving the roster, be it contract management or trades, help offset when the 49ers whiff on draft picks. And the positives have come much more often than the negatives. Positional value I do think the 49ers have understood and captured positional value as well when handing out contracts. The Niners have generally shied away from paying defensive backs and offensive linemen marquee money, though they’re willing to hand out contracts to the right players. We’ve seen a ton of defensive back moves and contracts age quite poorly over the past few years, which have really hurt a number of teams aspiring to be contenders. The 49ers have instead prioritized other positions, such as defensive line and wide receiver. Overall, though, the total number of factors all contribute to why the 49ers have been able to build a sustainable roster construction model that has outlasted a ton of its NFL counterparts. So, even when they’re struggling to draft well, the foundation for roster building remains there and can be capitalized on in different ways.
author: Rohan Chakravarthi

title: Brandon Aiyuk will report to 49ers facility after filing for reinstatement
summary: Brandon Aiyuk has turned in his paperwork to file for reinstatement, his new agent Drew Rosenhaus has said. Per ESPN’s Adam Schefter, Aiyuk will report to the 49ers’ facility on Friday. “Brandon is healthy and ready to get back on the field,” Rosenhaus said, per Schefter. Aiyuk has not featured in an NFL game since […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - OCTOBER 20: Brandon Aiyuk #11 of the San Francisco 49ers warms up prior to the start of the game against the Kansas City Chiefs at Levi's Stadium on October 20, 2024 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Thearon W. Henderson/Getty Images) | Getty Images Brandon Aiyuk has turned in his paperwork to file for reinstatement, his new agent Drew Rosenhaus has said. Per ESPN’s Adam Schefter , Aiyuk will report to the 49ers’ facility on Friday. “Brandon is healthy and ready to get back on the field,” Rosenhaus said, per Schefter. Aiyuk has not featured in an NFL game since suffering a torn ACL, MCL and meniscus in the 49ers’ loss to the Kansas City Chiefs on October 20, 2024. Aiyuk has remained on the reserve/left squad list this season, having initially been given that designation last December after he stopped showing up at the facility. The 49ers voided around $27 million in guaranteed money on Aiyuk’s contract in July last year after he failed to attend the required rehab sessions and team check-ins in the offseason. Aiyuk did not report to the 49ers’ training camp this July, leading to him being placed on the reserve/did not report list before being given the ‘left squad’ designation to start the season. The 2020 first-round pick was required to apply for reinstatement to the league to be able play again. Having done that, the 49ers are left with a decision, and a potentially tricky distraction ahead of their Week 9 matchup with the Las Vegas Raiders. It is now up to the 49ers to decide whether to keep Aiyuk, look to find a trade partner for him, or simply release him. Given the apparent breakdown in the relationship between Aiyuk and head coach Kyle Shanahan and general manager John Lynch, him staying on the team looks extremely unlikely. The 49ers, 6-1 and the current one seed in the NFC, do not need the sideshow of Aiyuk reintegrating with the team, despite the obvious talents that made him a star. The Washington Commanders have long been considered a likely trade partner. However, given his conduct over the past year, it remains to be seen if any team will be willing to give up any sort of draft capital to take a chance on Aiyuk. As such, the 49ers may be happy to just cut their losses and move on. Aiyuk was, at one point, the perfect Shanahan receiver and, from a talent perspective, would be ideal for a team dealing with injury issues at that spot. But, at this moment, with the promising position the 49ers enjoy and the baggage he brings, Aiyuk being anywhere near the team is the last thing they need.
author: Nicholas McGee

title: 49ers News: Less than a week until the trade deadline
summary: Inside the 49ers’ revamped hydrotherapy room, from cold tubs to an underwater treadmill (paywall)“An in-ground cold tub, which the previous version didn’t have. In addition to that tub, the room also has five single-person cold tubs. “There’s a lot more space,” McCaffrey said. “I think that was one of the problems. Now we’ve got two […]
full_text: Inside the 49ers’ revamped hydrotherapy room, from cold tubs to an underwater treadmill (paywall) “An in-ground cold tub, which the previous version didn’t have. In addition to that tub, the room also has five single-person cold tubs. “There’s a lot more space,” McCaffrey said. “I think that was one of the problems. Now we’ve got two pools, additional hot tubs, cold tubs. There’s more of everything.” A therapy pool with stairs and multiple levels. Because water supports a player’s body weight, there’s less impact on joints. The new pool includes a deep-water area in which rehabilitating players can do low- and non-impact running. A treadmill pool that lowers players into the water. That’s where players coming off of surgery usually begin their rehabilitation. A player can move onto the platform on crutches and slowly be lowered to a depth of up to six feet. Picture Han Solo being lowered into the carbonite chamber in “The Empire Strikes Back.” Better lighting and a dehumidifying system, which Bosa said makes it a more inviting space. “It’s just a much better place to be, much better vibe than the previous (version),” he said. “Now we’ve got plants in there.” 49ers rookie Gracen Halton loses starting job but gains mentor in DeForest Buckner (paywall) “Without knowing it, Buckner served as an early football role model for Halton. In the offseason leading up to his freshman season at Oklahoma, Halton said he watched Buckner, Dexter Lawrence II and a handful of other NFL defensive tackles work out at the Sooners’ facility with private trainer Mark Hall. Halton remembered looking on with wide eyes and open ears, imagining the possibility of one day being Buckner’s NFL peer. Four years later, they’re teammates. “I was just a freshman watching those guys training at our facility,” Halton said. “Now we on the same team in the league. It’s crazy.” The 49ers are reportedly ‘still looking for a receiver and a pass rusher’ “Schultz followed that up by saying, “But the biggest name around the league that people are really starting to get curious about is George Pickens in Dallas. He’s playing on the franchise tag. He has not been utilized the same way as last year. ” The market for a pass rusher may not involve as many names as wide receiver.” 49ers work out 8 defensive players ahead of Raiders matchup DB Christian Braswell DT Matthew Butler DT Aaron Graves DB Kyu Blu Kelly DB David Long DT Chris Williams DT Kristian Williams”

title: Week 9 NFL Power Rankings: Did the Niners fall after their bye week?
summary: The San Francisco 49ers enjoyed their bye week here in Week 8, and they remain tied for the NFL’s best record with the Buffalo Bills and Minnesota Vikings going into Week 9 at 6-1. San Francisco had their first loss of the season back in Week 7, as their injury-riddled team couldn’t beat the Atlanta […]
full_text: The San Francisco 49ers enjoyed their bye week here in Week 8, and they remain tied for the NFL’s best record with the Buffalo Bills and Minnesota Vikings going into Week 9 at 6-1. San Francisco had their first loss of the season back in Week 7, as their injury-riddled team couldn’t beat the Atlanta Falcons on the road in a 29-20 loss. Still, going into Week 8, they were seen by a few sources as the No. 1 team in the NFL still. Now, going into Week 9, has that changed? Let’s look at the latest NFL power rankings after another eventful week of games. ESPN: No. 2 The 49ers fell one spot from No. 1 to No. 2 in ESPN’s power rankings, with the Buffalo Bills claiming the top spot after a 36-10 win over the Baltimore Ravens this past weekend. We’ll get a very good look at the Bills this weekend, as they hit the road to face the Minnesota Vikings this week in a battle between 6-1 teams. Behind the Bills and the 49ers are the Jacksonville Jaguars, Denver Broncos, and Chicago Bears. The Jaguars jumped from No. 6 to No. 3 after a 42-7 blowout of the Indianapolis Colts. The Broncos jumped from No. 8 to No. 4 after their 28-24 win over the Kansas City Chiefs, who fell out of the top five from No. 4 to No. 6. And the Bears moved from No. 7 to No. 5 after beating the Seattle Seahawks 34-17 on Monday Night Football. The rest of the top 10 includes the Vikings (No. 7), Seahawks (No. 8), Lions (No. 9), and Bengals (No. 10). NFL.com: No. 2 The 49ers actually moved up a spot from No. 3 to No. 2 on the bye week, with the Bills being No. 1 here as well. Last week, the 49ers were No. 3 behind the Bills and the Vikings. Buffalo moved up one spot to No. 1, while Minnesota fell eight spots to No. 9 after their loss to the Detroit Lions. “San Francisco hit the bye at the ideal time, spending the week off processing its first loss while hoping to welcome back a collection of key contributors from injury,” NFL.com’s Nick Shook wrote. “If the 49ers can get healthier, they should remain in the top tier for the foreseeable future.” The Bears jumped here from No. 9 to No. 3, while the Jaguars and Lions rounded out the top five. Following them were the Broncos, Seahawks, Bengals, Vikings, and Chiefs. The Athletic: No. 2 The 49ers stayed at No. 2 here behind the Bills, as there was no change at the top. “The 49ers have the NFL’s most impressive collection of wins with victories over the Rams, Broncos and Seahawks,” The Athletic’s Josh Kendall and Chad Graff wrote. “But the last time we saw this team, Mike Evans was out with an Achilles injury and Christian McCaffrey was slowed by a hamstring issue. As always, coach Kyle Shanahan is at the mercy of the gods.” Here, the Broncos moved up from No. 6 to No. 3, while the Bears and Chiefs rounded out the top five. These five teams were already in the top six last week. The only other team in that group, the Minnesota Vikings, dropped from No. 4 to No. 8. Rounding out the top ten here was the Jacksonville Jaguars (No. 6), Detroit Lions (No. 7), Seattle Seahawks (No. 9), and the Cincinnati Bengals (No. 10). FOX Sports: No. 3 The Niners moved up from No. 5 to No. 3 here after dropped several spots last week following their loss to the Washington Commanders. “The bye week really might be the best thing that happened to this battered team, because they sure did need a chance to rest and get some people healthy,” FOX Sports’s Ralph Vacchiano wrote. “It remains to be seen if they did, but at least nobody else got hurt while they were watching TV this past weekend (presumably). “They get the Raiders and the Cowboys coming out of their break, giving them a chance to ease back into action before back-to-back home games against the Vikings and the Seahawks. Health is the Niners’ key, though, and so far that’s mostly been bad.” The Broncos moved from No. 4 to No. 2 here behind the Bills, while the Chicago Bears and Kansas City Chiefs rounded out the top five. CBS Sports: No. 2 Here, the 49ers moved up one spot to No. 2 behind the Bills, who also moved up one spot. “They come off a much-needed bye with added help up front thanks to the DeForest Buckner trade. This is a team that will make a strong Super Bowl push,” CBS Sports’s Pete Prisco wrote. The No. 1 team last week, Minnesota, fell to No. 6 after their loss to the Lions. Meanwhile, the Jaguars jumped into the top three here, while the Bears and Broncos rounded out the top five.
author: Rohan Chakravarthi
