title: NFL Power Rankings: Stacking all 32 teams for Week 9, plus best in-season trades
summary: How does every NFL team stack up heading into Week 9? We made our 1-32 list and picked the best trade deadline acquisitions of all time.
full_text:
If you've felt like games have been closer than ever in the 2026 NFL season , you're not wrong. There have been 71 games decided by one score (eight points or fewer), tied with 2022 for the most through Week 8 in NFL history, per ESPN Research.

 So how do teams start to really separate at this point of the season? Well, the easiest way might be by making big trades before  the Nov. 10 deadline . (Some teams have already been active , with the Bears adding former Titans DT Jeffery Simmons and the 49ers bringing back  DT  DeForest Buckner .)

 To preview how important the deadline can be, we asked our NFL Nation reporters to pick the best in-season trade acquisition by each team in their franchise's history. That includes the acquisition of draft picks who eventually became stars, like the Cowboys using a pick earned from the Herschel Walker trade to select running back Emmitt Smith in the 1990 draft.

 To form the 1-32 list, our power panel of more than a dozen NFL analysts evaluates how all 32 teams stack up against one another. Here are a few highlights from this week's rankings:

 
 The Broncos are in the top five of our rankings for the first time this season after defeating the Chiefs -- their fourth win while trailing in the fourth quarter this season. Quarterback Bo Nix now has 13 fourth-quarter comeback wins over his career, which is the most by any quarterback in their first three seasons since starts were first tracked in 1950. And Denver is now the favorite to win the AFC West on DraftKings . 
 The NFC North is the only division with all four teams in the top 15 of our rankings, starting with the Bears at No. 5 and ending with the Packers at No. 14. Minnesota dropped its first game of 2026 against Detroit, which scored the first fourth-quarter touchdown against Brian Flores' defense this season. The Bears, Packers and Lions also are all 4-1 in their past five games, as well .  
 Entering Sunday, the Ravens had -215 odds to make the playoffs on DraftKings. Those odds are now +280 (10th in the AFC) after their blowout loss to the Bills , and they're down six spots from last week's Power Rankings. Baltimore lost two quarterbacks to injury Sunday ( Lamar Jackson and Tyler Huntley ), which puts undrafted rookie Joe Fagnano  into the spotlight for their Thursday night matchup against Jacksonville (if he isn't out because of injury ). The Ravens have lost three straight games. 
 
 Let's get into the full list, starting with the a different No. 1 team from last week .

 

 
 Jump to a team: 
 ARI | ATL | BAL | BUF | CAR | CHI | CIN 
 CLE | DAL | DEN | DET | GB | HOU | IND 
 JAX | KC | LAC | LAR | LV | MIA | MIN 
 NE | NO | NYG | NYJ | PHI | PIT | SF 
 SEA | TB | TEN | WSH 

 
 

 

 1. Buffalo Bills (6-1) 
 Week 8 result: Beat the Ravens 36-10 
 Week 8 ranking: 2 

 Best in-season trade acquisition ever: LB Cornelius Bennett in 1987

 

 Dubbed the "Trade of the Decade," the Bills acquired Bennett as part of a 10-player, three-team deal that sent Hall of Fame running back Eric Dickerson to the Colts. Bennett became a fixture on the Bills' Super Bowl defenses, notching 52.5 sacks and 19 forced fumbles in nine seasons with Buffalo, including three seasons with All-Pro honors. Only Bruce Smith and Darryl Talley have more career tackles in a Bills uniform than Bennett. -- Nick Suss 

 
 

 

 2. San Francisco 49ers (6-1) 
 Week 8 result: Bye 
 Week 8 ranking: 1 

 Best in-season trade acquisition ever:  DE Fred Dean in 1981

 

 Apologies to RB Christian McCaffrey  ( acquired in 2022 ), but you can draw a direct line between the Niners landing Dean and the rise of their dynasty. Upon Dean's induction into the Pro Football Hall of Fame , former owner Eddie DeBartolo Jr. said "the greatness of the 49ers began with Fred Dean's arrival in San Francisco." The Niners sent a second-round pick to the Chargers in October 1981 for Dean with an eye toward bolstering the pass rush. Over the final 11 games, he recorded 12 sacks and earned first-team All-Pro honors. Dean added another in the playoffs as the Niners won their first Super Bowl (XVI) against Cincinnati. San Francisco won Super Bowl XIX as well, with Dean contributing four sacks in that postseason run. -- Nick Wagoner 

 
 

 3. Jacksonville Jaguars (5-2) 
 Week 8 result: Beat the Colts 42-7 
 Week 8 ranking: 6 

 Best in-season trade acquisition ever: WR Jakobi Meyers in 2025

 

 Of the eight in-season trades in which the Jaguars acquired a player for immediate help, adding Meyers last season stands out. Brian Thomas Jr . was out because of an ankle injury, Travis Hunter was out for the season because of a knee injury , Dyami Brown was dealing with a shoulder injury, Parker Washington had yet to emerge, and the Jaguars led the NFL in drops (19) when they sent fourth- and sixth-round picks to Las Vegas the day before the deadline. Meyers' precise route running and sure-handedness sparked an offense that averaged 22 points before his arrival to averaging 33 points after he joined the team. -- Michael DiRocco 

 
 

 4. Denver Broncos (6-2) 
 Week 8 result: Beat the Chiefs 28-24 
 Week 8 ranking: 8 

 Best in-season trade acquisition ever: WR Haven Moses in 1972

 

 The Broncos acquired Hall of Famer Gary Zimmerman just before the start of the 1993 regular season, so the wayback machine had to be fired up to get to the best in-season trade. The Broncos acquired Moses from the Bills via a one-for-one swap for Dwight Harrison. Moses played nine full seasons for the Broncos after the 1972 season, averaging at least 17 yards a catch in eight of those years and having 44 total touchdown catches. He is in the team's Ring of Fame and played on the franchise's first Super Bowl team in 1977. -- Jeff Legwold 

 
 

 5. Chicago Bears (6-2) 
 Week 8 result: Beat the Seahawks 34-17 
 Week 8 ranking: 7 

 Best in-season trade acquisition ever: DE Montez Sweat in 2023

 

 Three seasons before the Bears sent three draft picks , including two first-rounders, to Tennessee to acquire All-Pro defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons , GM Ryan Poles got aggressive in 2023 to land Sweat. Chicago sent a 2024 second-rounder to Washington in exchange for Sweat, who led both the Commanders (6.5) and Bears (6.0) in sacks in 2023, making him the first player in NFL history to lead two different teams in sacks in the same season. Sweat recorded his first double-digit-sack season and reached similar production in 2025, when he led Chicago with 10 sacks. Coach Ben Johnson called that season the best of Sweat's career. -- Courtney Cronin 

 
 

 6. Kansas City Chiefs (5-2) 
 Week 8 result: Lost to the Broncos 28-24 
 Week 8 ranking: 4 

 Best in-season trade acquisition ever: WR Kadarius Toney in 2022

 

 The Chiefs had one of the league's best offenses in 2022 and still added Toney, acquiring him from the Giants for a 2023 third-round pick and a 2023 sixth-round pick. He wasn't a major part of the offense, but he made contributing plays to help the Chiefs to the No. 1 seed in the postseason. The greatest game in Toney's career was Super Bowl LVII , when he scored a touchdown and generated a pivotal 65-yard punt return in the second half to help the Chiefs complete their comeback victory. That punt return is the longest in Super Bowl history. -- Nate Taylor 

 
 

 7. Minnesota Vikings (6-1) 
 Week 8 result: Lost to the Lions 19-15

 Best in-season trade acquisition ever: DE Jim Marshall in 1961

 

 As they began their inaugural season, the Vikings acquired five players from the Browns in exchange for second- and 11th-round picks in the 1962 draft. Marshall was among that group and went on to become one of the best players in franchise history. He set an NFL record that stood for decades by playing in 282 consecutive games, and he was a captain for 14 seasons that included four trips to the Super Bowl. Upon Marshall's death in 2025, Pro Football Hall of Fame quarterback Fran Tarkenton called him "the greatest leader…

title: Josh Allen-produced short doc on Buffalo storm gets release date, trailer
summary: The short documentary on the once-in-a-generation Buffalo blizzard will be released on Nov. 24.
full_text:
BUFFALO, N.Y. -- The unlikely pairing of Academy Award-winning director Ben Proudfoot and Buffalo Bills quarterback Josh Allen is bringing a quintessential Buffalo story to HBO Max.

 

 The documentary short "The Buffalo Miracle," directed by Proudfoot and executive-produced by Allen and his production company Out of Pocket Studios, is set to premiere on the streaming service on Nov. 24. It depicts the true story of Buffalo fast-food workers who opened their doors to strangers and neighbors as places of refuge during the historic Christmas-week blizzard of 2022.

 A once-in-a-generation storm that brought hurricane-force winds of up to 80 mph, 15-foot-high snowdrifts and wind chill temperatures around 30 below zero, the storm was a monster that meant whiteout conditions and loss of power and access to infrastructure across the region.

 

 The trailer plays on Buffalo's nickname as the "City of Good Neighbors," and highlights how common love for the Bills brings the whole town together, especially in December when the team is preparing for a playoff run. Allen led the Bills to a 13-3 record in 2022, but the Bills were on the road for a Week 16 matchup against the Chicago Bears during the blizzard's peak.

 Allen has become increasingly involved in film and production work in recent years. In addition to his frequent commercial work, he launched Out of Pocket Studios over the summer. The company already produces multiple programs for Paramount in addition to the upcoming documentary.

 Proudfoot is a two-time Oscar winner for the documentary shorts "The Queen of Basketball" and "The Last Repair Shop."

 The film will premiere the week of Thanksgiving, when Allen and the Bills will host Patrick Mahomes and the Kansas City Chiefs at Highmark Stadium for a primetime AFC showdown.

title: Panthers defenders: We're in 'great hands' after DC switch-up
summary: Promoted from defensive line coach to coordinator, Todd Wash already has the support of the unit's leaders.
full_text:
CHARLOTTE, N.C. -- Todd Wash has a second chance at calling plays in the NFL.

 The longtime Carolina Panthers defensive line coach was promoted to interim defensive coordinator on Friday following the dismissal of Ejiro Evero , who had been his boss since 2023. Wash -- who served as the  Jacksonville Jaguars ' defensive coordinator from 2016 to 2020 -- was emotional during his first meeting at the helm, according to several players on Tuesday, as he let the group feel his passion at the front of the room for the first time.

 "That first meeting that we had with him, he almost teared up in there," Panthers pass rusher Princely Umanmielen said. "Like you could just really see the passion he has for the game. Just real genuine passion for the game. He got up there and the way he talked to us, the way he presented what the defense is gonna look like, you could just tell how much passion he has and it really makes you want to play hard for him."

 Wash, who worked with general manager Dan Morgan and coach Dave Canales in Seattle from 2011 to 2012, was picked to replace Evero because of his experience as a coordinator. He helped lead the Jaguars to the AFC Championship Game following the 2017 season, when Jacksonville had the No. 2 defense in the NFL.

 

 After leaving Jacksonville in 2020, Wash spent the past six seasons working with defensive lines in Detroit and Carolina. He hadn't been on the defensive coordinator search radar over the past few years, and players said they could feel his excitement in regaining the role.

 "It really means a lot to him," veteran outside linebacker  Patrick Jones II  said. "Like you could tell, he was emotional about it. ... And when you see someone go up there and talk like that -- their passion -- it gets you really fired up. ... Like, 'I want to go to war for you. I want to go to war with you.' Cause it really means something when it really means a lot."

 Wash oversaw defensive tackle  Derrick Brown 's lone Pro Bowl season in 2023. The coach and the captain remain tight, and Brown, who had been an outspoken advocate for Evero, said Wash will value the input of his players based on his experience with him.

 "He listens to his players, allows you to have a voice and also takes what you have to say into consideration," Brown said. "I think from Day 1 [in 2023] that's the way he's been with me and our room. And you appreciate that as a player."

 The bulk of the locker room found out about Evero's dismissal Friday morning away from the facility. Multiple players said they were just waking up after a long, late flight back from Green Bay following the team's 27-19 loss to the Packers.

 "Dan Morgan gave me a call -- that was the first person I heard it from, which I really appreciated," longtime Evero pupil and starting safety Nick Scott said. "And the message was -- it was the decision they had to make, I respected it and I know they had a job to do. Wish [passing game coordinator Jonathan Cooley] and [Evero] the best of luck, thank them for the role they had in my career to this point, and now we're looking forward to this next game."

 

 "I was genuinely shocked," Umanmielen said. "Like I was genuinely surprised, especially it happening in the middle of the season. Something that I wouldn't have expected at all."

 The Panthers enter their Week 9 matchup on Sunday against the Denver Broncos with the league's 23rd-ranked defense, as the unit has given up 349.6 yards per matchup through seven games.

 The group also ranks 30th in rushing defense (140.7 yards allowed per game), 29th in sacks percentage (4.56% of dropbacks) and 20th in interception rate (1.66% of pass attempts).

 Wash will look to improve those numbers during the final 10 weeks. His background with defensive fronts is likely to lend itself to improving the run defense and pass rush during his interim tenure.

 "I guess you could say it's cool because you know he's going to have a little bias there with the D-line," Umanmielen said. "Him being a D-lineman himself, I'm assuming that he would want to see the D-line be successful game in and game out, so it's nice to have a coach with that bias."

 The Panthers are on a two-game skid and they're dealing with injuries on defense, including top pass rusher Jaelan Phillips (hamstring) and rookie fill-in starting cornerback Will Lee III (hamstring). But their hope is that a new voice at the top of the defense, and perhaps some minor scheme adjustments, can lead to better results.

 Wash and the defense will get the opportunity to make a positive reintroduction against Denver's 30th-ranked offense.

 "We're in great hands," Scott said. "This is a guy that really cares and loves his job -- is going to pour everything into it, just like we would. So, we have a bunch of guys that are extremely passionate about this game, this sport, this phase of the ball, so we're going to put all of our trust and faith in him, as well as each other, and do whatever we can to continue to build this defense and put this team in positions to win games."

title: Seven things Solak thinks for NFL Week 9: Bucs atop NFC South? RB trades coming?
summary: Get ready for Week 9 with takes on the Bucs' division chances, why RBs could dominate the trade deadline and which teams should at least ask about Justin Herbert.
full_text:
Are you excited for NFL Week 9 ? It's the last week before the trade deadline next Tuesday at 4 p.m. ET. It's also the official midway point of the season. Feel that little bite in the air? Playoff football will soon cometh.

 Every Tuesday of the NFL season , I'll turn the page from the previous week to the upcoming one with seven things I think. These aren't full-scale predictions. They aren't concrete takeaways from the past week of NFL action, either; those are fired off Sunday or Monday. Instead, these are the uncertain topics. They are things that might be true, but it'll probably take the next few games to find out. And at the bottom, you'll find a few extra half-thoughts ... just those little inklings I'm unable to shake.

 
 Subscribe: 'ESPN's Leaguewide' 

 
 This week, I'll start with my headliner expectation for the 2026 trade deadline, irresponsibly put my faith in a 3-5 Buccaneers team and wonder just how much the Chargers would get if they traded  Justin Herbert .

 

 
 Jump to: 
 RB trades are coming before the deadline 
 Cowboys should trade Pickens 
 Irving will lead the Bucs to NFC South title 
 Steelers are going to win the AFC North 
 Three teams should try to trade for Herbert 
 Campanile will be a head coach candidate 
 Bears could be dangerous with Simmons 
 Some extra trade inklings 

 
 

 

 I think ... the running back movement will be the story of the trade deadline  
 The splashiest name included in the 2026 NFL trade deadline rumor mill is Colts running back  Jonathan Taylor .

 He is a special player who can have the same impact on a healthy offense that Saquon Barkley had for the Eagles in 2024 and Derrick Henry for the Ravens in the same year. Barkley and Henry had rushing success rates of 35.4% and 37.8%, respectively, and averaged 4.2 and 4.3 yards per carry, respectively, in the two seasons before they joined their new squads. Over the past two seasons, Taylor has a 41.2% success rate and is averaging 4.7 yards per pop. His recent body of work, along with the glimmer of elite play we saw in the early parts of the 2025 season, indicates that he can be a transformative addition.

  

 As such, the Colts are -- unsurprisingly -- demanding a big return for Taylor. NFL Network's Ian Rapoport and ESPN's Adam Schefter reported that the Colts' asking price is something in line with the Christian McCaffrey trade package from 2023 -- a second-round pick, a third-round pick and some more capital.

 If Taylor gets dealt for that much compensation to a team such as the Vikings, Giants, Broncos or Bengals (or a surprise team such as the Packers and Seahawks), it's possible the running back trade market will freeze up. If the Colts get that much in return for Taylor, what could the Titans get for Tony Pollard or the Jets for  Breece Hall ?

 Jets head coach Aaron Glenn shut down trade speculation involving Hall after the 2-6 Jets' loss to the Raiders this past week, saying, "We're in the business of keeping good players, and he's one of our better players. So, Breece will still be here."

 I'm inclined to believe Glenn. Then again, Glenn could be on his way out, and I don't think general manager Darren Mougey would lament making Glenn look silly by trading Hall should he receive a big offer from a team that misses out on Taylor.

 Similarly, I find the reports that the Eagles would never trade Barkley reasonable, but not absolute. Barkley was asked if the front office told him he'd be with the Eagles beyond the deadline , and he responded, "It was mentioned to me." Of course, that's before the Eagles lost another game -- to the 1-4-1 Commanders. I would put the chances of Barkley not getting traded somewhere between 95-99%, but Roseman is the sort of GM to never say never.

 The more I look at the landscape, the more I see an environment ripe for running back trades. The need is great.

 Denver is entrusting a lot of backfield snaps to a fourth-round rookie in Jonah Coleman ( whom I like quite a bit) , but the Broncos need their running game to be more dangerous given the limitations on the Bo Nix -led passing attack. Quarterback  Kyler Murray  was Minnesota's leading rusher against the Lions, as the Vikings struggle to get their running game going to open their play-action pass attack. Josh Jacobs  returned for the Packers from the commissioner exempt list, but he still might be suspended and hasn't been the same since coming back. The Bengals are looking for an upgrade over Chase Brown , as are the Giants with  Cam Skattebo , whom they don't seem to trust to be a three-down player.

 

 But the market is paralyzed by Taylor, as all these teams stare down the Colts and their towering demands. Someone will soon break from the ranks and trade for Pollard, a steady, three-down back who has reminded the league of his characteristic energy after consecutive games of 100-plus rushing yards. (I vote for the Giants, as assistant coach Brian Callahan has familiarity with Pollard.) The Cardinals should trade someone off their roster, as Bam Knight , Tyler Allgeier and the soon-to-be-healthy James Conner  all don't need to split time while rookie Jeremiyah Love gets healthy . Jaguars running back  Chris Rodriguez Jr . has lost the timeshare to Bhayshul Tuten , but Rodriguez is still a solid player who would pair well with a twitchy counterpart (looking at you, Cincinnati).

 If I were general manager of the Vikings or the Packers -- both looking to make a deep NFC playoff run but terrified of handing the ball off more than 10 times a game -- I'd be making calls beyond the obvious options from the Colts and Titans.

 Raiders second-year running back Ashton Jeanty was all but benched in Week 8 -- rookie Mike Washington Jr. outcarried him 25-2 -- and Jeanty hasn't looked particularly healthy this season. Can a playoff contender acquire the former first-rounder for a Day 2 pick, rest him up and get him healthy for the postseason?

 The Rams are funneling carries to Blake Corum more boldly than ever; he has 29 touches to Kyren Williams ' 35 over the past two weeks, which are notably the two weeks after Williams said the Rams' energy was fluctuating drive over drive " probably because I'm not out there. " I think the Rams like their 1-2 punch, but I'd definitely call to make sure.

 The Chargers have three playable backs ( Omarion Hampton , Kimani Vidal and Keaton Mitchell ), and that is three more than their win total. The Seahawks also have three playable backs ( Zach Charbonnet , Jadarian Price and Emanuel Wilson ) on top of third-down pass protector George Holani . Travis Etienne Jr . will soon return from injured reserve to rejoin Alvin Kamara and Kendre Miller in the Saints' three-player backfield. Does Chuba Hubbard move if the Panthers fall to 3-5 next Sunday?

 

 There seems to be way more backs possibly available than during previous deadlines. The trade deadline frequently features running back movement. In four of the past nine seasons, at least two running backs were traded in October and November. In 2022, a whopping six running backs exchanged teams. This position has contracts that are fairly fungible and roles that can be easily catered to skill sets; it's easy to move them midseason.

 

 What I think is rare(r) this season is the need . Four clear contenders (Broncos, Bengals, Packers and Vikings) have serious run-game concerns, and there are running back depth charts that can be substantially improved. Taylor can go to only one of those teams, and the other three will be left scrambling for Pollard. Once that dust settles, the desperation could jack up the cost and muster a surprise, big-ticket trade.

 Or Taylor won't be dealt because the Colts hold firm on their demands and find no trade partner. And then, nothing else happens. But that wouldn't be an interesting column and sure would be a disappointment come Nov. 10 at 4 p.m. ET. So we won't think about that, will we?

 
 

 I think ... George Pickens forces his way…

title: How Gary Kubiak paved the way for his sons, Klint, Klay and Klein, in the NFL
summary: Klint, Klay and Klein Kubiak are all on their respective NFL journeys. But their father, Gary, helped each along the way.
full_text:
LEVI'S STADIUM HAS provided special memories for Gary Kubiak and his family. It was the place where he won Super Bowl 50 as the  Denver Broncos ' head coach. Ten years later, his eldest son, Klint, as an offensive coordinator also won in the same stadium, helping the Seattle Seahawks earn the Super Bowl LX title.

 And during the Las Vegas Raiders ' Week 9 game against the San Francisco 49ers , another family memory will be created in Santa Clara, California, on Sunday ( 4:25 p.m. ET, Fox ). On one sideline, Klint, 39, will be leading the Raiders as a first-time head coach. Across the field, his brother Klay, 38, will help 49ers head coach Kyle Shanahan as the offensive coordinator. Meanwhile, the youngest of the three brothers, Klein, 35, will sit in the press box doing advanced scouting ahead of the  Dallas Cowboys ' Week 10 matchup against San Francisco.

 "It's weird how the world works," Klein, a national scout/special projects for Dallas since 2022, told ESPN.

 

 Gary, 65, never imagined his three sons would follow his path of working in the NFL. But they were destined to.

 As Gary served as the offensive coordinator in Denver from 1995 to 2005, working for Kyle's father and former head coach, Mike, his kids were around football almost 24/7, forging their passion for the sport.

 Gary, who was quarterback John Elway's backup in Denver from 1983 to 1991, is also known for his four Super Bowl victories (three as an assistant and one as a head coach in 2016) with the Broncos and recording 63 wins as the  Houston Texans ' coach from 2006 to 2013. But his greatest accomplishment could very well be the football legacy he created with his kids.

 Klint, one of the league's most respected offensive minds, is the second head coach in his family and a key figure in the Raiders' rebuild. Klay, in the midst of his sixth season with the 49ers and second as the team's offensive coordinator, is on track to follow in his brother's footsteps as the next head coach in the Kubiak household. And Klein is building on a respectable career as a scout.

 Each brother's journey is unique. The commonality is Gary's impact and how they have embodied their father's ideologies along the way.

 "I knew if [Gary's kids] wanted to get into coaching, they'd be great because of everything that their dad did," former Broncos coach Mike Shanahan, a two-time Super Bowl champion, told ESPN. "[Gary] took as much pride as any football coach would take, knowing that when he got his opportunity, he didn't want to let anybody down. I think his kids take right after him.

 "It's pretty obvious why the Kubiaks have had so much success as a family."

 
 

 KLINT DIDN'T THINK he wanted to be a football coach. But when he sat in on the Texans' draft meetings in 2009, listening to his father and other coaches talk about defensive ends, he began to have a change of heart.

 "I think they were maybe studying [defensive end Jason] Pierre-Paul that day," Klint, a Texas native, said. "... I just saw this big room full of guys just talking football, and then when the meetings were over, I was in the coach's locker room, and it was my dad and all the coaches, and they were just sitting there and shooting the bull.

 "I just remember thinking at that moment, like, 'Man, this isn't such a bad job.'"

 Klint played wide receiver and defensive back at Colorado State from 2005 to 2009. After his playing days were over, Klint received a taste of the family business. He was an offensive quality control coach (2010-11) and a graduate assistant at Texas A&M (2012), working with wide receivers such as Mike Evans (new to the 49ers this season).

 Initially, Klint wanted to work on defense, given his playing background as a DB. Two weeks into the job, then-Texas A&M coach Mike Sherman, who also spent five seasons as the Green Bay Packers coach and was on Gary's staff in Houston, told Klint that he wanted someone else to take his job. And so Klint had to be an offensive graduate assistant.

 "I was really upset about it. ... Then it ended up being the best thing that ever happened to me," Klint said.

 David Beaty, the Aggies' wide receivers coach in 2012, said Klint wasn't your "normal graduate assistant." He said Klint was a self-starter, always going the extra mile, and incorporated his own ideas to make plays easier for the players.

 

 "[Klint] could've been the full-time wide receiver coach," Beaty told ESPN. "This guy's work ethic was second to none [to anyone] I've ever been around."

 Beaty called Klint a "football junkie." No one could beat Klint into the building in the morning, and no one knew if he ever went home. When the team returned to campus from road games, Klint went straight to the office to grade wide receivers while everyone else went home.

 Beaty added that Klint spent an enormous amount of time breaking down video of opponents' defensive fronts, coverages and blitzes, providing an accurate report for him and Kliff Kingsbury, the Aggies offensive coordinator at the time, to use.

 Even though Klint wasn't sure he wanted to be a head coach, Beaty saw the signs.

 "He was the best nurse that a doctor could have," Beaty said. "When you came in, all you had to do was grab the scalpel and go to work."

 Evans, who was a freshman at the time, said Klint instilled confidence in him by watching film and critiquing his game.

 "Klint is the man. I love that guy," Evans said. "When you're 17, 18 years old, you ain't thinking about, 'Oh, this guy's going to be a great head coach one day.' I'm just like, 'Man, he definitely knows what he's talking about. I should listen to him."

 But being a graduate assistant didn't pay enough. Klint was married to his wife, Tessa, and even though none of his four children were born yet, Klint felt like he was letting his family down and wanted to try something new. So he left Texas A&M and worked at an oil field in Texas. Two weeks into his new job, Klint realized he missed being a part of a team. Klint appreciated his time at the oil field, but he belonged in football.

 A few months later, in 2013, Kubiak became an offensive quality control coach for the Minnesota Vikings before transitioning back to the college level.

 

 In December 2014, Beaty became the coach at Kansas, and as he was filling out his staff, he reached out to Kubiak about becoming the Jayhawks' wide receivers coach.

 Kubiak's first full-time coaching job didn't feature any team success. The Jayhawks finished 0-12 -- one of three times in program history they compiled a winless record.

 While in Kansas, Klint was itching to return to the NFL, where he didn't have to worry about recruiting -- only football. To his benefit, an opportunity to work for Gary in Denver opened. Brian Callahan left his offensive assistant position for the Broncos to become the  Detroit Lions ' quarterbacks coach, leaving an opening on Gary's staff.

 Previously, Klint never wanted to work for his father. He was aware of the stigma attached to being a coach's kid. In Klint's words, he didn't want to feel like the son who automatically landed on third base because of his parent.

 Klint softened on the idea, viewing it as a chance to spend more time with his dad, but also learn from him. But if he took the Broncos' job, Klint was determined to be the hardest-working person in the building.

 "That's always been something really important to me," Klint said. "Like if I got a chance to work for my dad, I want to make sure I did it the right way."

 Beaty thought so highly of Klint that he was prepared to offer the offensive coordinator job to convince him to stay.

 However, Klint's heart was made up.

 Klint spent three years as the Broncos' offensive assistant. He went back to Minnesota, where he served as a quarterbacks coach (2019-20) and offensive coordinator (2021). Minnesota was 12th in points (25 per game) and 14th in total yards (362.8) in Klint's lone season as the offensive playcaller. Since then,…

title: Why Broncos rookie Jonah Coleman is primed to be Denver's primary running back
summary: Coleman was Denver's primary running back during Sunday's comeback against the Chiefs and could thrive against the Panthers on Sunday.
full_text:
ENGLEWOOD, Colo. -- In the weeks before the 2026 NFL draft, there was a scout or two who classified Jonah Coleman as a "than" player.

 They thought that Coleman, then a running back from the University of Washington, was faster than , more elusive than and a better receiver than many thought.

 The early returns say the fourth-round rookie, whose current résumé consists of 39 touches through eight games (30 carries for 134 rushing yards, nine receptions for 97 receiving yards), might be exactly what the 6-2 Denver Broncos need to kickstart an offense that has struggled to consistently move the ball and score points.

 "I don't think it's a surprise to us, we've seen it in practice, in a lot of different situations, he's just a talented kid," Broncos tackle Mike McGlinchey said. "I think he's only going to get better the more he's out there."

 

 While there has been what Broncos coach Sean Payton calls "internet gossip" about what the Broncos might or might not do to acquire a running back prior to the Nov. 10 trade deadline, Coleman has offered glimpses of being able to be Denver's primary ball carrier. He seems primed to fill that role again when the Broncos travel to face the 3-4 Carolina Panthers on Sunday ( 1 p.m. ET, Bank of America Stadium, CBS ).

 Coleman led the Broncos in both rushing yards (41 yards on 11 carries with a touchdown) and receiving yards (63 yards on five receptions) in Sunday's critical win over the AFC West rival Kansas City Chiefs . He accounted for all 56 yards on the Broncos' game-winning drive, with his 51-yard catch-and-run setting up his 5-yard touchdown run on the next play to put the Broncos ahead 28-24 with 1:56 left in the fourth quarter.

 Denver held on to cap a comeback from 11 points down entering the final period, its third second-half, double-digit comeback win of the season. And Coleman was the only running back to carry the ball for the Broncos in the final two quarters.

 "Just about going hard for one another," Coleman said. "... It was good to punch in the game-winner. ... Fourth quarter hit, we know what time it is."

 Coleman's big finish against the Chiefs was preceded by a 69-yard performance (54 rushing yards, 15 receiving) on 11 touches in Week 7 against Arizona, his first game after spending four weeks on injured reserve with an ankle injury. Coleman also had 10 carries for 39 rushing yards and a touchdown in a Week 2 comeback victory over the Jaguars, the only game he played prior to the injury.

 Payton said after the Arizona game that Coleman would "definitely" get more touches in the weeks ahead. So far, so good on that decree.

 Coleman played 49% of Denver's offensive snaps against the Cardinals and was bumped to 66% (41 of 62 snaps) against the Chiefs. While a two-game, post-injury sample size does not make a trend, it's clear Coleman is having an impact on an offense that sorely needs a difference maker. And Sunday could be a great opportunity for Coleman to build on his momentum, as the Panthers rank 30th in the NFL in rushing defense (140.7 rushing yards allowed per game) and are tied for 28th in yards allowed per carry (4.8).

 

 "I don't really count the carries," Coleman said. "Just make the best of the opportunities whenever I get the ball. ... I try to embrace whatever role it is to win."

 The Broncos' offense was reeling entering the fourth quarter against the Chiefs, gaining only 9 yards in the third quarter as Denver trailed 24-13. But Coleman had 75 of the Broncos' 136 fourth-quarter yards.

 Coleman's surge comes at an interesting time. The trade deadline is six days away, second-year running back RJ Harvey is on injured reserve for at least another three games and J.K. Dobbins  -- who has started seven of the Broncos' eight games this season -- has struggled so far. He has averaged fewer than 3 yards per carry in two of the past three games and three total games in 2026. He had only eight such games in his previous six NFL seasons.

 Dobbins, who missed seven games last season with a foot injury, said prior to the Chiefs game that his season-low six carries against Arizona were part of an overall plan to keep him fresh for later in the season and the playoffs. Dobbins had seven carries against Kansas City, all before halftime.

 "This organization has a plan for me and I'm always there to coach our young guys ... I want to see them succeed," Dobbins said. "I want to win the game, and I also want to win in the playoffs and eventually get to the Super Bowl ... so let's be smart about it.

 "If we're losing and I'm not getting the carries, s--- I'm going to be mad as f---. ... But if we're winning and it's working, I just want to win."

 

 The Broncos are still 26th in the league in rushing (92.6 yards per game) and 25th in runs of 10 or more yards (14). The latter is another area where Coleman has already flashed. He has taken five of his 30 carries this season for more than 10 yards (16.7%). That percentage is sixth among NFL running backs with at least 25 carries. Add Coleman's knack for pass protection (especially for a rookie), and he has seen an uptick in third-down snaps since Harvey's injury.

 "I did a lot of that in college," Coleman said. "Coming here, I felt like I was going to play a lot on third downs, that's what makes me special and different. I can do it all."

title: C.J. Stroud turned down a big contract. A bigger one awaits
summary: Sources say C.J. Stroud turned down a deal similar to Trevor Lawrence's. He's in line for a bigger one.
full_text:
HOUSTON -- The Houston Texans had reached a tipping point.

 Teams tend to attempt to sign key players to long-term deals between the start of training camp and Week 1 of the regular season. The Texans had been trying to do so with their star quarterback, C.J. Stroud , who has shown major promise but was coming off a career lowlight -- a four-interception first half in a playoff loss in New England.

 Before camp, Houston made an initial offer to Stroud that reached what sources called a "respectable" range -- not at the top of the quarterback market but well within the $50 million-per-year club that 13 quarterbacks now occupy. Two sources familiar with the negotiation recalled Houston's offer was similar to the deal Trevor Lawrence signed with Jacksonville two years ago, placing Stroud in the second tier of around $55 million per year.

 "They made a pretty good effort," a source said, noting Houston's Nick Caserio is one of the league's most aggressive general managers. The Texans made Will Anderson Jr . the NFL's highest-paid non-quarterback and Derek Stingley Jr . the league's highest-paid defensive back while also signing Danielle Hunter , Nico Collins and  Azeez Al-Shaair  to significant contract extensions.

 The way Stroud's 2025 campaign ended had fueled a firestorm of offseason chatter and a ping-pong game of different scenarios for Houston: pay him, trade him, let him play out his fourth year.

 A trade was not happening, something about which Caserio was publicly adamant.

 It turns out Stroud made a choice of his own in the weeks leading up to the regular season.

 Stroud and his agent, David Mulugheta, made a counteroffer. They did not demand that Stroud be the league's highest-paid quarterback, per a source. Stroud understands the business side of being an NFL player, from market pay for players at multiple positions, to team construction. He knows if he takes every penny possible, paying the players around him becomes harder.

 But despite the back-and-forth, a deal was not imminent. Meanwhile, Stroud had made clear he was comfortable playing without a new deal, per sources. "Unless there's a better offer, we're good," is how one source recalled the messaging from Stroud.

 Once Houston chose not to put together a deal Stroud couldn't refuse, he opened the year against the Buffalo Bills with one mindset: Time to bet on myself. 

 

 This was not viewed as a contentious negotiation, and both sides seemed at peace. This leaves Caserio with the task of projecting Stroud's upward trajectory after his 2027 fifth-year option, which is worth $25.9 million.

 "Nobody was reluctant on anything," Caserio said. "We had discussions. We made an offer. All right, couldn't quite come to a final resolution or agreement. That happens. It's not the first time, it's not the last time. Not going to be the first time. Again, nobody's discouraged. I have a lot of respect for C.J. and David Mulugheta and their group."

 Stroud's well-timed breakout -- and his competition next offseason 

 Two months later, Stroud's seasonlong parlay has been a winning ticket so far. And the 2023 No. 2 pick hasn't allowed the contract situation to affect his play.

 "Something I was taught when I first went to Ohio State was just keep the main thing the main thing," Stroud said. "Football has always been there and it's not going nowhere. I hope not. I'm very blessed to play this game every single week. Practice, walk-throughs, meetings, I don't take anything for granted. If you chase the deal or the contract, I think that's when you kind of lose yourself."

 He's fourth in passing yards (1,867), 10th in passer rating (100.7) and 13th in touchdowns (11) with only one interception. Advanced metrics are even rosier; he's second in expected points added and seventh in ESPN's Total QBR.

 

 "He looks like he was expected to look after his rookie year," an NFL coordinator said of Stroud's recent play.

 Houston sits at 2-5 because a once-elite defense has regressed drastically to 19th in points allowed (24.3) after finishing second (17.4) in 2025. The preseason narrative surrounding the Texans' Super Bowl hopes centered on Stroud reaching his potential paired with a dominant defense. But while Stroud is doing his part, the defense has allowed four late game-winning drives.

 Despite that faith in Stroud, Houston's failure to reach a deal with him puts the team at the mercy of rising quarterback costs.

 "I don't think anybody's really too worried about it," Caserio said. "He's played really good football, which isn't a surprise to anybody. I think there are very few people, maybe [coach DeMeco Ryans], myself, who supported him all offseason when he was essentially bad-mouthed for like four months about one bad half of football."

 

 Part of Stroud's conviction in playing out his rookie deal came from a forecast of an exploding market in 2027, multiple league sources said. Quarterbacks from the 2024 draft class -- the Chicago Bears' Caleb Williams , Washington Commanders' Jayden Daniels and Patriots' Drake Maye -- are among those eligible for new deals this offseason. Maye reached the Super Bowl in Year 2 and Daniels appeared in a conference championship as a rookie. Daniels' career has been similar to Stroud's, as he had a meteoric start followed by turbulence.

 Baltimore Ravens quarterback  Lamar Jackson will also enter the last year of his contract with an albatross cap hit of $84 million. Stroud, to his credit, has three playoff wins, all in the wild-card round. The more Stroud delivers, the higher his price climbs. One industry source projects that the quarterbacks named above could push the $70 million-per-year threshold. Stroud's place in that tier is looking promising.

 "He's making himself a lot of money," an AFC executive said. "New tax bracket. If he keeps playing like this and they somehow get in the playoffs and make a run, there's no reason why he can't be somewhere close to the highest paid." After all, Stroud's rookie year, when he set multiple records during a historic debut season, sparked assumptions that he would reset the market when contract-eligible. After up-and-down production the past two seasons, the tenor around Stroud's perception changed a bit. But this season, Stroud has held up his end of the bargain.

 The Texans' aggressive move to get Stroud help last month -- trading a second-round pick to Arizona for Marvin Harrison Jr ., Stroud's teammate at Ohio State -- signals faith in Stroud's long-term impact.

 Caserio has no concerns about the contract situation becoming tumultuous when the two sides revisit it in the offseason. In fact, the expectation is the Texans and Stroud will agree to a contract extension in the offseason, barring a massive unforeseen downturn in his play, according to a team source. The Texans' owners, Cal and Hannah McNair, love Stroud and don't mind paying the potential new market value, according to a team source.

 "Chasing the game, not chasing what people would think is like the bag or whatever," Stroud said. "I'm grateful that I have a lot of people who keep me focused on what's important in life."

 No reason for panic, but challenges near for Texans 
 
 
 An offseason impasse on a contract negotiation could create a ripple effect despite the presence of that fifth-year option. The fifth-year option is well below market -- especially for a player currently taking on multiple risks: of injury, of a potential slump like he sustained last winter, and of declining players around him. It's no secret that Houston has struggled to configure a strong offensive line. The Texans have used 25 different offensive combinations to start a game, which is the ninth most in the span since Stroud entered the league in 2023. Houston acquired running back  David Montgomery  in March via trade from Detroit and changed two starting spots on the line. The result: The Texans are rushing for 3.6 yards a carry and only 84.7 yards per game…

title: John Harbaugh pushing all the right buttons for Giants
summary: The coach's culture of accountability and expectations has New York (4-2-1) in first place in the NFC East.
full_text:
EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. -- The New York Giants entered their Week 8 bye week having matched their win total from last year -- before the midway point of the season. 
 
 Something has changed, beginning with the coach. John Harbaugh and his staff have pushed all the right buttons early this season while developing a culture and setting expectations. It has the Giants (4-2-1) in first place in the NFC East.   
 
 Accountability is vital in Harbaugh's program. This is crucial because it was considered a shortcoming of former coach Brian Daboll and how he led the team. These new Giants are at a point where it's acceptable and common during team meetings for Harbaugh or his assistants to call out individuals for mistakes during practice or games. 
 
 Uncomfortable, sure, but they don't let it fester. Instead, they make it imperative it gets fixed. Communication is key. 
 
 This was evident just last week when defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson was unhappy with his unit's effort in running to chase down plays in a 34-27 loss to the New Orleans Saints . The film showed players slacking and not putting in maximum effort to the whistle. Rather than addressing it individually or during the defensive meeting, it was addressed in front of the entire room. 
 
 
 
 "You confront it. Just like we do, we confront everything," Wilson said. "When you're in the meeting room, you show those plays. I look at guys that don't run to the ball, and I call them traitors because they're traitors to the defense. At the end of the day, when you have a traitor to the defense, you either have to make adjustments to get them off the field, you have to get somebody else on the field, or they have to correct their behaviors." 
 
 Harbaugh and his coaching staff haven't been shy about making lineup changes, if necessary. Already this season quarterback Jameis Winston , running back Cam Skattebo , center John Michael Schmitz Jr. , defensive linemen Darius Alexander and CJ Okoye , cornerback Paulson Adebo and safety Tyler Nubin have been removed from the lineup at times. Harbaugh doesn't like the word "benched," but in most cases that is effectively what it has been. Salary or veteran standing doesn't stand in the way either. Not in Harbaugh's program.   
 
 The only thing that seems to matter is what gives Harbaugh's team the best chance to win. That's how he explained the switch from Winston to J.J. McCarthy last week at quarterback. The move gave the Giants the best chance to beat the Houston Texans  that week. 
 
 As a matter of fact, Harbaugh was so nonchalant about the move that he didn't make any grand announcement to his team. Many of the players found out about the quarterback change when they started going over the game plan. 
 
 Mistakes on the field are a different animal. They are unacceptable and handled bluntly at team meetings.   
 
 "We have a bunch of good guys," Harbaugh said. "Our guys understand that we have to confront everything that has to do with our football, and if we do that, that comes from a place of love because we care enough, we all care enough, and we need to hear it too, as coaches, and we did from our players. There are plenty of things that our players talk to us about that they want to see done better from a coaching perspective, and if we have that kind of relationship, that kind of partnership, coaches and players, to me, you just have a chance to be successful because you build trust that way. 
 
 "I just am appreciative of the fact that everybody in the building made it about what's important, which is the football. That's what we have to continue to do, and we will continue to do that. We've all seen it be successful." 
 
 Not every coach handles it the same way but it's easier to accept given Harbaugh's results in Baltimore and now early in New York. Daboll once held a team meeting after a blowout loss to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers where he only showed the positive plays. 
 
 Different strokes for different folks.   
 
 
 
 "I would say some of [my coaches] have handled it like Harbaugh, some of them haven't. It really just depends on your coaching style and how you want to handle it," veteran offensive lineman Aaron Stinnie said. "But I think guys are taking really good to it and like it. I think it helps. It helps keep everyone accountable and stay on the same page. 
 
 "There's definitely a way to do it and he does a good job of having it in a constructive manner. Just being upfront and honest. Everything is transparency." 
 
 This is what the Giants were buying when hiring Harbaugh. They got a coach with a track record of success who knows what it takes to win football games. It's no accident they are 3-1-1 in games decided by one score or less one year after finishing 1-7 in those such games last season. 
 
 Harbaugh has found ways to get the most out of his players, whether it be calling out guys for lack of effort at team meetings or demoting someone like Skattebo for fumbling. Skattebo rebounded by setting a career high with 124 rushing yards in a 27-21 win against the Houston Texans on Sunday.   
 
 "I don't know if it's philosophy so much," Harbaugh said of his tactics. "It's just a week-to-week feel thing with your guys." 
 
 Harbaugh can downplay it all he wants. This is what players such as tight end Isaiah Likely , who came over with him from Baltimore, said back in the spring that he does best. The new Giants coach is a wizard with his messaging and so far he's getting the most out of his players, teams and coaches. 
 
 It has resulted in the Giants winning despite losing their quarterback, Jaxson Dart , and best defensive player,  Brian Burns , due to injury. It has cornerback Deonte Banks playing the best football of his career after two disastrous seasons. It has offensive coordinator Matt Nagy scheming players open with regularity despite being on his third starting quarterback in seven games and Wilson transforming in and out of being a blitz-happy team depending on the week and opponent. 
 
 Key to this success is the way they are handling business. 
 
 "If you're not doing something to help the team and you're hurting the team, if your effort is bad, if you have a lack of toughness, it gets pointed out. And it gets pointed out in front of everybody, not only in a defensive meeting. It gets pointed out in the full team meeting," Wilson said. "When you have behaviors that's unacceptable, we're not going to accept it. And if you don't change the behaviors, we have to change the players." 
 
 The message is being received.

title: Aaron Glenn says Breece Hall is Jets' starter despite Braelon Allen's emergence
summary: Braelon Allen has rushed for the second-most yards behind Bucky Irving in Breece Hall's five-game absence.
full_text:
FLORHAM PARK, N.J. -- Is Braelon Allen better than Breece Hall ?

 Since replacing the injured Hall in Week 4, Allen has churned out more rushing yards than the best five-game stretch in Hall's career -- 504 to 409.

 With Hall poised to return, likely this week, the New York Jets have a running back controversy. We're not talking about a garden variety controversy, either. Tuesday's looming NFL trade deadline adds another layer of intrigue, with Hall's name prominent in the rumor mill.

 Despite the narratives and Allen's emergence, coach Aaron Glenn said Hall isn't going anywhere.

 

 "Listen, Breece is still a part of this team," Glenn said Monday. "I understand how the noise happens when things like this happen. I've said it before: We're in the business of keeping good players, and he's one of our better players. So Breece will still be here."

 Glenn said the same thing last year, when trade speculation was rampant, and the Jets wound up committing to Hall with a three-year, $43.5 million contract extension earlier this year. That should have quieted the trade talk, and it did for a few months, but the whispers are loud again because of Allen.

 What makes this different than last year is that Allen was recovering from major knee surgery before the trade deadline. All the Jets had was Hall and  Isaiah Davis , who had played sparingly to that point. Hall attracted interest in the trade market -- he was open to being dealt -- but the Jets never received an offer that blew them away. Besides, they still viewed him as a foundational performer.

 This time, general manager Darren Mougey might want to consider offers. If  Jonathan Taylor  is traded, the running back-needy teams that missed out on the  Indianapolis Colts ' star surely will call the Jets to check on Hall's availability. If they have unease on Hall's contract, which includes $29 million in guarantees, this will present an opportunity to offload him and hand the job to Allen, eliminating the controversy.

 Still, Allen's on a heater. He rushed for a career-high 147 yards in Sunday's 38-33 loss against the Las Vegas Raiders , becoming the first Jets running back since Chris Ivory in 2015 to produce back-to-back 100-yard games.

 Allen is 10th in rushing yards (565), tied for fifth in yards after contact (2.64 per carry) and seventh in yards per carry (5.0). The only player in the NFL with more rushing yards over the past five games is the  Tampa Bay Buccaneers ' Bucky Irving (548).

 While Hall brings more home run speed, Allen is more consistent on a down-to-down basis, a power back with deceptive outside speed. His friend and mentor, Baltimore Ravens star Derrick Henry , calls him "man-child." 

 Good call. Allen is 6-foot-1, 242 pounds, and still only 22 years old. He's one of the bright spots in the Jets' 2-6 start -- with the Kansas City Chiefs (5-2) up next Sunday ( 1 p.m. ET, CBS ) on the road.

 

 "I try to be as versatile as possible. I'm able to do a little bit of everything," Allen told ESPN. "I came from Wisconsin. In my three years, I had three different offensive coordinators and each of them had a different run scheme.

 "I'm used to wide zone, which was my freshman year. Second year was all downhill, a tight zone, gap scheme. Then, my last year, was the Air Raid. So I have a background of doing everything. I feel like that's a strong part of my game. As big as I am, I can play on the perimeter."

 The Jets run a mix of zone and man schemes (mostly zone), with Allen displaying the necessary acceleration to thrive in a zone blocking scheme. Now the question is, what happens to his workload when Hall returns? Fantasy managers have a keen interest.

 Glenn has said repeatedly that Hall's status hasn't changed.

 "Breece is our starter -- he's always been our starter -- but Braelon is going to get touches too," Glenn said.

 There's a lot of gray area in that statement. Hall might be the starter, but will he continue to get 73% of the carries? That was the split for the first three games before he went down with a quadriceps injury late in the Week 3 loss to the Detroit Lions .

 It would be an unpopular move if Glenn goes back to the way it was. If he's operating a true meritocracy, he will give Allen at least an equal share of the workload. He said, "It doesn't matter which guy's in there," noting that both are capable of being featured.

 

 Glenn enjoyed a close-up view of an effective two-back system during his time with the Lions, who used David Montgomery and Jahmyr Gibbs . He would love to replicate that with the Jets, who could have the Hall-Allen tandem for at least one more year.

 Allen, still on his rookie contract, is signed through 2027. Hall is under contract through 2028, though his 2028 base salary ($14.2 million) isn't guaranteed. Conceivably, the Jets could move on from Hall, 25, in 2028, re-upping with Allen and making him the RB1. He would still be only 24.

 Hall hasn't talked to the media since his injury. He also deleted his social media account, where he has known to post cryptic messages, on Sunday. Allen hasn't lobbied to maintain his current role, although he acknowledged he has the type of back who excels in high-volume situations.

 "I feel like I've always prided myself on getting stronger as the game goes on," Allen said. "I think I've always made, going back to college, always made my hay in the second half of games."

 It will be interesting to see how the Jets play this -- if Hall still is around.

title: Sam Darnold is struggling under pressure, but Seahawks patient with O-line
summary: Seattle's trade for Quenton Nelson last week shuffled the offensive line ahead of its decisive loss to the Bears. Will the pass protection get better?
full_text:
SEATTLE -- When Seattle Seahawks  general manager John Schneider  acquired All-Pro left guard Quenton Nelson in a trade last week, he knew the full effects of the move wouldn't be felt right away.

 Nelson was being thrown into an unfamiliar system in the middle of the season, and his arrival would force  Grey Zabel to move to right guard.

 "The maneuvering and all that," Schneider told Seattle Sports 710-AM before kickoff against the Chicago Bears , "it's going to take a minute for all those guys to get comfortable."

 Schneider's pregame analysis proved painfully true as the Seahawks' offense struggled in a 34-17 loss to the Bears -- Seattle's most lopsided defeat since December 2024. The loss dropped the defending Super Bowl champions to 4-4, putting them 2.5 games behind the San Francisco 49ers  in the NFC West standings.

 Most concerning was quarterback Sam Darnold 's continued struggles under pressure. He was pressured on 14 of his 39 dropbacks and completed just one of 11 attempts for 13 yards and an interception while under duress, according to ESPN Research. A week after he did not take a sack in Seattle's 20-3 win over the previously unbeaten Kansas City Chiefs , Chicago dropped Darnold three times while registering six official QB hits. 

 It was a perfect storm of factors that led to a messy offensive effort. Their reconfigured offensive line also had backup Josh Jones at left tackle facing a Bears front that just added All-Pro defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons via trade and got edge rusher Montez Sweat back from a two-game suspension .

 Zach Charbonnet made his season debut, while fellow Seahawks running back  Jadarian Price  returned from injured reserve, but they combined for only 52 rushing yards on 16 attempts (3.25 yards per carry).

 "I think there [is] a little bit of a learning curve with the new group, the new alignments," coach Mike Macdonald said Tuesday on his Seattle Sports radio show. "There are a couple coaching points that are going to happen. [The mistakes] should be fewer and far between from week to week."

 

 Macdonald called sacks a team stat and cautioned against the assumption that whenever a quarterback gets hit, the offensive line must be to blame. Charbonnet, for instance, got beat by a blitzing linebacker on the Bears' third sack. But the first one came via a quick and decisive win by Simmons over Zabel, a second-year player who made his first start at right guard since his freshman season in college.

 "It's a tough transition to flip sides in the middle of the week, but at the end, no excuses," Zabel said. "Could've played better. I will play better. We move forward from here."

 Also to blame was Darnold's tendency to hold the ball longer Monday night. Against Kansas City, his average time before a throw was 2.45 seconds, easily his fastest since returning in Week 3 from his glute injury. Against Chicago, it was 2.89 seconds -- though at times, that was a result of having nowhere to throw the ball.

 "When I get the ball out quick, it's all about knowing where to go with the football," he said. "Just being decisive, knowing when I need to move on in progression and doing that. Talking about this game specifically, got to watch the tape, obviously. I feel like there were opportunities to get the ball out, and I just didn't."

 Darnold now has nine interceptions this season, which is tied for second most in the NFL despite him playing just six full games. His pick in the fourth quarter Monday night involved some misfortune, as his scramble throw to an open receiver was tipped by defensive end Austin Booker and directly to James Lynch right after it left Darnold's hand.

 The play exemplified how his interception problem is partly a pressure problem. He has been under duress on 38.3% of his dropbacks this season, the sixth-highest rate in the NFL. When pressured, he's completing only 31.3% of his passes (29th), with two touchdowns to five interceptions (26th) and a QBR of 3.9 (27th). Last season, Darnold's pressure rate was 30.4% (21st highest). When under duress, he completed 50% of his passes (tied for sixth best) with seven touchdowns to seven interceptions (21st) and a QBR of 16.4 (20th).

 

 "Sam's a warrior, man," Macdonald said on his radio show. "Do we want Sam to play better? Yeah. Do we need Sam to play more efficient football? Yes. But he also freaking battled his tail off after getting hit. I hope everybody understands what type of courage that takes and toughness that this guy has to be able to play through the things that he was able to play through. So there's urgency to get better for sure, but I think we can respect what Sam's doing physically as well."

 Macdonald said left tackle Charles Cross , who went down with an ankle injury  in Week 7, has a chance to return this week to start against the Arizona Cardinals . Cross did not practice last week, meaning he has yet to log a rep with Nelson next to him at left guard.

 "It's great to have Quenton," Macdonald said. "We're psyched. You can definitely see there's a lot of really great plays where he's moving people and cutting people out and doing Quenton Nelson things, which is really great.

 "It's just, we've got to make it all come together."
